life|01-01||Άγιος Βασίλειος ο Μέγας||Basil was born around 330 in Caesarea of Cappadocia, into a family with a deep Christian tradition; his siblings included Gregory of Nyssa and Macrina. He studied in Caesarea, in Constantinople and in Athens, where he became a friend of Gregory the Theologian. // He gave up his brilliant career as a rhetorician and chose the ascetic life in Pontus. There he wrote the rules for the monastic community, which influenced almost all Eastern monasticism. In 370 he became Bishop of Caesarea. // He defended the right faith against Arianism and wrote important theological works, such as "On the Holy Spirit". He founded a large charitable complex, the "Basiliad", with a hospital and a shelter for the poor. He died on 1 January 379, and for this reason his memory is celebrated on the first day of the year; the liturgy that bears his name is celebrated ten times a year.

life|01-17||Όσιος Αντώνιος ο Μέγας||Anthony was born around 251 in Egypt, into a wealthy family. After the death of his parents he heard in church the Gospel words "sell what you have and give to the poor", and he distributed his property. // He lived first near his village and then in the desert, ever farther away, in order to pray and to struggle against temptations. Many followed his example and gathered around him, and so he is regarded as the father of asceticism. // He died around 356, at an age of more than a hundred years. His life was written by Athanasius the Great, and this text spread throughout the Christian world.

life|01-25||Άγιος Γρηγόριος ο Θεολόγος||Gregory was born around 329 in Arianzus of Cappadocia; his father was Bishop of Nazianzus. He studied in Caesarea, in Alexandria and in Athens, where he became a friend of Basil. // He preferred the life of contemplation, but the Church needed him: in Constantinople he preached the famous "Theological Orations" on the Holy Trinity and helped to strengthen the Orthodox faith in the capital. In 381 he briefly became Patriarch of Constantinople and presided over the Second Ecumenical Council. // He resigned after disagreements and returned to his birthplace, where he wrote poems and letters. He died around 390. He is one of the Three Hierarchs and is called "the Theologian", like the evangelist John.

life|01-30||Οι Τρεις Ιεράρχες||The feast was established in the 11th century, when in Constantinople there was a dispute over which of the three great fathers was the greatest: Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian or John Chrysostom. According to tradition, the three saints appeared to John Mauropous, Bishop of Euchaita, and told him that they are one before God and that they should be celebrated together. // The three were great theologians and orators of the 4th century, who united Greek learning with the Christian faith. In Greece the day is a feast of letters and of schools.

life|02-10||Άγιος Χαράλαμπος||Charalambos was a priest in Magnesia in Asia Minor and, according to tradition, he had reached a very advanced old age when, under the Emperor Septimius Severus (around 202), he was arrested for teaching Christ. // His persecutors tortured him, but he did not deny his faith, and according to tradition he healed the sick and brought to the faith those who saw him. In the end he was beheaded. // The people honor him as a protector against epidemics and diseases, especially against the plague, and for this reason his memory is great in many parts of Greece.

life|03-25||Ο Ευαγγελισμός της Θεοτόκου||The feast commemorates the moment when the Archangel Gabriel announced to Mary in Nazareth that she would give birth to the Son of God, as the Gospel according to Luke relates. Nine months before Christmas, the day is the beginning of the mystery of the Incarnation. // In Greece, 25 March is also the national anniversary of the Revolution of 1821, because according to tradition Germanos, Metropolitan of Old Patras, raised the banner at the Monastery of Agia Lavra on that day. Thus the religious and the national feast coincide.

life|04-23||Άγιος Γεώργιος||George was born, according to tradition, in Cappadocia to Christian parents and served as an officer in the Roman army. During the persecution of Diocletian he publicly confessed his faith and was imprisoned. // His torturers subjected him to many torments, but he did not yield, and in the end he was beheaded around 303 in Nicomedia. Tradition says that he was buried in Lydda in Palestine. // His memory is very widespread: he is honored as the protector of the army and of shepherds, and the icon of the horseman slaying the dragon symbolizes the victory of good over evil. If 23 April falls before Pascha, the feast is transferred to the Monday of Bright Week.

life|05-21||Άγιοι Κωνσταντίνος και Ελένη||Constantine was born around 272 and in 306 was proclaimed emperor by his soldiers. In 312 he defeated Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge and, according to tradition, saw the sign of the cross in the sky. With the Edict of Milan (313) he granted freedom to Christian worship. // In 325 he convened the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea, and in 330 he inaugurated Constantinople as the new capital. He was baptized shortly before he died, in 337. // His mother Helena traveled to the Holy Land and, according to tradition, found the Precious Cross; she founded churches in Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives. The two are honored as equal-to-the-apostles.

life|06-24||Το Γενέθλιο του Αγίου Ιωάννη||John was born to Elizabeth and the priest Zechariah at an advanced age, six months before the birth of Christ. He grew up in the desert of Judea and preached repentance on the banks of the Jordan. // He baptized Jesus in the Jordan and presented him as "the Lamb of God". For this reason he is called the Forerunner and the Baptist. // Herod Antipas imprisoned him because he rebuked him for his unlawful marriage, and beheaded him. The memory of his birth is celebrated on 24 June, and the Klidonas, a custom with fires and predictions, is connected with this day.

life|06-29||Άγιοι Απόστολοι Πέτρος και Παύλος||Peter was a fisherman from Bethsaida and one of the first disciples of Jesus; Christ named him "Peter", that is, rock. After Pentecost he led the first Christian community and preached in Antioch and in Rome. // Paul was born in Tarsus and was a Pharisee who persecuted the Christians, until on the road to Damascus he had an experience that changed his life. He made three great missionary journeys in Asia Minor and in Greece and founded churches, among other places in Philippi, in Thessaloniki and in Corinth. His epistles belong to the New Testament. // According to tradition, both were martyred in Rome under Nero, around 64-67.

life|07-20||Προφήτης Ηλίας||Elijah was a prophet of the kingdom of Israel in the 9th century BC, from Tishbe of Gilead. He opposed the worship of Baal, which King Ahab and Jezebel supported. // On Mount Carmel he proposed to the prophets of Baal to test which god would light the fire on the sacrifice, and Elijah's God answered. The Book of Kings relates that he was taken up into heaven in a chariot of fire. // In Greece the chapels of the Prophet Elijah are usually built on mountaintops, because the people associate him with the sky, the rain and the lightning.

life|07-26||Αγία Παρασκευή||Paraskevi was born in Rome in the middle of the 2nd century to pious parents and was named so because she was born on a Friday. She dedicated her life to teaching the faith. // In the time of the Emperor Antoninus they arrested her and subjected her to tortures. According to tradition, she came out of the torments unharmed and healed the blind, and for this reason she is honored as the protector of the eyes. She died by beheading. // Many churches bear her name and her memory is very great in Greece.

life|07-27||Άγιος Παντελεήμων||Panteleimon was born in Nicomedia at the end of the 3rd century and was originally named Pantaleon. He studied medicine and became a physician at the court of the Emperor Maximian. // The priest Hermolaus brought him to Christianity. From then on he healed the sick free of charge, in the name of Christ, and many came to believe through this. Envious colleagues denounced him and during the persecution of Diocletian he was beheaded, around 305. // He is called "Panteleimon" ("he who has compassion on all") and is one of the Holy Unmercenaries; he is honored as the protector of physicians and of the sick.

life|08-06||Η Μεταμόρφωση του Σωτήρος||The feast commemorates the event recounted by the first three Gospels: Jesus went up a high mountain, which tradition identifies with Tabor, with the disciples Peter, James and John. There his face shone like the sun and his clothes became white as light. // Moses and Elijah appeared and spoke with him, and a voice from a cloud said: "This is my beloved Son". The Orthodox Church sees in the Transfiguration the revelation of the uncreated light of the divinity.

life|08-15||Η Κοίμηση της Θεοτόκου||The feast of the Dormition of the Theotokos, the "Dekapentavgoustos" (15 August), is the greatest feast of the Panagia. Tradition says that the apostles were miraculously gathered in Jerusalem to be present at her falling asleep and at the translation of her body. // The feast is prepared for by a fifteen-day fast, from 1 August. In Greece it is celebrated with great festivity, especially on Tinos, where thousands of pilgrims go to the church of Panagia Evangelistria.

life|08-29||Η Αποτομή της Κεφαλής||John the Forerunner rebuked the tetrarch Herod Antipas because he had taken Herodias, his brother's wife, as his wife. Herod imprisoned him in the fortress of Machaerus. // On his birthday, the daughter of Herodias danced before the guests and the king promised her whatever she might ask. At the urging of her mother she asked for the head of John, and Herod ordered the beheading. // The day is a strict fast: the faithful do not eat meat and do not engage in entertainment.

life|09-08||Το Γενέθλιο της Θεοτόκου||According to the apocryphal Protoevangelium of James, Mary was born to Joachim and Anna, a couple who had no children until their old age and received the child as an answer to their prayer. // The feast is the first of the church year, which begins on 1 September. It marks the beginning of salvation, because Mary was born to become the mother of Christ.

life|09-14||Η Ύψωση του Τιμίου||The feast refers to the finding of the Precious Cross by Helena, the mother of Constantine, and to its elevation by Bishop Macarius, so that the faithful might see it. // In 614 the Cross was taken by the Persians, and in 628 the Emperor Heraclius recovered it and brought it back to Jerusalem. The day is a strict fast. // In many parts of Greece basil is distributed, which tradition says grew at the place where the Cross was found.

life|10-26||Άγιος Δημήτριος||Demetrius was, according to tradition, a high official in Thessaloniki at the end of the 3rd century and publicly confessed the Christian faith. The Emperor Maximian imprisoned him and put him to death with spears, around 306. // His tomb became a place of pilgrimage and over it was built the great basilica of Saint Demetrius. The people believed that he protected the city during sieges and honor him as the patron saint of Thessaloniki. // His memory is connected with the "Agiodimitriatiko" season, the beginning of winter in popular tradition.

life|11-09||Άγιος Νεκτάριος||Nectarios was born in 1846 in Selymbria in Thrace with the name Anastasios Kefalas. He studied in Athens and became a monk at the Nea Moni of Chios. In 1889 he was ordained Metropolitan of Pentapolis in Egypt. // The reputation of his goodness provoked envy and he was removed from Alexandria. He settled in Athens, where he served as a preacher and as director of the Rizarios School. // In 1904 he founded on Aegina the women's Monastery of the Holy Trinity and lived there until his death, in 1920, as a simple monk. He was canonized in 1961 and is one of the best-loved saints of the 20th century.

life|11-13||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Χρυσόστομος||John was born around 349 in Antioch, to a father who was a military man. He became a student of the rhetorician Libanius, and later a monk and deacon. // In 398 he became Archbishop of Constantinople. The power of his speech gained him the epithet "Chrysostom", that is, "golden-mouthed". He preached against luxury and injustice, and his homilies on wealth and almsgiving became well known. // His criticisms annoyed the Empress Eudoxia and some bishops, and he was exiled twice. He died in 407, at Comana in Pontus, on the march of his exile. The liturgy that bears his name is celebrated almost every Sunday.

life|11-21||Τα Εισόδια της Θεοτόκου||The feast is based on the apocryphal tradition that the parents of Mary, Joachim and Anna, brought her to the Temple of Jerusalem when she was three years old, in order to dedicate her to God, and that she was brought up there. // The commemoration inaugurates the period of preparation for Christmas.

life|11-25||Αγία Αικατερίνη||Catherine was, according to tradition, an educated daughter of a noble family from Alexandria in the early 4th century. With her wisdom she defeated in debate many philosophers whom the emperor had summoned, and several of them came to believe. // She refused to sacrifice to the gods and to marry the emperor, and in the end she was beheaded, around 305. According to tradition, angels carried her body to Mount Sinai, where the Monastery of Saint Catherine was built. // She is honored as the patron saint of students and of philosophers.

life|11-30||Άγιος Ανδρέας ο Απόστολος||Andrew was from Bethsaida and a fisherman in Galilee, the brother of Peter. He was a disciple of John the Forerunner and the first to follow Jesus, and for this reason he is called "the First-Called". // He preached in Asia Minor, on the Black Sea and in Greece. According to tradition, he was crucified in Patras on an X-shaped cross, which is called "Andrew's cross". // He is honored as the founder of the Church of Byzantium and as the patron saint of Patras. The church of Saint Andrew in Patras is one of the largest in Greece.

life|12-04||Αγία Βαρβάρα||Barbara was, according to tradition, the daughter of a rich pagan, Dioscorus, who kept her shut up in a tower. There she heard about Christ and was baptized in secret. // Her father denounced her to the authorities when he learned of her faith, and after torments he himself beheaded her. Tradition says that Dioscorus was struck by lightning. // She is honored as a protector against lightning and explosions, and for this reason she is the patron saint of artillerymen and miners. In many places they prepare the "varvara", a sweet made of wheat.

life|12-05||Όσιος Σάββας||Sabbas was born in 439 in Cappadocia and became a monk from a young age. At the age of 18 he went to Palestine, where he lived with Venerable Euthymius. // He founded the Great Lavra, near Jerusalem, which from him was named the Monastery of Saint Sabbas. It is one of the oldest monasteries of the East that are still functioning. // He defended the teaching of Chalcedon and died in 532, at the age of 93. His monastery preserves his relics.

life|12-06||Άγιος Νικόλαος||Nicholas was born around 270 in Patara of Lycia to wealthy parents and became Bishop of Myra. He was known for his kindness and charity: it is said that he secretly gave gold coins to the three daughters of a poor man, so that they would not remain without a dowry. // During the persecution of Diocletian he was imprisoned, and, according to tradition, he took part in the First Ecumenical Council. He died around 343. // He is honored as the protector of sailors and of children, and from him came the Santa Claus of the Western tradition. Many chapels on islands and shores bear his name.

life|12-12||Άγιος Σπυρίδων||Spyridon was born in Cyprus, at the end of the 3rd century, and was a shepherd and farmer who became Bishop of Trimythous. He was a simple man, known for his kindness and his hospitality to strangers. // He took part in the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea in 325 and, according to tradition, explained the dogma of the Trinity with a roof tile: fire, water and earth in one. He died around 348. // His relic is kept in Corfu, where he is honored as the patron saint of the island, and the processions of Spyridon are among the best known in Greece.

life|12-15||Άγιος Ελευθέριος||Eleutherius was born in Rome at the end of the 1st century and, according to tradition, became, while still young, bishop of Illyricum under the Emperor Hadrian. His mother, Anthia, was a Christian. // He was arrested during the persecution and cruelly tortured, but, according to tradition, remained unharmed by the torments. In the end he was put to death. // He is honored as the protector of pregnant women and of childbirth, and many Greeks bear the name Eleutherios.

life|12-25||Η Γέννηση του Κυρίου||The feast commemorates the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, as it is related by the Gospels of Matthew and Luke: Mary gave birth to Christ in a cave-manger, because there was no room in the inn, and the shepherds and the magi came to worship him. // 25 December was established as the date of the feast in the 4th century. The feast is preceded by a forty-day fast, and is followed by the Twelve Days, which reach as far as Theophany. // In Greece the carols, the Christ-bread and the decorated boat or tree make up the customs of the day.

life|12-27||Άγιος Στέφανος ο Πρωτομάρτυς||Stephen was one of the seven deacons whom the apostles chose in Jerusalem to care for the poor, as the Acts of the Apostles relate. He was full of faith and wisdom and worked miracles among the people. // He was accused of blasphemy and led before the Sanhedrin, where he gave a long speech about the history of Israel. They took him outside the city and stoned him, while he prayed for his executioners. // He was the first Christian martyr, and for this reason he is called the Protomartyr. Present at the stoning was Saul, the later Apostle Paul.

life|01-02||Όσιος Σεραφείμ του Σαρώφ||Seraphim was born around 1754 in Kursk in Russia, into a family of merchants, with the name Prokhor Moshnin. He entered the monastery of Sarov while young and later lived for many years as a hermit in a hut in the forest. // After a long period of silence he opened his door to people. He received everyone with a smile and greeted them with the words "Christ is risen, my joy". He taught that the aim of the Christian life is the acquisition of the Holy Spirit. // He died in 1833 and was canonized in 1903. He is one of the best-loved saints of Russia.

life|01-10||Άγιος Γρηγόριος ο Νύσσης||Gregory was born around 335 in Cappadocia and was the brother of Basil the Great and of Macrina. He studied rhetoric and at first taught, until his family persuaded him to serve the Church. // In 372 he became Bishop of Nyssa. At first he was unjustly accused and exiled, but he returned and took part in the Second Ecumenical Council of 381. He wrote many theological and ascetical works, such as "On the Making of Man" and the "Life of Moses". // He died around 395. The Greek fathers regard him as one of the deepest thinkers of the early Church.

life|01-12||Αγία Τατιανή||Tatiana lived in Rome in the 3rd century, the daughter of a Christian official, and served as a deaconess. In the time of the Emperor Alexander Severus she was arrested because she confessed her faith and refused to sacrifice to the gods. // According to tradition, her torturers were unable to break her and, in the end, she was beheaded. She is the patron saint of students in Russia, where her memory is celebrated as "Students' Day".

life|01-28||Όσιος Εφραίμ ο Σύρος||Ephrem was born around 306 in Nisibis in Mesopotamia and became a deacon of its church. When the city was captured by the Persians, he moved to Edessa, where he taught and wrote until the end of his life. // He never became a priest, out of humility. He wrote many hymns and homilies in Syriac, and for this reason he is called the "Harp of the Holy Spirit". The prayer "O Lord and Master of my life", which is read during Great Lent, is his. // He died around 373, while caring for the sick during an epidemic.

life|02-02||Η Υπαπαντή του Κυρίου||The feast commemorates what the Gospel according to Luke relates: forty days after the birth of Christ, Mary and Joseph brought him to the Temple of Jerusalem, as the Law prescribed. // There he was met by the righteous Simeon, who had waited for years for the Messiah, and took him in his arms. He thanked God and spoke the words "Now lettest thou thy servant depart, O Master", which are sung every evening at Vespers. With him was also the prophetess Anna. // The name "Hypapante" means "meeting".

life|02-05||Αγία Αγάθη||Agatha was born in Catania in Sicily and, according to tradition, was a young woman from a noble family, who had dedicated her life to Christ. During the persecution of Decius, around 251, she refused the proposal of the magistrate Quintianus and was imprisoned. // They tortured her cruelly, but she did not deny her faith and died in prison. She is honored as the protector of Catania and as the protector of women.

life|02-08||Άγιος Θεόδωρος ο Στρατηλάτης||Theodore was, according to tradition, a military commander in Heraclea of Pontus in the early 4th century, under the Emperor Licinius. It is said that he killed a dragon that terrorized the region. // When Licinius asked him to sacrifice to the gods, he refused, and they tortured him and beheaded him, around 319. He is one of the "military" saints and his memory is very great in Greece.

life|02-23||Άγιος Πολύκαρπος||Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna, was a disciple of the evangelist John and one of the "Apostolic Fathers". The church of Smyrna had him as its leader for decades. // Around 155 he was over eighty years old when they arrested him. The magistrate asked him to deny Christ, and he answered that he had served him for eighty-six years and that Christ had done him no harm. They burned him and stabbed him. // The "Martyrdom of Polycarp" is among the oldest Christian texts on martyrdom.

life|03-04||Όσιος Γεράσιμος ο Ιορδανίτης||Gerasimus was born in Lycia in the 5th century and went to Palestine, where he became an ascetic in the desert of the Jordan. He founded a monastery near the river, with a system that combined communal life and solitary prayer. // Tradition says that he removed a thorn from the paw of a lion, and from then on the animal followed him. For this reason the saint is depicted with a lion. He died around 475.

life|03-09||Οι Άγιοι Τεσσαράκοντα Μάρτυρες||The forty soldiers served in Sebaste in Armenia, in the army of Licinius, and were Christians. Around 320 they refused to sacrifice to the idols. // Their commander condemned them to remain naked all night on the frozen lake, with a bath of warm water on the shore for anyone who renounced. One gave up, but a guard, who saw signs in the sky, took his place and believed. // The next day they burned them and threw the relics into the lake. Their memory, which falls in Great Lent, gives courage to the faithful.

life|03-14||Όσιος Βενέδικτος||Benedict was born around 480 in Nursia in Italy and studied in Rome, but left and became a hermit at Subiaco. He founded monasteries and around 529 built the monastery of Monte Cassino. // He wrote his "Rule", a text with instructions for the life of the monastic community, based on prayer, work and obedience. It became the foundation of Western monasticism. // He died around 547. The Orthodox Church honors him as a venerable saint, from the time when the two Churches were united.

life|03-30||Όσιος Ιωάννης της Κλίμακος||John lived in the 6th-7th century and, while still young, became a monk on Mount Sinai. He lived for many years as a hermit and later became abbot of the monastery of Sinai. // He wrote the "Ladder", a book with thirty steps of the spiritual life, from the renunciation of the world to love. The book is read every year during Great Lent and his memory is celebrated on the fourth Sunday of the Fast, as well as on 30 March.

life|05-09||Προφήτης Ησαΐας||Isaiah lived in the 8th century BC in Jerusalem and was one of the great prophets of Israel. The book that bears his name contains prophecies about justice, judgment and hope. // Christians honor him especially because his prophecies, such as that of Emmanuel ("Behold, a virgin shall conceive") and that of the Servant of the Lord, are regarded as foretelling Christ. According to tradition, he died a martyr's death under King Manasseh.

life|05-11||Άγιοι Κύριλλος και Μεθόδιος||The brothers Constantine (Cyril) and Methodius were born in Thessaloniki in the 9th century. Cyril was a philosopher and teacher in Constantinople, and Methodius a governor and later a monk. // In 863 the ruler of Moravia asked Byzantium for missionaries. The two brothers created the Glagolitic alphabet, from which the Cyrillic derived, and translated the Bible and the worship into the Slavonic language. // Cyril died in 869 in Rome and Methodius in 885 as an archbishop. They are honored as the "Apostles of the Slavs" and as patrons of Europe.

life|05-15||Όσιος Παχώμιος ο Μέγας||Pachomius was born around 292 in Upper Egypt to pagan parents and served as a soldier. He was impressed by the kindness of the Christians who helped the soldiers, and was baptized. // He became an ascetic and then founded at Tabennisi the first cenobitic monastery, where the monks lived together and had a common rule, common possessions and common labors. At the end of his life his monasteries had thousands of monks. // He died around 348 of an epidemic. He is honored as the father of cenobitic monasticism.

life|07-05||Όσιος Αθανάσιος ο Αθωνίτης||Athanasius was born around 920 in Trebizond and became a monk at Kyminas in Bithynia. In 960 he went to Athos, where until then hermits had lived. // With the support of the Emperor Nikephoros Phokas he founded in 963 the Great Lavra, the first organized monastery of the Holy Mountain, and wrote the rule for it. Thus began the monastic polity of Athos. // He died around 1001, when the dome of a church that was being built collapsed.

life|07-11||Αγία Ευφημία||Euphemia was born in Chalcedon in Asia Minor and, according to tradition, refused to sacrifice to the gods during the persecution of Diocletian, around 303. They tortured her greatly and she died in martyrdom. // At the Fourth Ecumenical Council, in 451, which took place in Chalcedon, in the church of the saint, the fathers placed two confessions of faith inside her relic, and according to tradition the confession of orthodoxy remained in her hands. For this reason she is called "Panefimos" (All-Praised).

life|07-12||Όσιος Παΐσιος ο Αγιορείτης||Paisios was born in 1924 in Farasa of Cappadocia, with the name Arsenios Eznepidis, and his family came as refugees to Konitsa. He served as a radio operator in the army and asked to become a monk. // He lived on the Holy Mountain and on Sinai, and in his last years at Panagouda in Thessaloniki, where he received thousands of people who sought advice. He was known for his simplicity and his love for people. // He died on 12 July 1994 and was canonized by the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 2015.

life|08-24||Άγιος Κοσμάς ο Αιτωλός||Kosmas was born in 1714 in a village of Aetolia and studied at the Athonias School. He became a monk on the Holy Mountain and then began to travel as a teacher of the nation. // For twenty years he traveled through Epirus, Macedonia and Albania, preached the Gospel in plain Greek and founded schools, because he believed that education is needed to save the nation. // The powerful feared him. They arrested him and hanged him on 24 August 1779, near the river Apsos, in Albania. He was canonized in 1961.

life|08-27||Όσιος Φανούριος||Phanourios is a saint whose icon was discovered, according to tradition, on Rhodes, among the ruins of a wall. His name, "Phanourios", means "he who reveals", and it is said that he helps in finding lost things. // The faithful make a phanouropita and offer it in memory of his mother, so that her sins may be forgiven. No reliable historical information about his life is known.

life|09-02||Άγιος Μάμας||Mamas was a shepherd in Caesarea of Cappadocia in the 3rd century, the son of Christian parents who had died in prison. He lived in the desert and, according to tradition, wild animals approached him calmly. // During the persecution of Aurelian, around 275, he was thrown to wild beasts and tortured, and died a martyr's death. He is honored as the protector of shepherds and of dairy producers, and is the patron saint of Morphou in Cyprus.

life|09-04||Προφήτης Μωυσής||Moses was the great leader and lawgiver of the Israelites. He was born in Egypt and was rescued from the waters of the Nile, and was brought up in the court of Pharaoh. // On Mount Horeb God spoke to him from the burning bush and sent him to free his people. He led the Israelites out of Egypt, they crossed the Red Sea and at Sinai he received the Ten Commandments. // He died on Mount Nebo, before they entered the Promised Land. The first five books of the Bible, the Pentateuch, are attributed to him.

life|10-03||Άγιος Διονύσιος ο Αρεοπαγίτης||Dionysius was an Athenian judge on the Areopagus, and was one of the few who believed when the Apostle Paul preached there, as the Acts of the Apostles write. // According to tradition he became the first bishop of Athens and died a martyr's death. The works that bear his name, probably written in the 5th-6th century, had a significant influence on Christian theology and mysticism. // He is the patron saint of Athens.

life|10-07||Άγιοι Σέργιος και Βάκχος||Sergius and Bacchus were officers of the Roman army, friends of one mind, and were secretly Christians. When they refused to take part in a pagan sacrifice, around 303, they were publicly humiliated. // Bacchus died from a beating and Sergius was beheaded at Resafa in Syria. His tomb became an important place of pilgrimage, and the city was renamed "Sergiopolis". In Constantinople the church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus was built in their honor, which today is called Little Hagia Sophia.

life|10-16||Άγιος Λογγίνος||Longinus was a Roman centurion who was at Golgotha at the time of the crucifixion. When he saw the signs, the earthquake and the darkness, he said: "Truly this was the Son of God". // Tradition says that he later believed in Christ, was baptized and went to Cappadocia, where he preached the Gospel. He was arrested and beheaded. In the iconography of the Crucifixion he is depicted with the spear.

life|10-20||Άγιος Αρτέμιος||Artemius was a high-ranking official of the Roman army and served the Emperor Constantine and his son Constantius. In the days of Julian the Apostate, around 363, he publicly confessed his faith and silenced the emperor with his words. // They tortured him and beheaded him. He is honored as the protector of patients who suffer pains in the abdomen and the waist.

life|10-28||Η Αγία Σκέπη της Θεοτόκου||The feast commemorates a vision that Venerable Andrew the Fool for Christ saw in the 10th century in the church of Blachernae in Constantinople. According to tradition, he saw the Theotokos praying above the congregation and spreading her veil to protect it. // In Greece, 28 October is also the national anniversary of the "No" of 1940, and the two commemorations became linked, because the people considered that the Panagia sheltered Greece in the war.

life|11-01||Άγιοι Κοσμάς και Δαμιανός||The brothers Cosmas and Damian were born in Asia to a Christian mother, Theodota. They were physicians and healed the sick free of charge, and for this reason they are called "Unmercenaries", that is, "without money". // They healed many people and animals in the name of Christ and many believed. During the persecution of Diocletian they were arrested and put to death. There are three pairs of Holy Unmercenaries with this name, and the one of 1 November is the one of Asia.

life|11-11||Άγιος Μηνάς||Menas was an Egyptian soldier in the Roman army. When the persecution of Diocletian began, he abandoned military service and became a hermit. Around 296 he appeared at a public spectacle and publicly confessed Christ. // They tortured him and beheaded him. The place of his tomb, near Alexandria, was made a place of pilgrimage, and in Heraklion of Crete the great church of Saint Menas is the church of the patron saint of the city.

life|11-12||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Ελεήμων||John was born in Amathus of Cyprus, at the end of the 6th century, and was married with children. When he lost his family, he dedicated his life to the Church. // In 610 he became Patriarch of Alexandria. He gave everything to the poor and called them "his masters", because, he said, they would help him enter paradise. When the Persians captured Alexandria, he returned to Cyprus, where he died around 620.

life|11-17||Άγιος Γρηγόριος ο Θαυματουργός||Gregory was born around 213 in Neocaesarea of Pontus and studied law and philosophy, and had Origen as his teacher. Around 240 he became bishop of the city, when it had very few Christians. // The preaching and the miraculous acts attributed to him made almost the whole city Christian, and for this reason he remained known as the "Wonderworker". He died around 270.

life|12-07||Άγιος Αμβρόσιος||Ambrose was born around 339 in Gaul, into a family of Roman officials, and became governor of Liguria with his seat in Milan. When the bishop of the city died, the people asked for him as bishop, although he was not even baptized. // As Bishop of Milan from 374 he defended the right faith and the independence of the Church against the emperors. He baptized Augustine. He wrote hymns and homilies. // He died in 397. He is one of the great fathers of the West.

life|12-11||Όσιος Δανιήλ ο Στυλίτης||Daniel was born around 409 in Mesopotamia and was a monk. He visited Symeon the Stylite and decided to imitate his ascetic life. // He settled on a pillar outside Constantinople, where he lived for almost thirty-three years until his death, around 493. He received visitors, even emperors, and gave them advice. The faithful saw him as a wonderworker.

life|12-20||Άγιος Ιγνάτιος ο Θεοφόρος||Ignatius was Bishop of Antioch at the end of the 1st century and, according to tradition, a disciple of the apostles. He is called "Theophoros" ("God-bearer") because, as is said, he bore God in his heart. // In the days of Trajan he was arrested and sent with soldiers to Rome. On the way he wrote seven letters to churches, which are among the most important texts of the early Church. He asked that they not save him, and in Rome he was thrown to the wild beasts, around 107-110.

life|12-22||Αγία Αναστασία η Φαρμακολύτρια||Anastasia was born in Rome, the daughter of nobles, and had been taught the Christian faith by her mother. She married a pagan, but, according to tradition, lived apart and cared for imprisoned Christians. // During the persecution of Diocletian, around 304, she was arrested and put to death. She is called "Pharmakolytria" ("Deliverer from Poisons") because, as is believed, she heals those who have been poisoned or are afflicted by diseases.

life|01-03||Προφήτης Μαλαχίας||Malachi lived in the 5th century BC, after the return of the Jews from the exile in Babylon. His name means "my messenger" and his book is the last of the Twelve Prophets. // He criticized the priests and the people for their lukewarm worship and called for justice and faith. He prophesied that a messenger would be sent who would prepare the way of the Lord; Christians interpret this as foretelling John the Forerunner.

life|01-04||Σύναξη των Αγίων Εβδομήκοντα||According to the Gospel of Luke, Christ chose seventy disciples in addition to the twelve and sent them two by two to the cities he intended to visit, to preach the kingdom of God. // Tradition preserves their names and many of them are regarded as founders and bishops of the first churches. The Church honors them all together on one common feast, while some also have their own commemoration during the year.

life|01-05||Αγία Συγκλητική||Syncletica was born in Alexandria in the 4th century, into a wealthy family. After the death of her parents and her brother she distributed her property and lived in a tomb outside the city. // There she struggled with fasting and prayer and women who sought guidance gathered around her. The "Sayings" attributed to her are among the important texts of women's monasticism. She died at an advanced age, around 400.

life|01-06||Τα Άγια Θεοφάνεια||The Gospels relate that Jesus, at about the age of thirty, went to the Jordan to be baptized by John. As soon as he came out of the water, heaven opened, the Spirit descended like a dove and a voice said "This is my beloved Son". // For this reason the feast is called Theophany (manifestation of God) and Lights. The Church celebrates the Great Blessing of the Waters and in seaside towns they throw the cross into the sea, and the young men dive to catch it. The feast closes the Twelve Days of Christmas.

life|01-07||Σύναξη του Αγίου Ιωάννη||On the day after the feast of the Baptism, the Church honors the one who baptized Christ. John was the son of the priest Zechariah and of Elizabeth and lived in the desert of Judea, clothed in a garment of hair and feeding on locusts and honey. // He preached repentance and baptized in the Jordan. He is the last prophet of the Old Testament and the first witness of Christ; his memory continues in the name Yannis, one of the most widespread names in Greece.

life|01-08||Όσιος Γεώργιος ο Χοζεβίτης||George was born in Cyprus and later became a monk at the monastery of Choziba, in the desert of Judea, near Jericho, around the 7th century. // He lived with great humility and ascetic strictness, and the monastery in which he served remains known to this day as the monastery of Saint George the Chozebite, built on a rock above the ravine.

life|01-09||Άγιος Πολύευκτος||Polyeuctus was an officer of the Roman army in Melitene of Armenia, in the middle of the 3rd century, and a friend of Nearchus, who was a Christian. After the conversation with his friend he believed in Christ. // During the persecution of Decius/Valerian he openly confessed his faith, tore down idols and was beheaded. His church in Constantinople, built by the princess Anicia Juliana, was among the most splendid of the time of Justinian.

life|01-11||Όσιος Θεοδόσιος ο Κοινοβιάρχης||Theodosius was born in Cappadocia in 423 and went to Jerusalem and the desert of Judea, where he lived near Venerable Symeon the Stylite. // He founded a cenobitic monastery near Bethlehem, which became great: it had churches for monks of different languages, a hospital and a guesthouse. He supported the right faith of Chalcedon against the Emperor Anastasius. He died in 529 at the age of 105.

life|01-13||Άγιοι Ερμύλος και Στρατονίκος||Hermylus was a deacon in Singidunum (present-day Belgrade) and Stratonicus was his friend and attendant. In the days of Licinius, around 315, they were accused as Christians. // They were tortured and thrown into the river Danube, where they died. Their relics were found by Christians and were venerated.

life|01-14||Αγία Νίνα||Nina was born in the 4th century in Cappadocia, according to tradition, and went to Iberia, present-day Georgia. There she lived humbly and healed the sick with her prayers. // She also healed the queen, and King Mirian III believed and became a Christian around 330; thus Georgia became a Christian country. Nina is the equal-to-the-apostles and the patron saint of the Georgians.

life|01-15||Όσιοι Παύλος ο Θηβαίος||Paul was born in the Thebaid of Egypt around 228 and fled to the desert to escape the persecution of Decius. He lived in a cave for about ninety years, almost without being seen by anyone. // Anthony the Great visited him shortly before he died, around 341. Jerome wrote his life and made him known as the first hermit. John the Hut-Dweller lived later, in the 5th century, in Constantinople: he left his rich home and lived as a beggar in a hut in his own father's house.

life|01-16||Προσκύνηση της Τιμίας Αλύσεως||The Acts of the Apostles relate that Herod Agrippa arrested Peter and bound him with chains in prison, and that an angel freed him. // Tradition says that the chains were preserved by the Christians. Their memory has been celebrated since the ancient Church, and the West honors them with the church of San Pietro in Vincoli in Rome.

life|01-18||Άγιοι Αθανάσιος και Κύριλλος||Athanasius was born around 296 in Alexandria and took part as a young deacon in the First Ecumenical Council. He became Patriarch of Alexandria in 328 and steadfastly defended the divinity of Christ against Arius. He was exiled five times and died in 373. // Cyril became Patriarch of Alexandria in 412. He was a leading figure at the Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus (431), where Nestorius was condemned and the title Theotokos for Mary was confirmed. He died in 444. Their memory is celebrated together.

life|01-19||Όσιος Μακάριος ο Αιγύπτιος||Macarius was born around 300 and became a monk in Scetis in Egypt. He spent more than sixty years in the desert and became the spiritual father of many monks. // Spiritual homilies survive in his name, which significantly influenced the Christian mystical tradition. He died around 390.

life|01-20||Όσιος Ευθύμιος ο Μέγας||Euthymius was born in 377 in Melitene of Cappadocia and grew up in the Church near the bishop of the city. He went to Palestine in 405 and lived in the desert of Judea. // He founded a monastery, received many disciples, among them Sabbas, and supported the right faith of Chalcedon. He died in 473 at the age of 96.

life|01-21||Όσιος Μάξιμος ο Ομολογητής||Maximus was born around 580 in Constantinople and served at the imperial court before becoming a monk. He wrote important theological and mystical works. // He opposed Monothelitism, the teaching that Christ has only one will, and for this reason he was tried in Constantinople. They cut out his tongue and cut off his right hand and exiled him to Lazica, where he died in 662.

life|01-22||Απόστολος Τιμόθεος||Timothy was born in Lystra in Asia Minor, to a Jewish mother and a Greek father, and became a co-worker of Paul. He accompanied him on his journeys to Macedonia and to Greece. // Paul wrote him two epistles, which belong to the New Testament. According to tradition, he became Bishop of Ephesus and was martyred around 97, when he tried to stop a pagan festival.

life|01-23||Άγιος Κλήμης Αγκύρας||Clement was Bishop of Ancyra in Galatia. During the persecution of Diocletian, around 306, he was arrested and imprisoned. // According to tradition, they tortured him greatly and sent him from city to city, until he died a martyr's death.

life|01-24||Οσία Ξένη||Xenia was born in Rome at the end of the 5th century and grew up in a rich family. Before the marriage that had been arranged for her, she left secretly with two of her servant girls and went to Kos. // There she lived humbly and ascetically, with the name Xenia (that is, stranger), and people knew her for her hospitality and her prayer. The people honor her as the protector of strangers and of the poor.

life|01-26||Όσιος Ξενοφών||Xenophon was a rich official of Constantinople, in the days of Justinian, married to Maria. They had two sons, John and Arcadius, and sent them to study in Berytus. // After adventures, Xenophon and Maria became monastics, and their sons as well. The four met later in Jerusalem, and the family lived with great faith and love for humanity.

life|01-27||Η Μετακομιδή των λειψάνων του Αγίου Ιωάννου του Χρυσοστόμου||John Chrysostom died in 407 at Comana in Pontus, in exile. Patriarch Proclus, his disciple, persuaded the Emperor Theodosius II to honor him. // In 438 his relics were transferred to Constantinople, and the emperor, according to tradition, asked forgiveness for the injustice done by his parents. The people received them with splendor and they were placed in the church of the Holy Apostles.

life|01-29||Η Μετακομιδή των λειψάνων του Αγίου Ιγνατίου||Ignatius, Bishop of Antioch, was martyred in Rome around 107 and his relics were taken by the Christians. // Later, in the days of Theodosius II, his relics were transferred with honors to Antioch, and the church celebrated this commemoration. For his life see also his commemoration on 20 December.

life|01-31||Άγιοι Κύρος και Ιωάννης||Cyrus was born in Alexandria and was a physician, while John was a soldier from Edessa. During the persecution of Diocletian, Cyrus hid in Arabia, where he healed the sick without payment. // John came to find him. They were arrested together with a Christian woman and her daughters and were put to death around 311. In their church near Alexandria, according to tradition, many healings took place.

life|02-01||Άγιος Τρύφων||Tryphon was born in Phrygia and, according to tradition, from a young age had the gift of healing people and animals by prayer. He brought many to the faith. // During the persecution of Decius, around 250, he was brought to Nicaea, tortured and beheaded. He is honored as the protector of gardeners and of vine-growers, and the people celebrate his day with the "pruning" of the vine, the Tryfonari.

life|02-03||Άγιος Συμεών ο Θεοδόχος||Symeon was an elder of Jerusalem, righteous and devout, who was awaiting the Messiah. According to the Gospel of Luke, it had been revealed to him that he would not die before he saw Christ. // When Mary and Joseph brought Jesus to the temple, on the fortieth day, Symeon took him in his arms and spoke the hymn "Now lettest thou thy servant depart". Beside him was the prophetess Anna, a widow of eighty-four years, who did not leave the temple.

life|02-04||Όσιος Ισίδωρος ο Πηλουσιώτης||Isidore was born in Alexandria around 360 and became a monk on the mountain near Pelusium. He was a disciple of John Chrysostom. // He left about two thousand letters, with interpretation of Scripture, practical advice and criticism of those who hold power. He died around 435.

life|02-06||Όσιος Φώτιος ο Μέγας||Photius was born around 810 in Constantinople, into a noble family, and was one of the most educated people of Byzantium. He became patriarch in 858. // He was a leading figure in the dispute with Rome and supported the mission of Cyril and Methodius to the Slavs, as well as the spread of Christianity among the Bulgarians and the Rus. His "Myriobiblos" is a work with summaries of books that he read. He died in 893.

life|02-07||Όσιος Παρθένιος||Parthenius was born in Melitopolis of Bithynia, the son of a deacon, and became Bishop of Lampsacus in the days of Constantine the Great. // He became known for his kindness and charity, for caring for the poor and for fighting idolatry. He died in the 4th century.

life|02-09||Άγιος Νικηφόρος ο Μάρτυς||Nikephoros was a layman in Antioch, a friend of a priest, Sapricius, with whom, however, he had quarreled. Later he asked forgiveness, but Sapricius refused. // During the persecution of Valerian, Sapricius was led to martyrdom, and Nikephoros came forward and offered to die in his place. Sapricius denied the faith, and Nikephoros was beheaded, around 260. He is the example of forgiveness.

life|02-11||Άγιος Βλάσιος||Blaise was a physician and Bishop of Sebaste in Armenia. During the persecution of Licinius, around 316, he lived in a cave where wild animals also visited him, because he healed them. // Hunters found him and led him to the governor, and he was beheaded. He is honored as the protector of animals and of livestock breeders; in the West his protection is invoked against ailments of the throat.

life|02-12||Άγιος Μελέτιος||Meletius was born in Melitene of Armenia and became Bishop of Sebaste and then of Antioch, in 360. The Emperor Constantius quickly exiled him because he supported the right faith. // In 381 he presided over the Second Ecumenical Council of Constantinople, where he died. Gregory of Nyssa and John Chrysostom delivered funeral orations for him.

life|02-13||Όσιος Μαρτινιανός||Martinian was born in Caesarea of Palestine and, at the age of eighteen, became a hermit on a mountain near the sea. // According to tradition, he resisted harsh temptations and later lived on a small island. He died in the 5th century.

life|02-14||Όσιος Αυξέντιος||Auxentius was born in Syria and served at the court of Theodosius II. Leaving military life, he became a monk near Chalcedon, on Mount Skopos (Eastern Olympus). // He took part in the Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon in 451, where he supported the right faith. He died around 470.

life|02-15||Απόστολος Ονήσιμος||Onesimus was a slave of Philemon in Colossae, who ran away from his house and found Paul in prison. Paul brought him to Christ and sent him back to his master with a letter, asking him to receive him "no longer as a slave, but as a beloved brother". // The epistle to Philemon is the shortest of Paul's. Tradition says that Onesimus became a bishop and was martyred in Rome.

life|02-16||Άγιος Πάμφιλος||Pamphilus was born in Berytus and became a presbyter in Caesarea of Palestine, where he founded a large library and copied books of Scripture. Eusebius, the historian of the Church, was his friend and biographer. // During the persecution of Maximinus, in 309, he was martyred together with others. In prison he had written a defense of Origen.

life|02-17||Άγιος Θεόδωρος ο Τήρων||Theodore was a young soldier in Amaseia of Pontus. When he refused to sacrifice to the gods, around 306, he set fire to a temple and, according to tradition, they burned him alive. // Later, in the days of Julian the Apostate, Theodore appeared to Patriarch Eudoxius and warned him that the emperor had sprinkled the foodstuffs of the market with the blood of idol sacrifices. So the faithful ate koliva (boiled wheat), and for this reason on the first Saturday of Lent we eat koliva in his memory.

life|02-18||Άγιος Λέων, Πάπας Ρώμης||Leo was born in Tuscany and became Bishop of Rome in 440. He became known for his defense of Rome: in 452 he met Attila and persuaded him to withdraw, and in 455 he reduced the destruction caused by Gaiseric. // The "Dogmatic Letter" (Tome) that he sent in 449 became the basis of the teaching of the Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon (451) on the two natures of Christ. He died in 461.

life|02-19||Απόστολοι Άρχιππος και Φιλήμων||Philemon was a rich man of the city of Colossae, who became a Christian through Paul and opened his house for the church. Archippus is mentioned in the epistle to the Colossians as a deacon. // According to tradition, Philemon became Bishop of Gaza and, together with his wife Apphia and Archippus, they were martyred in the days of Nero, when the mob stoned them.

life|02-20||Άγιος Λέων, επίσκοπος Κατάνης||Leo was born in Ravenna and became Bishop of Catania in Sicily, in the early 8th century. According to tradition, he became known for his kindness and his miracles. // He fought sorcery and helped the poor and the sick. He died around 780.

life|02-21||Άγιος Ευστάθιος||Eustathius was born in Side of Pamphylia and became Bishop of Beroea and then of Antioch, around 324. At the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea (325) he was among the leading figures against Arius. // The followers of Arius falsely accused him and the emperor exiled him to Thrace, where he died around 337. He wrote homilies and interpretations of Scripture.

life|02-22||Η εύρεση των λειψάνων||Near Constantinople lay the relics of Christian martyrs, which had been buried in the church of Eugenius, and the Church celebrates their discovery. // The finding of the relics gave the city protection and the people came to the church to venerate them.

life|02-24||Α΄ και Β΄ εύρεση της τιμίας κεφαλής||After the beheading of John the Forerunner, his head, according to tradition, was buried by Herodias in a secret place. Later it was found in Jerusalem by two monks, and, according to tradition, the second finding took place at Comana. // The Church honors the discoveries and the pilgrimages connected with the relic. On the basis of this commemoration, the church of the Venerable Head in Constantinople became a place of pilgrimage.

life|02-25||Άγιος Ταράσιος||Tarasius was born in Constantinople and was an official of the court, before becoming patriarch in 784, while still a layman. // With the agreement of the Empress Irene he convened the Seventh Ecumenical Council of Nicaea in 787, which restored the veneration of icons. He was also active against the practice of buying ecclesiastical offices. He died in 806.

life|02-26||Όσιος Πορφύριος||Porphyry was born in Thessaloniki, around 347, and lived as an ascetic in Egypt and in Jerusalem. In 395 he became Bishop of Gaza, where most of the inhabitants were pagans. // With the help of the Empress Eudoxia and the Emperor Arcadius, he destroyed the idols and built a church on the site of the temple of Marnas. He died in 420.

life|02-27||Όσιος Προκόπιος ο Δεκαπολίτης||Procopius was born in Decapolis of Isauria and became a monk and confessor. In the days of the iconoclast Leo III he defended the icons. // He was arrested, imprisoned and tortured, and died around 750.

life|02-28||Όσιος Βασίλειος ο Ομολογητής||Basil was abbot of a monastery in Constantinople and, in the period of the second iconoclasm, insisted on the veneration of icons. // They beat him and exiled him, and he died around 750, in the village where he lived in exile.

life|02-29||Όσιος Κάσσιανος ο Ρωμαίος||Cassian was born in Scythia, around 360, and became a monk in Bethlehem. He went to Egypt, where he met the hermits, and then to Constantinople and to Rome. // He founded two monasteries in Marseilles and wrote the "Institutes" and the "Conferences", with the teachings of the Fathers of the desert, which became a source for Western monasticism. He died around 435.

life|03-01||Αγία Ευδοκία||According to her life, Eudokia lived in Heliopolis (Baalbek) of Lebanon and had riches and a luxurious life. A monk, Germanus, spoke to her about Christ and baptized her. // She dedicated her property to the poor and became a nun. She was arrested in the days of Trajan, around 114, and beheaded.

life|03-02||Όσιος Νικόλαος ο Πλανάς||Nicholas Planas was born in 1851 on Naxos and came to Athens, where he became a priest in 1879. He served in the church of Agia Zoni and the Holy Unmercenaries for over fifty years. // He was known for his meekness and his charity; he gave whatever he had to the poor and the sick, and the Athenians called him "Papa-Planas". He died in 1932 and was canonized by the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 1992.

life|03-03||Άγιοι Εύτροπιος||Eutropius, Cleonicus and Basiliscus were military men and friends of Basiliscus, and Basiliscus was a nephew of Saint Theodore the Tyro. // During the persecution of Maximian, in Amaseia of Pontus, around 308, they confessed their faith and were martyred in various ways.

life|03-05||Άγιος Κόνων||Conon was from Isauria and was martyred in the middle of the 3rd century. According to tradition he was a simple gardener, who brought many to the faith by his example. // He was arrested in the time of Decius, tortured and died.

life|03-06||Οι Άγιοι Τεσσαράκοντα Δύο Μάρτυρες του Αμορίου||In 838 the caliph Mutasim captured Amorium in Phrygia. The officers who defended the city, among them the general Aetius, were taken prisoner and transported to Samarra. // They spent seven years imprisoned and were offered to change their religion. They refused, and in 845 they were beheaded.

life|03-07||Οι Άγιοι Μάρτυρες της Χερσώνος||Ephraim, Basileus, Eugenius, Elpidius, Agathodorus, Capito and Aetherius were bishops who were sent from Jerusalem to Cherson in Crimea to preach the Gospel. // Several of them were martyred in the early 4th century by the pagans of the city.

life|03-08||Όσιος Θεοφύλακτος||Theophylact was Bishop of Nicomedia in the days of iconoclasm. Because he defended the icons, the Emperor Leo V exiled him. // He died in exile, around 840, having spent many years in privation.

life|03-10||Άγιος Κόδρατος||Codratus was a disciple and a Christian of Corinth, and was martyred together with others, Cyprian, Dionysius, Anectus and Paul. // During the persecution of Decius (250), the group was arrested and put to death, and Corinth honors them.

life|03-11||Άγιος Σωφρόνιος||Sophronius was born in Damascus around 560 and was a wise monk and writer. In 634 he became Patriarch of Jerusalem. // He resisted Monothelitism and, in 637, when the caliph Umar besieged Jerusalem, he surrendered the city by agreement. He died a little later, in 638.

life|03-12||Όσιος Θεοφάνης ο Ομολογητής||Theophanes was born in Constantinople around 760 and lived at court, but became a monk and founded the monastery of Megas Agros. He wrote the "Chronographia", a historical work. // During the iconoclasm of Leo V he was imprisoned and exiled to Samothrace, where he died in 818.

life|03-13||Η Μετακομιδή των λειψάνων του Αγίου Νικηφόρου||Nikephoros became Patriarch of Constantinople in 806 and was a historian and theologian. During the second iconoclasm he was exiled and died in 828. // In 846, in the time of the Empress Theodora, who restored the icons, his relics were transferred with honors to Constantinople.

life|03-15||Άγιος Αγάπιος||Agapius and six other Christians were martyred in Caesarea of Palestine in the early 4th century, in the days of Diocletian. // They were thrown to wild beasts and then thrown into the sea.

life|03-17||Όσιος Αλέξιος ο άνθρωπος του Θεού||Alexis was born, according to tradition, in Rome, the son of a rich senator. On the day of his wedding he left secretly and went to Edessa, where he lived as a beggar near the church. // After seventeen years he returned to Rome, but they did not recognize him, and he lived under the staircase of his parents' house. After his death they found a letter with his story. His life had a great resonance in Byzantium and in the West.

life|03-18||Άγιος Κύριλλος, Αρχιεπίσκοπος Ιεροσολύμων||Cyril was born around 315 and became Bishop of Jerusalem in 349. He was exiled three times because of the Arians. // He left eighteen "Catecheses", which were given to new Christians before baptism, and five "Mystagogical Catecheses", which explain the mysteries. He took part in the Second Ecumenical Council in 381 and died in 386.

life|03-19||Άγιοι Χρύσανθος και Δαρεία||Chrysanthus was the son of a senator in Rome, who became a Christian and married Daria, a priestess of Athena, who also believed. // They lived together like siblings and brought many to the faith. In the days of Numerian (284) they were arrested and put to death.

life|03-20||Οι Όσιοι Πατέρες που σφαγιάστηκαν||Many monks lived in the monastery of Saint Sabbas in Palestine. Around 796 and 797, Arab raiders invaded the monastery and killed twenty monks. // The people honor them as martyrs. Their names are preserved in the synaxaria.

life|03-21||Άγιος Ιάκωβος ο Ομολογητής||James was a bishop and confessor in the days of iconoclasm, and was exiled because he refused to condemn the icons. // He died around 840, having suffered tortures and exile.

life|03-22||Άγιος Βασίλειος, πρεσβύτερος Αγκύρας||Basil was a priest of Ancyra and preached with courage against Arianism. In the days of Julian the Apostate he openly denounced idolatry. // They arrested him and tortured him, and in 362 he died a martyr's death.

life|03-23||Άγιος Νίκων||Nikon was a military man from Naples, who became a Christian and a monk. According to tradition, together with a group of 199 disciples, he was martyred in Sicily, in the days of Decius, around 250. // The sources for their lives are incomplete.

life|03-24||Όσιος Ζαχαρίας||Zacharias was a monk and ascetic of Palestine in the 5th century. According to the synaxaria, he had great humility and abounded in prayer. // On 24 March the Church also celebrates the forefeast of the Annunciation.

life|03-26||Σύναξη του Αρχαγγέλου Γαβριήλ||Gabriel is the angel who, according to the Gospel of Luke, announced to Zechariah the birth of John and to Mary the birth of Christ. // On the day after the feast of the Annunciation, the Church celebrates the archangel, as it does with others who are connected with a great event.

life|03-27||Οσία Ματρώνα||Matrona was born in Perge in Pamphylia and became a servant in a family in Constantinople. Her mistress was harsh toward her, because Matrona would go secretly to pray. // She left and became a nun in a monastery, dressed in men's clothing, and later founded a convent in Constantinople. She died around 492, at the age of more than one hundred years.

life|03-28||Όσιος Ιλαρίων ο Νέος||Hilarion was born in Cappadocia, around 760, and became a monk. He became abbot of the Pelekete monastery in Bithynia. // During Iconoclasm he was exiled and imprisoned, and he died around 845.

life|03-29||Άγιος Μάρκος, επίσκοπος Αρεθουσίων||Mark was Bishop of Arethusa in Syria in the 4th century. In the time of Julian the Apostate he destroyed a pagan temple. // Later the pagans cruelly tortured him, and he died around 362.

life|03-31||Άγιος Υπάτιος||Hypatius was Bishop of Gangra in Paphlagonia and took part in the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea in 325. // Later, heretics who opposed him attacked and killed him, according to tradition.

life|04-01||Οσία Μαρία η Αιγυπτία||Mary was born in Egypt around 344 and at the age of twelve left for Alexandria, where she lived for seventeen years a life that she herself considered sinful. She traveled with pilgrims toward Jerusalem. // She could not enter the Church of the Resurrection, and an icon of the Theotokos led her to repent. She crossed the Jordan and lived in the desert for forty-seven years, until the monk Zosimas found her and gave her Holy Communion. She died around 421. Her life is read on the Thursday of the fifth week of Lent.

life|04-03||Όσιος Νικήτας ο Ομολογητής||Nikitas was born in Bithynia around 760 and became abbot of the Medikion monastery. // During the second Iconoclasm he was imprisoned and exiled, because he did not renounce the icons. He died around 824.

life|04-04||Όσιος Ιωσήφ ο Υμνογράφος||Joseph was born in Sicily around 816 and, when the Arabs took the region, his family took refuge in the Peloponnese. He became a monk and went to Thessaloniki and to Constantinople. // During the Iconoclasm of Theophilos he went to Rome and was captured by pirates in Crete. He was freed and wrote more than a thousand canons and hymns, which are sung at the services of the feasts. He died in 886.

life|04-06||Άγιος Ευτύχιος||Eutychius was born in Phrygia around 512 and became a monk in Amaseia in Pontus. In 552 he became Patriarch of Constantinople. // He presided over the Fifth Ecumenical Council in 553. Because of a disagreement with Justinian he was exiled in 565, but he returned in 577. He died in 582.

life|04-07||Άγιος Καλλιόπιος||Kalliopios was a Christian who was arrested in the persecution of Diocletian, around 304, and did not deny his faith. // According to the Synaxarion, he was martyred by being crucified upside down. The sources for his life are few.

life|04-08||Απόστολοι Ηρωδίων||Herodion, Agabus, Rufus, Asyncritus, Phlegon and Hermes were disciples of the apostles and belong to the Seventy. Paul mentions them in his epistle to the Romans. // Agabus prophesied the famine in the days of Claudius and that Paul would be bound in Jerusalem, according to the Acts. According to tradition, they became bishops of various cities.

life|04-09||Άγιος Ευψύχιος||Eupsychius was a nobleman of Caesarea who had recently married. In the time of Julian the Apostate, around 362, he was among the Christians who destroyed a pagan temple. // He was arrested and beheaded.

life|04-10||Άγιοι Τερέντιος||Terence, Pompeius, Africanus, Maximus and other Christians were arrested in Carthage in the time of Decius and were martyred. // The church of Carthage honored them from very early on.

life|04-11||Άγιος Αντίπας||Antipas was Bishop of Pergamum, whom the Christians regarded as a disciple of John the Theologian. The Apocalypse mentions him as "my faithful martyr," who was killed in Pergamum. // The people consider him a protector from toothache, and invoke him for this reason.

life|04-12||Άγιος Βασίλειος, επίσκοπος Παρίου||Basil was Bishop of the city of Parium on the Hellespont in the 8th century. He opposed the iconoclasts. // He was exiled and died in exile. The Church honors him as a confessor.

life|04-13||Άγιος Μαρτίνος||Martin was born in Italy and became Bishop of Rome in 649. He convened the Lateran Council, which condemned Monothelitism. // Emperor Constans II arrested him and brought him to Constantinople. He was tried and exiled to Cherson, where he died in 655 from hunger and hardships.

life|04-14||Απόστολοι Αρίσταρχος||Aristarchus was from Thessaloniki and accompanied Paul on his journeys, and was imprisoned with him. Pudens and Trophimus were also co-workers of Paul. // According to tradition, Aristarchus became Bishop of Apamea and was martyred in Rome, together with Paul.

life|04-15||Αγίες Βασίλισσα και Αναστασία||Basilissa and Anastasia were women of Rome and, according to tradition, disciples of the apostles Peter and Paul. They cared for imprisoned Christians. // In the time of Nero they were arrested and died as martyrs.

life|04-16||Αγίες Αγάπη||The three sisters Agape, Irene and Chione were from Thessaloniki and, when Diocletian ordered the Christian books to be burned, they took some with them and hid in the mountains. // They were arrested around 304 and were martyred in Thessaloniki. They are honored in the city.

life|04-17||Άγιος Σίμων, επίσκοπος Περσίας||Simeon was Bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon in Persia. In the time of King Shapur II (340) he refused to worship the sun and to pay tax. // He was martyred together with many clergy and laypeople.

life|04-18||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Νεομάρτυρας των Ιωαννίνων||John was a young man from Ioannina, who worked as a shepherd or a servant. In 1526 he was accused of having become a Muslim and denied it. // They burned him alive in Ioannina. The people honor him as a new martyr and protector of the city.

life|04-20||Όσιος Θεόδωρος ο Τριχινάς||Theodore lived in Constantinople in the 4th century and was an ascetic of very severe discipline. He wore a hair garment, and from this he took the name "Trichinas." // He was known for his prayers, and many went to visit him.

life|04-22||Όσιος Θεόδωρος ο Σικεώτης||Theodore was born in Sykeon in Galatia, around 540, and from a young age prayed in the church of Saint George. He lived as a hermit and healed the sick. // He became Bishop of Anastasioupolis, but resigned and returned to the monastery. He died in 613. He was a friend of Emperor Maurice.

life|04-24||Άγιος Σάββας ο Στρατηλάτης||Sabbas was a Gothic officer of the Roman army. He was arrested because he was a Christian and did not want to eat food sacrificed to idols. // In the time of Aurelian, in 272, Sabbas was thrown into the river and drowned.

life|04-25||Άγιος Μάρκος ο Απόστολος||Mark, who was also called John, was from Jerusalem, and in the house of his mother the first Christians gathered. He accompanied Paul and Barnabas on the first journey and later Peter. // According to tradition, he wrote the second Gospel, which is based on the accounts of Peter, and founded the Church of Alexandria. He was martyred there, around 68. He is the patron saint of Venice.

life|04-26||Άγιος Βασίλειος, επίσκοπος Αμασείας||Basil was Bishop of Amaseia in Pontus. In the time of Licinius, around 322, he denounced the persecutions of the Christians. // He was arrested and beheaded in the Black Sea region of Pontus.

life|04-27||Άγιος Συμεών, επίσκοπος Ιεροσολύμων||Simeon was the son of Clopas, the brother of Joseph, and therefore a relative of Christ. He became Bishop of Jerusalem after James, around 62. // In the time of Trajan he was accused of being a Christian and, at the age of about one hundred and twenty, he was crucified, around 107.

life|04-28||Απόστολοι Ιάσων||Jason was from Tarsus and a relative of Paul. Thessaloniki hosted Paul in the house of a certain Jason, as the Acts write. // According to tradition, Jason and Sosipater went to Corfu, and there became bishops. They were martyred on the island, and are honored as its protectors.

life|04-29||Οι Άγιοι Εννέα Μάρτυρες της Κυζίκου||Theogenes, Eunicus, Dometius and other Christians of Cyzicus, in Asia Minor, were arrested in the time of Diocletian. // After tortures, they were put to death, and they are honored as martyrs.

life|04-30||Άγιος Ιάκωβος ο Απόστολος||James was the son of Zebedee and brother of John, a fisherman from Galilee. Jesus named them "Boanerges," "sons of thunder." He was one of the three disciples who saw the Transfiguration. // The Acts relate that Herod Agrippa beheaded him, around 44, and he is the first of the twelve to be martyred. The tradition that he preached in Spain is the origin of the pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela.

life|05-01||Προφήτης Ιερεμίας||Jeremiah was born into a priestly family, in Anathoth, and was called as a prophet at a young age, around 627 B.C. He prophesied in Jerusalem in the years before its destruction by the Babylonians, in 586 B.C. // He warned the people to change their lives and suffered imprisonment and persecutions. He left the book that bears his name and the "Lamentations." Tradition says that he died in Egypt.

life|05-02||Η Μετακομιδή των λειψάνων του Αγίου Αθανασίου||Athanasius died in Alexandria in 373. His relics were later transferred to Constantinople, in the time of Constantine Porphyrogenitus, in 950. // The Church celebrates the translation in order to honor the defender of the right faith.

life|05-03||Άγιοι Τιμόθεος και Μαύρα||Timothy was a reader in a village of Egypt and had recently married Maura. In the time of Diocletian, the governor asked Timothy to hand over the sacred books. // He refused and was tortured. Maura gave courage to her husband and shared in the martyrdom. They were crucified in 286.

life|05-04||Αγία Πελαγία||Pelagia was a young woman of Tarsus in Cilicia, at the end of the 3rd century. According to the Synaxarion, Diocletian (or one of his officials) asked to marry her, but she had dedicated herself to Christ. // She refused and was martyred around 287.

life|05-05||Αγία Ειρήνη||Irene was, according to the Synaxarion, the daughter of the pagan Licinius and was born with the name Penelope. Her teacher, Apellianos, brought her to Christianity and she was baptized. // Her father tortured her and left her to the horses, and, after many trials, she was led to death. In Greece she is especially honored, and many girls bear her name, which means "peace."

life|05-06||Δίκαιος Ιώβ||The book of Job tells the story of a righteous and wealthy man of the land of Uz, who lost everything: his children, his flocks and his health. // His friends tried to persuade him that he was at fault, but he did not blame God and asked that his righteousness be heard. In the end God restored everything to him. He is a symbol of patience. Christians also honor him, and the patience of Job is read during Holy Week.

life|05-07||Το σημείο του Τιμίου Σταυρού||On May 7, 351, as Cyril, Bishop of Jerusalem, relates in his letter to Emperor Constantius, a luminous cross appeared above Golgotha and extended as far as the Mount of Olives. // The whole city saw the sight, and many, both Christians and non-Christians, believed. The Church celebrates the event.

life|05-08||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Θεολόγος||John was the son of Zebedee and brother of James, a fisherman from Galilee, and the disciple whom Christ especially loved. He was present at the Transfiguration, in Gethsemane and on Golgotha, where Jesus entrusted his mother to him. // According to tradition, he lived in Ephesus and was exiled by Domitian to Patmos, where he wrote the Apocalypse. In Ephesus he wrote the Gospel and three epistles. He died in deep old age, around 100. He is called "the Theologian" because he spoke profoundly about the divinity of Christ.

life|05-10||Απόστολος Σίμων ο Ζηλωτής||Simon was one of the twelve apostles and is called "the Zealot," perhaps because he had a connection with the movement of the Zealots, or because of his zeal. The Gospels do not say much about him. // According to tradition, he preached in Egypt and in other lands and was martyred.

life|05-12||Άγιοι Επιφάνιος||Epiphanius was born around 315 in Palestine and became a monk, and in 367 Bishop of Salamis in Cyprus. He wrote the "Panarion," a work against the heresies. He died in 403. // Germanus was born in Constantinople and became patriarch in 715. He opposed the iconoclast Leo III and resigned in 730. He died around 733. Their memory is celebrated together.

life|05-13||Αγία Γλυκερία||Glykeria was a young woman of Heraclea in Thrace, the daughter of an official. In the persecution of Antoninus (2nd century) she refused to sacrifice to the gods. // They threw her to wild beasts and she was martyred. Her relics were later transferred to Constantinople.

life|05-14||Άγιος Ισίδωρος||Isidore was a soldier and a Christian in Chios, in the time of Decius, around 251. He was arrested and, according to the Synaxarion, beheaded. // He is the patron saint of Chios, and his church on the island is among the best-known places of pilgrimage.

life|05-15||Όσιος Παχώμιος ο Μέγας||Pachomius was born in 292 in Upper Egypt to pagan parents. In the army he met Christians who helped them, and he too became a Christian. // He founded the first cenobitic monastery at Tabennisi and wrote his rule. He died in 346.

life|05-16||Όσιος Θεόδωρος ο Ηγιασμένος||Theodore was a disciple of Pachomius, and became abbot after him. He was known for his kindness and humility. // He was the continuer of cenobitic monasticism in Egypt, and he died in 368.

life|05-17||Απόστολοι Ανδρόνικος και Ιουνιάς||Paul, at the end of his epistle to the Romans, greets Andronicus and Junias, his relatives and fellow prisoners, whom he calls "of note among the apostles" and who became Christians before him. // Andronicus, according to tradition, became Bishop of Pannonia.

life|05-19||Άγιος Πατρίκιος||Patricius was Bishop of Prusa in Bithynia. In the time of Julian the Apostate, in 362, he was arrested together with three companions, Acacius, Menander and Polyaenus. // They did not deny their faith and were beheaded.

life|05-20||Άγιος Θαλλέλαιος||Thalelaios was a physician and came from Lebanon or Cilicia. He healed the sick free of charge and in this way taught Christ. // In the time of Numerian (284) he was arrested, tortured and put to death. In Thessaloniki he is honored, and he is also called Thaleleos.

life|05-22||Άγιος Βασιλίσκος||Basiliscus was a nephew of Theodore the Recruit and a soldier. In the time of Maximian, around 308, he confessed his faith. // He was martyred at Comana in Pontus. Tradition says that John Chrysostom, who died there in exile, saw Basiliscus in a vision.

life|05-23||Όσιος Μιχαήλ ο Ομολογητής||Michael was Bishop of Synada in Phrygia. In the second Iconoclasm, in the time of Leo V, he was exiled because he defended the icons. // He died around 821, at the age of more than sixty, in exile.

life|05-24||Όσιος Συμεών ο εν τω Θαυμαστώ Όρει||Symeon was born in Antioch in 521 and at the age of five climbed onto a pillar, where he lived for years. Later he moved to the "Wondrous Mountain," near Antioch. // He was known for his miracles and his clairvoyance. He died in 596.

life|05-25||Η Τρίτη εύρεση||John the Forerunner was beheaded by Herod, and tradition says that his head was found three times. The third finding took place after Iconoclasm and they transferred it to Constantinople. // On May 25 the Church celebrates the event.

life|05-26||Απόστολος Κάρπος||Carpus was a Christian of Troas who hosted Paul. Paul writes to Timothy to bring him the cloak that he left at the house of Carpus, and the books. // According to tradition, he was one of the Seventy and became Bishop of Beroea in Thrace.

life|05-27||Όσιος Ιωάννης ο Ρώσος||John was a Russian soldier of Peter the Great and was captured by the Tatars in the war of 1711, and sold to the Turks. He served as a slave in Prokopi in Cappadocia. // He lived in a stable, but was always joyful and prayed. His master came to respect him. He died in 1730. His relics were transferred in 1924 by the refugees to Nea Prokopi in Euboea, where they are venerated.

life|05-29||Αγία Θεοδοσία||Theodosia was a pious woman of Constantinople. In 729, when Emperor Leo III ordered the icon of Christ to be taken down from the Chalke Gate of the palace, she, at the head of a group of women, tried to prevent it. // They arrested her and she was martyred. She is among the first victims of Iconoclasm.

life|05-30||Όσιος Ισαάκιος||Isaac was a monk in Constantinople and founded the monastery of Dalmatou. In the time of the Arian emperor Valens he defended the right faith. // He became the spiritual father of many, and he is honored for his zeal in the struggle. He died around 406.
life|05-31||Άγιος Ερμείας||Hermias was a soldier at Comana in Pontus, who openly confessed Christ in the time of Antoninus. // After tortures, he was beheaded, around 160.

life|06-01||Άγιος Ιουστίνος ο Φιλόσοφος||Justin was born in Flavia Neapolis (Nablus) in Palestine, around 100, and sought the truth in various philosophical schools. He met an elderly Christian and became a Christian. // He opened a school in Rome and wrote the "Apologies" addressed to Emperor Antoninus and the Senate, and the "Dialogue with Trypho." He was arrested and beheaded around 165, with companions. He is called "philosopher and martyr."

life|06-02||Άγιος Νικηφόρος ο Ομολογητής||Nikephoros was born in Constantinople, around 758. He was an official and a historian, and in 806 he became patriarch, while still a layman. // In the Iconoclasm of Leo V he refused to condemn the icons, and was exiled in 815 to the monastery he had founded on the Bosphorus. He wrote historical and theological works. He died in 828.

life|06-03||Άγιος Λουκιλλιανός||Lucillian was a pagan priest and became a Christian at Prisa in Bithynia. In the time of Aurelian, in 270, he was arrested. // After the tortures, he was put to death together with four young boys who had believed through him.

life|06-04||Όσιος Μητροφάνης||Metrophanes was the first known bishop of Constantinople, around 315-325. He became Bishop of Byzantium when he was already an old man. // Because of his age he could not attend the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea and sent a representative. He died in 325.

life|06-05||Άγιος Δωρόθεος||Dorotheus was Bishop of Tyre, at the end of the 3rd century. He was exiled in the persecution of Diocletian, and later in the time of Julian. // He wrote historical and moral works and died around 362, in deep old age.

life|06-06||Όσιος Ιλαρίων ο Νέος||Hilarion was born in Dalmatos in Bithynia and became a monk. He founded monasteries in the region. // In the time of the iconoclasts he suffered imprisonments and exile. He died around 845.
life|06-07||Άγιος Θεόδοτος||Theodotus was Bishop of Ancyra, in the time of Diocletian. He cared for imprisoned Christians and buried the martyrs. // He was arrested and beheaded around 303.

life|06-08||Η Μετακομιδή των λειψάνων του Αγίου Θεοδώρου||Theodore the General is honored in Heraclea in Pontus and his relics were transferred to Euchaita, and later to Constantinople. // The Church celebrates their translation.
