life|06-09||Άγιος Κύριλλος, Πατριάρχης Αλεξανδρείας||Cyril was a nephew of Patriarch Theophilus and took the throne in 412. At the Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus (431) he played a leading role against Nestorius, who taught that Mary is not Theotokos. // He left many exegetical and doctrinal works. He died in 444. His principal commemoration is on January 18, together with Athanasius the Great.

life|06-10||Άγιοι Αλέξανδρος και Αντωνίνα||Antonina was a Christian of Alexandria, who was taken to a brothel because she refused to sacrifice to the idols, in the time of Diocletian. // The soldier Alexander helped her escape, exchanging clothes with her. Both were martyred around 313.

life|06-11||Άγιοι Απόστολοι Βαρθολομαίος||Bartholomew was one of the twelve and, according to many, is identified with Nathanael from Cana, of whom Christ said, "Behold, an Israelite indeed." According to tradition, he preached in Armenia and in India. // Barnabas was born in Cyprus, with the name Joseph, and the apostles named him "son of encouragement." He went with Paul to Antioch and to Cyprus, and later with Mark. He was martyred in Salamis in Cyprus. Founder of the Church of Cyprus.

life|06-12||Όσιος Ονούφριος||Onuphrius lived in the desert of the Thebaid, according to his life written by Paphnutius. He spent sixty years alone. // It is said that an angel cared for him and that he had no clothes, only his hair and beard which covered him. He died in the 4th century.

life|06-13||Αγία Ακυλίνα||Aquilina was twelve years old, from Byblos in Phoenicia, and preached Christ to her peers. They denounced her to the governor, who in the time of Diocletian ordered her to be tortured. // She died as a martyr, around 293.

life|06-14||Προφήτης Ελισσαίος||Elisha was a farmer and Elijah called him by throwing his mantle over him. He followed the prophet and, when Elijah was taken up, he took the mantle and continued the work. // The books of Kings relate many of his miracles, such as the healing of Naaman from leprosy. He lived in the 9th century B.C.

life|06-15||Προφήτης Αμώς||Amos was a shepherd and a cultivator of sycamore figs from Tekoa, near Bethlehem, in the 8th century B.C. God called him to prophesy in the northern kingdom of Israel. // He denounced the injustice and the oppression of the poor by the rich and reminded that worship is not enough without justice.

life|06-16||Άγιος Τύχων||Tychon was born in Amathus in Cyprus, the son of a poor potter, and became bishop of the city in the 5th century. // He was known for his charity and, according to his life, for his miracles in the vineyards and in the fields. He is honored as the patron of vine growers.

life|06-17||Άγιοι Μανουήλ||The three Persian brothers, Manuel, Sabel and Ishmael, were sent by the king of Persia as ambassadors to Julian the Apostate. // They found the emperor sacrificing and rebuked him. They were arrested and killed in Chalcedon, around 362.

life|06-18||Άγιοι Λεόντιος||Leontius, Hypatius and Theodulus were soldiers from Phoenicia. In the time of Vespasian (1st century) they confessed Christ. // They were tortured and thrown to wild beasts, and died as martyrs in Tripoli in Phoenicia.

life|06-19||Απόστολος Ιούδας||Jude or Thaddaeus was a relative of the Lord and a brother of James, the first Bishop of Jerusalem. His epistle, a short epistle of the New Testament, warns about false teachers. // According to tradition, he preached in Armenia and in Persia and was martyred.

life|06-20||Άγιος Μεθόδιος||Methodius was Bishop of Olympus and later of Patara in Lycia, and a writer of the 3rd century. The "Symposium," a dialogue that extols virginity, is his best-known work. // According to tradition, he was martyred at the end of the 3rd century or in 311, in Chalcis in Syria.

life|06-21||Άγιος Ιουλιανός ο Μάρτυς της Ταρσού||Julian was a Christian of Cilicia. In the time of Diocletian, around 305, the governor Marcian arrested him. // After many tortures, they put Julian in a sack with snakes and threw him into the sea.

life|06-22||Άγιος Ευσέβιος||Eusebius was Bishop of Samosata in Syria, from 361. He was a friend of Meletius of Antioch and of Basil the Great. // He defended the Orthodox faith against the Arians, and was exiled to Thrace. When he returned, he was killed in 380 by a woman who threw a roof tile at him.

life|06-23||Αγία Αγριππίνα||Agrippina was a young woman of Rome, and in the time of Valerian (253) she was martyred because she was a Christian. // Her relics were transferred to Sicily and the people honored them.

life|06-25||Αγία Φεβρωνία||Febronia was a nun and abbess in a convent of Nisibis in Mesopotamia. She lived in the time of Diocletian. // She was arrested in 304, and despite the tortures and the offers she did not deny Christ. She was beheaded.

life|06-26||Όσιος Δαβίδ||David was born in Thessaloniki, in the 6th century, and became a monk. He lived for three years on an almond tree near the city. // The emperor honored him and invited him to Constantinople, but he died on the way. His monastery in Thessaloniki still exists.

life|06-27||Όσιος Σαμψών||Sampson was born in Rome, into a wealthy family, and was a physician. He moved to Constantinople and became a priest. // He founded a hostel for the poor and the sick, near Hagia Sophia. Justinian, who honored him, gave him money. He died around 530.

life|06-28||Η Μετακομιδή των λειψάνων των Αγίων Κύρου και Ιωάννου||The Unmercenary Saints Cyrus and John were martyred in Alexandria. In 414 Patriarch Cyril transferred their relics to Menouthis, near Canopus. // There, according to tradition, many healings took place.

life|06-30||Σύναξη των Αγίων Δώδεκα Αποστόλων||The twelve apostles are the disciples whom Christ chose: Peter and Andrew, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot and Judas. // After the death of Judas, Matthias was chosen by lot. After Pentecost the apostles preached the Gospel to the world. The Church celebrates them all together on the day after Peter and Paul.

life|07-01||Άγιοι Κοσμάς και Δαμιανός||Cosmas and Damian were brothers and physicians, from Rome (tradition distinguishes three pairs of Unmercenaries with these names). They healed without payment and in this way brought many to Christ. // They were martyred in Rome, around 284, in the time of Carinus. They are honored as patrons of physicians.

life|07-02||Η Κατάθεση της Τιμίας Εσθήτος||According to tradition, two noblemen, Galbius and Candidus, brought from Palestine the robe of the Theotokos and placed it in the church of Blachernae, in the time of Leo I (around 458). // The Church celebrates the deposition and honors the protection of the Theotokos in Constantinople.

life|07-03||Άγιος Υάκινθος||Hyacinth was an official at the court of Trajan and a Christian, from Caesarea in Cappadocia. He was accused of not eating food sacrificed to idols. // He was martyred in the time of Trajan (2nd century) by hunger and tortures.

life|07-04||Άγιος Ανδρέας, αρχιεπίσκοπος Κρήτης||Andrew was born in Damascus around 660 and became a monk in Jerusalem. He became a deacon in Constantinople and then Archbishop of Gortyna in Crete. // He wrote homilies and hymns, and the "Great Canon," which is sung on the Thursday of the fifth week of Lent and is the longest canon of the Church. He died in 740.

life|07-06||Όσιος Σισώης||Sisoes was born in Egypt and became a monk in Scetis, and then on the Mountain of Anthony. He was among the best-known ascetics. // The "Sayings of the Fathers" preserve many of his words, which show humility and repentance. He died around 429.

life|07-07||Αγία Κυριακή||Kyriaki was born in Nicomedia, and her parents, Dorotheus and Eusebia, named her so because she was born on a Sunday. In the persecution of Diocletian, around 289, she confessed Christ. // They tortured her greatly, and finally she died. She is especially honored in Greece, and many churches bear her name.

life|07-08||Άγιος Προκόπιος||Procopius was born in Jerusalem and was called Neanias. An official of the Romans, he was sent to Alexandria. // On the way, as his life says, he saw a cross in the sky and became a Christian. He refused to sacrifice to the gods and was the first martyr of Diocletian in Palestine, in 303.

life|07-10||Οι Άγιοι Μάρτυρες της Νικοπόλεως||Forty-five Christians in Nicopolis in Armenia, in the time of Licinius (around 320), did not deny their faith. // They were put to death in various ways. The Church honors them together.

life|07-13||Σύναξη του Αρχαγγέλου Γαβριήλ||Gabriel is the angel who appears in the book of the prophet Daniel and in the Gospels, as a messenger of God. He announced to Mary the birth of Christ. // The Church celebrates him twice during the year, on March 26 and on July 13, and on November 8 with the other angels.

life|07-14||Απόστολος Ακύλας||Aquila was a Jew from Pontus and a tentmaker. He lived in Rome with his wife Priscilla, but was expelled by Claudius and went to Corinth. // There he hosted Paul, who worked with them. He accompanied them to Ephesus and is among his close co-workers.

life|07-15||Άγιοι Κήρυκος και Ιουλίττα||Julitta was a Christian of Iconium, who fled with her three-year-old child Cyricus when the persecution began. In Tarsus she was arrested. // The governor took the child, who however kept shouting that he was a Christian, and threw him down the stairs. Julitta was tortured and beheaded, around 305.

life|07-16||Άγιος Αθηνογένης||Athenogenes was a bishop and physician in Pidachthoe in Cappadocia, and was martyred with ten of his disciples in the time of Diocletian. // It is said that, before he died, he wrote the hymn "O Gladsome Light of the holy glory," which is sung every evening at Vespers.

life|07-17||Αγία Μαρίνα||Marina was born in Antioch in Pisidia, the daughter of a pagan priest. Her nurse brought her to Christianity, and her father cast her out. // The governor Olybrius fell in love with her, and when she refused, he tortured her and beheaded her, in 304 or 307. In Greece she is honored as the protector of children and of the sick.

life|07-19||Αγία Μακρίνα||Macrina was born in 327 in Caesarea in Cappadocia and was the eldest of the ten children of the family. She was betrothed, but her fiancé died and she did not marry. // She became a teacher of her siblings and founded a community of women in Pontus. Gregory of Nyssa wrote her life. She died in 379, a few months after Basil.

life|07-21||Όσιος Συμεών ο δια Χριστόν σαλός||Symeon was born in Edessa in Syria and together with his friend John became a monk. After thirty years, he went to Emesa. // He pretended to be mad in order to hide his holiness and in this way accepted contempt, while he helped the poor and the people. He died around 590.

life|07-22||Αγία Μαρία η Μαγδαληνή||Mary came from Magdala in Galilee and Christ had healed her. She followed Jesus and was present at the crucifixion. // When she went to the tomb, on Sunday morning, the Risen Christ appeared first to her and sent her to tell the disciples. For this reason she is honored as equal to the apostles. According to tradition, she died in Ephesus.

life|07-23||Άγιος Απολλινάριος||Apollinaris was, according to tradition, a disciple of Peter who was sent to Ravenna, where he became the first bishop of the city. // Many believed through him and he suffered much from the pagans. He died around 79. Ravenna honors him with the basilica of Sant'Apollinare.

life|07-24||Αγία Χριστίνα||Christina was from Tyre, the daughter of an official, who tortured her when she became a Christian. // Finally she died by arrows, around 287 (or in the time of Diocletian).

life|07-25||Η Κοίμηση της Αγίας Άννας||Anna and Joachim are, according to the Protoevangelium of James, the parents of the Theotokos, who had no children until their old age. // The Church honors Anna with many feasts. It regards her as the protector of mothers. Her church in Constantinople was built by Justinian.

life|07-28||Απόστολοι Πρόχορος||Prochorus and Nicanor were two of the seven deacons of Jerusalem, together with Stephen, as the Acts mention. // According to tradition, Prochorus became Bishop of Nicomedia and Nicanor was martyred in Cyprus.
life|07-29||Άγιος Καλλίνικος||Kallinikos was Bishop of Gangra in Paphlagonia. Little is known about his life. // The Church honors him as a martyr and confessor.

life|07-30||Απόστολοι Σίλας||Silas or Silvanus was one of the leaders of the church of Jerusalem and accompanied Paul on the second journey. He was with him at Philippi and at Thessaloniki. // Crescens, Epaenetus and Andronicus are mentioned in the epistles of Paul as his co-workers.

life|07-31||Δίκαιος Ευδόκιμος||Eudokimos was born in Cappadocia, in the time of Theophilos, and belonged to a noble family. He was known for his charity. // He died young, around 840, and the people honor him as an example of kindness.

life|08-01||Προοδός του Τιμίου Σταυρού||August 1 is the beginning of the fast of the Dormition, and the Church brings out the Precious Cross for veneration, as a "procession." // On the same day the seven Maccabee brothers and their mother Solomone are honored, who according to the book of Maccabees were martyred under Antiochus IV (2nd century B.C.) because they did not deny the Law.

life|08-02||Η Μετακομιδή των λειψάνων του Πρωτομάρτυρος Στεφάνου||The relics of Stephen were found in the village of Kafargamala near Jerusalem in 415, after a vision of the priest Lucian. // They were transferred to Jerusalem and later, in 439, to Constantinople, in the time of Theodosius II.

life|08-03||Όσιοι Ισαάκιος||Isaac was a Syrian monk who came to Constantinople in the time of Valens. Dalmatos was a soldier who left his family and became his disciple, and later abbot of the monastery. // Faustus was the son of Dalmatos. The three defended the right faith, and their monastery in Constantinople became known as the monastery of Dalmatou.

life|08-04||Οι Άγιοι Επτά Παίδες της Εφέσου||In the time of Decius, around 250, seven young men of Ephesus, Christians, hid in a cave to escape the persecution, and they were walled in. // According to tradition, they fell asleep and woke after almost two hundred years, in the time of Theodosius II, when Christianity was by then accepted. In the Middle Ages the event became known throughout the world, and in the Quran.

life|08-05||Όσιος Ευσίγνιος||Eusignius was a soldier in the time of Constantine the Great and lived many years. In the time of Julian, he was already over ninety years old. // He openly confessed his faith before Julian and was beheaded in Antioch.
life|08-07||Όσιος Δομέτιος||Dometius was born in Persia and became a Christian. In Syria he became a monk and was a priest. // In the time of Julian, one of the imperial men killed him, around 363.
life|08-08||Άγιος Αιμιλιανός||Aemilianus was Bishop of Cyzicus and a confessor in the time of the iconoclasts, around 800. // Emperor Leo V exiled him. He died in exile, around 820.

life|08-09||Απόστολος Ματθίας||Matthias was among the disciples who followed Jesus from the beginning. After the Ascension, the apostles cast lots between Matthias and Barsabbas to replace Judas, and the lot fell on Matthias, as the Acts say. // According to tradition, he preached in Judea and in Ethiopia and was martyred.

life|08-10||Άγιος Λαυρέντιος||Lawrence was an archdeacon of Rome, in the time of Pope Sixtus II. After the arrest of Sixtus in 258, Emperor Valerian asked Lawrence for the treasures of the Church. // He distributed the money to the poor and pointed to the poor as the "treasures of the Church." According to tradition, they roasted him on a grill, in 258.

life|08-11||Άγιος Εύπλος||Euplus was a deacon of Catania in Sicily. In the time of Diocletian, in 304, he was arrested because he had the Gospel with him. // The governor interrogated him and, when he refused to hand it over, beheaded him.

life|08-12||Άγιοι Φώτιος και Ανίκητος||Photius and Anicetus were nephew and uncle, from Nicomedia. In the time of Diocletian, they confessed Christ. // After tortures, they died as martyrs, around 305.

life|08-13||Απόδοση της Μεταμορφώσεως||The feast of the Transfiguration (August 6) lasts a week and the Church concludes it today, with the "leave-taking." // On this day it also remembers Venerable Maximus the Confessor, who died on August 13, 662 in exile, after the tortures.

life|08-14||Προεόρτια της Κοιμήσεως||The eve of the feast of the Dormition of the Theotokos is the forefeast and the Church prepares with hymns. // On this day the prophet Micah (8th century B.C.) is also honored, who prophesied that from Bethlehem would come the ruler of Israel.

life|08-16||Άγιος Διομήδης||Diomedes was born in Tarsus in Cilicia and was a physician. He became a Christian and healed the sick with prayer. // In the time of Diocletian, around 298, he was arrested and beheaded in Nicaea.
life|08-17||Άγιος Μύρων||Myron was Bishop of Crete and was known for his care for the sick and the poor. They honor him as the patron of Crete. // He died around 350, in deep old age.

life|08-18||Άγιοι Φλώρος||Florus and Laurus were twins, from Illyria, and worked as stonemasons. They were called to build a temple of idols and, as the life says, they built a church. // The rulers killed them, around 170. They are honored as protectors of horses and of livestock breeders.

life|08-19||Άγιος Ανδρέας ο Στρατηλάτης||Andrew was a high-ranking officer in the Roman army and, according to his life, fought victoriously in Cilicia against the Persians. // He was baptized together with 2,593 of his soldiers. Maximian pursued them. Andrew and his men were killed, around 300, in the Taurus.

life|08-20||Προφήτης Σαμουήλ||Samuel was born of Hannah, who had prayed for many years for a child, and was dedicated from a young age to the temple of Shiloh. // He became the last judge and the prophet who anointed the first two kings of Israel, Saul and later David, around the 11th century B.C. Two books of the Old Testament bear his name.

life|08-21||Απόστολος Θαδδαίος||Thaddaeus was one of the twelve, also known as Lebbaeus and Judas of James. According to tradition, he preached in Edessa in Mesopotamia and healed King Abgar. // Tradition says that he was martyred in Armenia.

life|08-22||Άγιος Αγαθόνικος||Agathonicus was a Christian of Nicomedia, in the time of Diocletian, and was martyred with Zoticus and others, who were thrown into the sea. // The sources are few; the Church honors him as a martyr of the 4th century.

life|08-23||Η Απόδοση της εορτής της Κοιμήσεως||The feast of the Dormition has eight days after the feast and the Church concludes the celebration on August 23. // The hymns of the day repeat the troparia of the Dormition.

life|08-25||Απόστολος Τίτος||Titus was a Greek, a disciple and co-worker of Paul, who sent him to Corinth. Paul wrote him an epistle, which belongs to the New Testament. // According to tradition, Paul left him in Crete, where he became the first bishop and died in deep old age. On the same day the Church also celebrates the translation of the relics of Bartholomew.

life|08-26||Άγιοι Αδριανός και Ναταλία||Adrian was an officer in Nicomedia. Seeing the courageous stance of the Christians during the persecution of Maximian, he too confessed Christ, and they imprisoned him. // His wife Natalia, who was secretly a Christian, supported him in prison and cared for him. Adrian was martyred in 306 and Natalia died shortly after.

life|08-28||Όσιος Μωυσής ο Αιθίοπας||Moses was a slave from Ethiopia, who was dismissed for robbery, and became the leader of a band of robbers. Then he repented and became a monk in Scetis. // He became known for his humility. The text of the Sayings says that, when he was accused at a council, he went on his own carrying a leaking basket of sand, to show that his sins follow him. He died around 405, as a martyr, in an attack by barbarians.

life|08-30||Άγιοι Αλέξανδρος||Alexander was Patriarch of Constantinople at the beginning of the 4th century, who resisted Arius. John IV the Faster (6th century) and Paul the Younger (8th century) were also patriarchs. // The Church honors all three together, because they defended the right faith.

life|08-31||Η Κατάθεση της Τιμίας Ζώνης||According to tradition, the belt of the Theotokos was kept in Jerusalem and, in the time of Emperor Arcadius (around 400), was transferred to Constantinople and placed in a church. // The Church celebrates its deposition, and the belt is regarded as a protection. Today it is kept at the Vatopedi Monastery on Mount Athos.

life|09-01||Αρχή της Ινδίκτου||September 1 is the first day of the ecclesiastical year. In Byzantium it was the beginning of the "indiction," the fifteen-year tax cycle, and it remained the New Year's Day until about 1800. // On this day the Venerable Symeon the Stylite is also commemorated. He was born around 390 in Syria and lived on a pillar near Antioch for thirty-seven years. Many pilgrims and emperors sought his counsel. He died in 459.

life|09-03||Άγιος Ανθίμος||Anthimus was Bishop of Nicomedia and was leading the Church of the city when Diocletian's persecution began in 303. He continued to celebrate the services and to teach in secret. // He was arrested and beheaded, together with many Christians of the city.

life|09-05||Προφήτης Ζαχαρίας||Zechariah was a priest in the Temple of Jerusalem, married to Elizabeth, childless and advanced in years. According to the Gospel of Luke, when he was burning incense in the Temple, the angel Gabriel appeared and announced to him that he would have a son, John. // Because he did not believe, he remained mute until the birth of the child, when he wrote "His name is John," and he spoke and praised God. Tradition says that he was killed in the Temple by men of Herod.

life|09-06||Το θαύμα του Αρχαγγέλου Μιχαήλ||At Chonae (the ancient Colossae in Phrygia) there was a church of the Archangel Michael near a spring with healing water. The pagans tried to destroy it and diverted two rivers toward the church. // According to tradition, the Archangel struck the rock, and the water of the rivers disappeared into a chasm. Thus he saved the church and the pilgrim Archippus, who looked after it.

life|09-07||Προεόρτια του Γενεθλίου||On the eve of the feast of the Nativity of the Theotokos the Church observes the forefeast, with hymns that prepare for the event. // In Cyprus the Saint Sozomenos is honored, a young shepherd from Galata who became a monk and, according to tradition, was martyred around 300. His church is in the village of Orounta.

life|09-09||Άγιοι Θεοπάτορες||Joachim and Anna are the parents of the Virgin Mary, and are called "Theopators" (God-fathers, the ancestors of God). The Protoevangelium of James, an apocryphal text of the 2nd century, relates that they were elderly and childless, and they prayed. // The angel announced to them that they would have a child, and Mary was born. The Church honors them on the day after her nativity.

life|09-10||Αγίες Μηνοδώρα||The three sisters Menodora, Metrodora and Nymphodora lived together in a place near Nicomedia in Bithynia, in prayer and fasting. // In the time of Maximian they were arrested and martyred, around 305.

life|09-11||Οσία Θεοδώρα της Αλεξανδρείας||Theodora was married in Alexandria, in the time of Zeno. After a transgression, she repented and left her home. // Wearing men's clothes, she became a monk at the monastery of Saint Sabbas and spent many years under the name Theodore. Only after her death, around 491, was it discovered that she was a woman.

life|09-12||Άγιος Αυτόνομος||Autonomus was a priest and bishop in Bithynia. In the time of Diocletian he left Italy and founded a church in Bithynia. // The pagans killed him at the altar, around 313.

life|09-13||Τα Εγκαίνια του Ναού της Αναστάσεως||The Empress Helena and Constantine the Great built in Jerusalem the complex of the Holy Sepulchre and Golgotha. The dedication took place in 335, on September 13. // The next day the Exaltation of the Cross is celebrated.

life|09-15||Άγιος Νικήτας ο Μεγαλομάρτυς||Nicetas was a Goth who became a Christian through Ulfilas, the bishop of the Goths. When King Athanaric persecuted the Christians, Nicetas was arrested and thrown into the fire, around 372. // His relics were taken to Mopsuestia in Cilicia.

life|09-16||Αγία Ευφημία||Euphemia was born in Chalcedon, of a noble family, and in the time of Diocletian she confessed Christ, around 303. After many tortures, she died. // Her church in Chalcedon hosted the Fourth Ecumenical Council in 451. The Church celebrates the same saint also on July 11.

life|09-17||Αγίες Πίστις||Sophia (that is, "wisdom") was a widow in Rome, in the time of Hadrian (2nd century), with three daughters: Faith, Hope and Love, twelve, ten and nine years old. The names are the three Christian virtues. // They were arrested because they were Christians. The girls were martyred one after the other, and the mother stayed at their tomb, and died after three days.

life|09-18||Όσιος Ευμένιος||Eumenius was born in Gortyn and became bishop of the city, and went to Asia. He was known for his ascetic life. // He died at a great old age and the people of Crete honor him as a wonderworker.

life|09-19||Άγιος Τρόφιμος||Trophimus was from Antioch in Pisidia. In the time of Diocletian (276, according to some sources), the governor Dion interrogated him. // Trophimus, Sabbatius and Dorymedon died as martyrs and the Christians buried their relics.

life|09-20||Άγιος Ευστάθιος ο Μεγαλομάρτυς||Placidas, as he was called before he became a Christian, was a senior officer of Trajan. According to tradition, while hunting a deer, he saw the Cross between its antlers and heard the voice of Christ. // He was baptized and took the name Eustathius. He lost his wealth and his family, but after adventures he was reunited with his wife Theopiste and his sons Agapius and Theopistus. In the time of Hadrian they refused to offer sacrifice and were put to death.

life|09-21||Απόστολος Κοδράτος||Quadratus was Bishop of the Athenians in the time of Hadrian, around 125. He wrote an Apology for the Christian faith, which he gave to the emperor, and it was the first one, which Eusebius mentioned. // The Prophet Jonah, according to the book that bears his name, was sent by God to Nineveh to preach repentance, and, after first trying to flee, was thrown into the sea and swallowed by a great fish, from which he emerged after three days. The Church sees in the story a prefiguration of the Resurrection.

life|09-22||Άγιος Φωκάς||Phocas was a gardener in Sinope in Pontus and very hospitable. According to his life, he welcomed the soldiers who were looking for him and did not know him. // When they told him that they were searching for Phocas, he showed them around, and in the morning he presented himself. He was beheaded, around 117. Sailors honor him.

life|09-23||Η σύλληψη του Αγίου Ιωάννου||The feast recalls that, according to the Gospel of Luke, the angel announced to Zechariah, in the Temple, that his wife Elizabeth would bear a son. // The Conception of the Forerunner, nine months before his birth (June 24), has been celebrated since the 5th-6th century.

life|09-24||Αγία Θέκλα||Thecla was born in Iconium and, according to the "Acts of Paul and Thecla," upon hearing Paul preach, she believed and refused to marry her fiancé. // They condemned her to be burned, but, according to tradition, she was saved by rain. She accompanied Paul and later lived in Seleucia in Isauria. She is honored as the Protomartyr among women, in the 1st century.

life|09-25||Οσία Ευφροσύνη||Euphrosyne was the daughter of a wealthy man of Alexandria, and her father wanted to marry her off. According to her life, she left secretly and became a monk under the name Smaragdus, in a men's monastery. // Her father searched for her for years and met "the monk Smaragdus" without recognizing her. Only after her death, around 470, was it revealed who she was.

life|09-26||Μετάσταση του Αγίου Ιωάννη||John the Theologian, according to tradition, lived in Ephesus until about the age of one hundred and was the only one of the twelve who died a natural death. // On the day of his death he departed from his disciples and they found that he had died, and his tomb remained empty. The Church calls him "the Theologian" and "the beloved disciple."

life|09-27||Άγιος Καλλίστρατος||Callistratus was a soldier of Carthage, in the time of Diocletian, and a Christian. According to his life, he was martyred with forty-nine companions, around 300. // They were thrown into the sea in sacks, and, according to tradition, their relics came out intact and the Christians buried them.

life|09-28||Όσιος Χαρίτων||Chariton was born in Iconium and became a confessor in the time of Aurelian, around 275. He went to Palestine and founded three monasteries, Pharan, Douka and Souka. // He is considered the founder of the "lavra," the monastic way of life with separate cells around a common church. He died around 350.

life|09-29||Όσιος Κυριακός||Cyriacus was born in Corinth in 448 and left for Palestine. He lived in the lavra of Euthymius and Gerasimus. // He lived in the desert until the age of one hundred and nine, and died in 557.

life|09-30||Άγιος Γρηγόριος ο Φωτιστής||Gregory was born in Armenia around 257 and grew up a Christian in Cappadocia. When he returned, King Tiridates III threw him into a pit for years, because he refused to worship the idols. // When the king fell ill and was healed through the prayers of Gregory, he was baptized, around 301, and Armenia became the first country to officially adopt Christianity. Gregory became its first bishop, and died about 331.

life|10-01||Όσιος Ρωμανός ο Μελωδός||Romanos was born in Emesa in Syria, around 490, and became a deacon in Beirut and later in Constantinople. // According to tradition, one night, while he was sleeping, the Theotokos gave him a scroll to eat, and in the morning he chanted in church his first kontakion, "Today the Virgin." He wrote many kontakia, hymns in the form of poetic homilies. He died about 556.

life|10-02||Άγιος Κυπριανός||Cyprian was a magician in Antioch and had tried with sorcery to win Justina, a young Christian woman, on behalf of a suitor. He did not succeed and became convinced of the power of Christ. // He was baptized, became a bishop and, together with Justina, was arrested in Nicomedia and beheaded, in 304.

life|10-04||Άγιος Ιερόθεος||Hierotheus was an Athenian judge, like Dionysius, and was among the first Athenians who followed Paul. // According to tradition, he became Bishop of Athens and was present at the Dormition of the Theotokos. Dionysius mentions him as his teacher.

life|10-05||Αγία Χαριτίνη||Charitina was a slave in Amisos in Pontus, and worked for Claudius, a powerful man. Because she was a Christian, she was denounced to Diocletian. // After tortures she died about 304.

life|10-06||Άγιος Θωμάς ο Απόστολος||Thomas was one of the twelve, also called "the Twin." In the Gospel of John he did not believe that Christ had risen, until he saw him and touched his wounds, and said "My Lord and my God." // Tradition says that he preached in Persia and traveled to India, where he founded churches and was martyred. The Christians of Kerala honor him as their founder.

life|10-08||Οσία Πελαγία||Pelagia was an actress and dancer in Antioch in the 5th century and was very well known for her beauty and her way of life. Bishop Nonnus, who wept for her sin, once heard her preach. // Pelagia repented, was baptized, and went to the Mount of Olives, where she lived dressed in men's clothes as a hermit under the name Pelagius, until her death.

life|10-09||Απόστολος Ιάκωβος του Αλφαίου||James the son of Alphaeus was one of the twelve, and Matthew was, according to tradition, his brother. The Gospels say very little about him. // According to tradition, he preached in Judea and in Egypt and was martyred.

life|10-10||Άγιοι Ευλάμπιος||Eulampius and his sister Eulampia were from Nicomedia. In the persecution of Maximian, Eulampius confessed Christ and they tortured him. // His sister ran to help him, she too saw the martyrdom and was martyred in 303.

life|10-11||Απόστολος Φίλιππος ο Διάκονος||Philip was one of the seven deacons whom the apostles chose in Jerusalem. After the death of Stephen he preached in Samaria and baptized the Ethiopian eunuch, on the road to Gaza, as the Acts relate. // He lived in Caesarea of Palestine with his four prophetess daughters, and tradition makes him Bishop of Tralles.

life|10-12||Άγιοι Πρόβος||Probus, Tarachus and Andronicus were Christians who were arrested in the persecution of Diocletian and interrogated in Tarsus, around 304. // After many ordeals, they were thrown to wild beasts in Mopsuestia, and were martyred in Anazarbus.
life|10-13||Άγιοι Κάρπος||Carpus was Bishop of Thyatira and Papylus a deacon, and they lived in Pergamum. // In the time of Decius, around 250, they refused to offer sacrifice and were martyred.

life|10-14||Οσία Παρασκευή η νέα||Paraskevi was born in Epivates in Thrace in the 11th century, of pious parents. From childhood she gave whatever she had to the poor. // She went to the Jordan and then returned to Thrace. She died young, and the faithful say that she healed people. Her relics were also taken to Iași in Romania in 1641, where the people venerate them.

life|10-15||Όσιος Ευθύμιος ο Νέος||Euthymius was born in the East in 823, near Ankyra, and became a monk on Olympus. Later he went to Mount Athos. // He founded a monastery near Thessaloniki. He died in 898.

life|10-17||Προφήτης Ωσηέ||Hosea lived in the 8th century B.C. in the northern kingdom of Israel. God asked him to marry a woman who was not faithful, so that his marriage would become a symbol of God's relationship with the people. // His book speaks of the love of God who forgives. "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice," he says, and Christ repeats the words in the Gospels.

life|10-18||Άγιος Λουκάς ο Απόστολος||Luke came from Antioch in Syria, was a physician and, as it appears, a pagan who became a Christian. He became a companion of Paul and followed him to Rome. // He wrote the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. Tradition says that he painted icons of the Theotokos, and for this reason he is also honored as the patron of painters. He died, according to tradition, in Thebes in Boeotia, at the age of eighty-four.

life|10-19||Προφήτης Ιωήλ||Joel was a prophet in Jerusalem, perhaps in the 5th or 4th century B.C. His book begins with an invasion of locusts, which is described as a day of judgment. // He prophesied that God would send his Spirit upon all. Peter refers to this prophecy on the day of Pentecost, in the Acts.

life|10-21||Όσιος Ιλαρίων ο Μέγας||Hilarion was born in 291 in Gaza, and studied in Alexandria, where he became a Christian. He visited Anthony the Great in the desert and then became the founder of monasticism in Palestine. // Late in his life he went to Cyprus, where he died in 371. Jerome wrote his life. In Cyprus there is a castle that bears his name.

life|10-22||Άγιος Αβέρκιος||Abercius was Bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia, in the 2nd century. He traveled to Rome and to Syria. // An inscription that he himself wrote for his tomb, the "Inscription of Abercius," is one of the oldest Christian texts that have survived. He died about 167.

life|10-23||Άγιος Ιάκωβος ο Απόστολος||James was "the brother of the Lord," and the Acts show him leading the Church of Jerusalem and presiding at the Apostolic Council, in 49. // The Catholic Epistle that bears his name insists that "faith without works is dead." According to the historian Josephus, the high priest had him stoned in 62. The liturgy that bears his name is the oldest of the Church.

life|10-24||Άγιος Αρέθας||Arethas was the leader of the Christian community of Najran, in southern Arabia. The king of the Jewish Himyarites, Dhu Nuwas, captured the city in 523. // He refused to deny Christ and was killed together with many others. The Church honors them as the martyrs of Najran. The event led the king of Ethiopia to intervene.

life|10-27||Άγιος Νέστωρ||Nestor was a young Christian of Thessaloniki, a friend of Saint Demetrius. According to tradition, Demetrius gave him his blessing, and Nestor defeated the giant Lyaeus in combat, in the stadium. // Maximian, angered by the victory, put him to death around 306.

life|10-29||Οσία Αναστασία η Ρωμαία||Anastasia was born in Rome and was a high official of the court of Justinian, in the 6th century. The emperor wanted to marry her off. // She fled secretly to Alexandria, and lived in the desert of Scetis with Daniel, hiding that she was a woman. She died about 567, and only then did her story become known.

life|10-30||Άγιοι Ζηνόβιος||Zenobius was a bishop and physician in Aegae in Cilicia, and his sister Zenobia followed him in his work. They healed without payment. // In the time of Diocletian, around 285, they refused to offer sacrifice to the gods and were martyred.

life|10-31||Απόστολοι Στάχυς||Paul, at the end of his Epistle to the Romans, greets Stachys ("my beloved"), Ampliatus, Urbanus ("my fellow worker"), Narcissus, Apelles ("approved in Christ") and the household of Aristobulus. // According to tradition, they were among the seventy disciples and became bishops of various cities. Stachys became the first Bishop of Byzantium.

life|11-02||Άγιοι Ακίνδυνος||Acindynus, Pegasius, Aphthonius, Elpidephorus and Anempodistus were Christians of Persia. In the time of King Shapur II, around 341-345, they were arrested because they did not worship the sun and fire. // After tortures, they were put to death. With them thousands of Christians of Persia were martyred.

life|11-03||Άγιοι Ακεψιμάς||Acepsimas was an elderly bishop of Ionia in Persia, and Joseph was his presbyter. Aithalas was a deacon. // They were arrested around 380 and tortured to make them deny Christ. Acepsimas died in prison and the others were beheaded.

life|11-04||Όσιος Ιωαννίκιος ο Μέγας||Joannicius was born in 754 in Bithynia. He was a shepherd and served in the army of Constantine V for a time. // Afterwards he became a monk on Olympus, and became known for his clairvoyance and for his steadfastness in the Orthodox faith during Iconoclasm. He died in 846, at the age of 92.

life|11-05||Άγιοι Γαλακτίων||Galaction and Episteme were married in Emesa in Syria, and each lived as a monastic. Galaction was a monk and Episteme took care of the poor. // In the time of Decius they were arrested, tortured and beheaded, around 250.

life|11-06||Άγιος Παύλος ο Ομολογητής||Paul was born in Thessaloniki and was the successor of Bishop Alexander as Patriarch of Constantinople (337). He opposed the Arians and supported Nicaea. // He was exiled many times through the intervention of Constantius and died in exile in Cucusus in Armenia in 350, according to tradition strangled.

life|11-07||Οι Άγιοι Τριάντα Τρεις Μάρτυρες||Leontius and thirty-two other soldiers, who served in Melitene in Armenia, confessed their faith. // In the time of Diocletian, around 297, they were put to death.

life|11-08||Σύναξη των Ταξιαρχών||The Archangels are Michael and Gabriel, with all the orders of angels. Michael is mentioned in the book of Daniel and in the Apocalypse as the leader of the angelic powers. // In Greece many churches and monasteries honor the Archangels, such as the monastery of the Archangel Michael Panormitis on Symi.

life|11-10||Απόστολοι Ολυμπάς||Paul, in his Epistle to the Romans, greets Olympas, Rhodion, Sosipater, Tertius, who wrote the epistle, and Erastus, the treasurer of the city of Corinth, and Quartus. // Tradition counts them among the seventy disciples, and makes them bishops. Sosipater preached in Corfu.

life|11-14||Άγιος Φίλιππος ο Απόστολος||Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Peter and Andrew. Jesus called him with the words "Follow me." He immediately brought Nathanael as well. // In the Gospel of John, he asks Christ, "Show us the Father." According to tradition, he preached in Scythia and in Phrygia and was martyred in Hierapolis. The day after his feast the Nativity Fast begins, which is why it is called "Philippiatika."

life|11-15||Άγιοι Γουρίας||Gurias and Samonas were from Edessa in Mesopotamia. In the time of Diocletian, in 297, they refused to offer sacrifice to the gods and were shut up in prison. // Abibus was a deacon and was martyred in 322, in the time of Licinius. All three are honored in Edessa.

life|11-16||Απόστολος και Ευαγγελιστής Ματθαίος||Matthew, who was also called Levi, was a tax collector in Capernaum. Jesus saw him at the tax office and said to him "Follow me," and Matthew rose and followed him. // The first Gospel, which bears his name, was written for Jewish Christians. According to tradition, he preached in Judea and in Ethiopia and was martyred.

life|11-18||Άγιος Πλάτων||Plato was a young man from Ancyra and, from childhood, a Christian. In the time of Diocletian he helped the Christians and was arrested in 306. // After tortures, he was beheaded. The Church honors him as a martyr.

life|11-19||Προφήτης Αβδιού||Obadiah is the author of the shortest book of the Old Testament, with just one chapter. // The book deals with the punishment of Edom, because it took advantage of the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C., and prophesies that "the kingdom shall be the Lord's."

life|11-20||Προεόρτια των Εισοδίων||On the eve of the feast of the Entry of the Theotokos into the Temple the Church observes the forefeast. // On this day the Venerable Gregory the Decapolite is also commemorated, who was born in Irenopolis in Isauria around 780. He traveled to many places, from Thessaloniki to Rome, preached and defended the icons. He died in 842 in Constantinople.

life|11-22||Απόστολοι Φιλήμων||Philemon, Archippus and Apphia were Christians of Colossae. The gathering of the church took place in the house of Philemon, and Paul wrote him the epistle about Onesimus. // Tradition says that all three were honored with martyrdom in the time of Nero, and that Philemon and Apphia were husband and wife.

life|11-23||Άγιοι Αμφιλόχιος||Amphilochius was born about 340 in Cappadocia, was a cousin of Gregory the Theologian and a friend of Basil the Great. He became Bishop of Iconium in 373. // Basil dedicated to him the work "On the Holy Spirit." Amphilochius took part in the Second Ecumenical Council and died about 395. Gregory was Bishop of Acragas in Sicily, at the end of the 6th century, and was known for his piety and learning.

life|11-24||Άγιος Κλήμης, Πάπας Ρώμης||Clement was the third or fourth Bishop of Rome, at the end of the 1st century. Tradition considers him a disciple of Peter and Paul. // He wrote an epistle to the Church of Corinth, around 96, to calm a dispute. It is among the oldest Christian texts after the books of the New Testament. According to tradition, he was exiled to the Crimea by Trajan, and was killed.

life|11-26||Όσιος Στυλιανός||Stylianos was born in Paphlagonia, in the 6th century, and lived as an ascetic. According to his life, he healed children through his prayer. // The people honor him as the protector of children, and Stylianos is depicted with an infant in his arms.

life|11-27||Άγιος Ιάκωβος ο Πέρσης||James was an official at the court of the king of Persia Yazdegerd I, and a Christian. To keep his position he denied his faith. // His mother and his wife rebuked him, he repented, and when King Bahram V had him tortured, James's limbs were cut off, one by one. He died in 421, and has remained known as "the Dismembered."

life|11-28||Άγιος Στέφανος ο Νέος||Stephen was born in Constantinople in 715 and became a monk on Mount Auxentius, where he lived as a hermit. He was the best-known opponent of the iconoclast Constantine V. // The emperor shut him up in prison, and on November 28, 764 the mob dragged him out and pulled him through the streets, and he died.

life|11-29||Άγιος Παράμονος||Paramon was a Christian of Bithynia. In the time of Decius, around 250, he was arrested together with 370 Christians. // Tradition says that all were killed on the same day, in Bithynia. Paramon was their leader.

life|12-01||Προφήτης Ναούμ||Nahum was a prophet in Judea, in the 7th century B.C., from Elkosh. His book prophesies the fall of Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrians, which took place in 612 B.C. // It shows that God renders justice to unjust nations and protects his own.

life|12-02||Προφήτης Αββακούμ||Habakkuk lived in Judea around 600 B.C., at the time when the Babylonians became a power. His book begins with the question why God permits injustice. // The answer is "the righteous shall live by my faith," a phrase which Paul cites in the Epistle to the Romans. His "Ode" closes the book and is chanted in the Church.

life|12-03||Προφήτης Σοφονίας||Zephaniah prophesied in Jerusalem in the years of King Josiah, at the end of the 7th century B.C. // His book speaks of the "day of the Lord," a day of judgment and, at the same time, of hope for the humble of the people, whom God will preserve.

life|12-08||Όσιος Πατάπιος||Patapius was born in Thebes in Egypt, and became a monk, and then went to Constantinople, in the 7th century. // He lived with severe asceticism in a cell near the church of Blachernae. He died about 650 and his church near the Wall became a place of pilgrimage.

life|12-09||Η Σύλληψη της Θεοτόκου||The feast is based on the tradition of the Protoevangelium of James that Mary was conceived by Anna, who until then had been childless, after her prayers. // The feast has existed in the East since the 7th century and is celebrated nine months before the nativity of the Theotokos (September 8).

life|12-10||Άγιοι Μηνάς, Ερμογένης||Menas, Hermogenes and Eugraphus were Christians of Alexandria. Menas was a man of proven worth and Eugraphus was secretary to Hermogenes, governor of Egypt. // In the persecution of Maximian, they were the ones who confessed Christ and were put to death, around 313.

life|12-13||Άγιοι Ευστράτιος||Eustratius, Auxentius, Eugenius, Mardarius and Orestes were Christians from Armenia. In the time of Diocletian, around 296, they did not deny their faith. // After tortures they were put to death. On the same day Saint Lucy of Syracuse is honored, who was martyred in 304 and is honored as the protector of the eyes and of light.
life|12-14||Άγιοι Θύρσος||Thyrsus, Leucius and Callinicus were Christians who confessed Christ in Apollonia in Bithynia, in the time of Decius. // They were tortured and beheaded around 249.

life|12-16||Προφήτης Αγγαίος||Haggai prophesied in Jerusalem in 520 B.C., after the Jews returned from the captivity of Babylon. The work of rebuilding the Temple had stopped. // He urged the leader Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua to begin again, and the Temple was completed in 516 B.C.

life|12-17||Προφήτης Δανιήλ||Daniel was a young nobleman of Jerusalem, who was taken captive to Babylon, around 605 B.C. He became an adviser to the king, because he interpreted dreams. // His three friends, Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael ("the Three Holy Youths"), were thrown into a blazing furnace, because they refused to worship a golden statue, and came out unharmed. Daniel was thrown into the lions' den and was saved. In the Church, the Three Holy Youths are chanted in Holy Week and at Christmas.

life|12-18||Άγιος Σεβαστιανός||Sebastian was born in Milan, and was an officer of the imperial guard. He secretly helped the imprisoned Christians. // Diocletian ordered him to be shot with arrows, but he survived and a Christian woman healed him. He presented himself again to the emperor and they killed him with clubs, around 288. He is honored as a protector against the plague.

life|12-19||Άγιος Βονιφάτιος||Boniface was the servant of a wealthy Roman woman, Aglaida, and they lived together in debauchery. Later, both repented. // Boniface went to Tarsus to help the Christian martyrs, and was arrested and put to death, in 307.

life|12-21||Αγία Ιουλιανή||Juliana was a young woman of Nicomedia, and was betrothed to a pagan nobleman, Eleusius. She refused to marry him unless he became a Christian. // She was arrested and tortured in the time of Maximian and beheaded, about 305.

life|12-23||Οι Άγιοι Δέκα Μάρτυρες της Κρήτης||Theodulus, Saturninus, Euporus, Gelasius, Eunician, Zoticus, Pompius, Agathopus, Basil and Evaresthus were Christians of Crete. // In the time of Decius, in 250, they confessed Christ in Gortyn and were beheaded in the city. The Church of Crete honors them as its protectors.

life|12-24||Αγία Ευγενία||Eugenia was the daughter of Philip, the Roman governor of Alexandria, and became a Christian. She left with two servants, dressed as a man, and became a monk in a monastery. // She became abbot. A woman falsely accused her of immorality, and Eugenia revealed that she was a woman. Later, in Rome, she was martyred about 258. On the same day is the Eve of Christmas.

life|12-26||Η Σύναξη της Υπεραγίας Θεοτόκου||On the day after the feast of the Nativity of Christ, the Church honors the Most Holy Theotokos, who gave birth to Christ. The people thank her and gather to glorify her. // The "Synaxis" was the first feast that followed the Nativity, and it already exists from the 4th century.

life|12-28||Οι Άγιοι Είκοσι Χιλιάδες Μάρτυρες||According to tradition, in Nicomedia, on the day of Christmas in 303, Diocletian learned that thousands of Christians had gathered in a church to celebrate. // He ordered the doors to be shut and fire to be set. All died. Their memory is celebrated a few days after Christmas.

life|12-30||Αγία Ανυσία||Anysia lived in Thessaloniki and was rich and a Christian. One day, as she was going to church, a soldier tried to tear off her veil, because she did not have the mark of idolatry. // Anysia refused and spat at him, and the soldier killed her with his sword, in 304.

life|12-31||Οσία Μελάνη||Melania was born in Rome around 383, of a wealthy family. She married young, and, when she lost two children, the couple decided to live in asceticism. // She distributed her enormous fortune to the poor and to churches. She went to Egypt and to Palestine and founded a monastery on the Mount of Olives. She died in 439, after a pilgrimage to Rome and Jerusalem.

life|01-24||Όσιος Νεόφυτος ο Έγκλειστος||Neophytus was born in 1134 in Lefkara in Cyprus, of a poor family, and from childhood wanted to become a monk. His father had betrothed him, but he left and became a monk at the monastery of Saint Chrysostomos, at Koutsovendis. // After a journey to the Holy Places, he settled in a cave near Paphos, which he dug himself and which was called the Enkleistra. Monks gathered around him, and he founded a monastery. // He wrote the "Typikon" of the monastery and many works, among them a description of the trials of Cyprus at the hands of the Franks and Isaac Komnenos. He died after 1214. The frescoes of the Enkleistra are among the most important of the 12th century.

life|05-12||Άγιος Επιφάνιος, Επίσκοπος Κωνσταντίας||Epiphanius was born about 315 near Eleutheropolis in Palestine and became a monk in Egypt. He returned to Palestine and founded a monastery. // In 367 he became Bishop of Constantia (Salamis) and led the Church of Cyprus. He wrote the "Panarion," a work against heresies, and the "Ancoratus." He was a strict defender of the right faith and did not hesitate to enter into disputes, such as with John Chrysostom. // He died in 403, on a sea voyage, returning from Constantinople. Cyprus honors him as one of its great hierarchs.

life|06-11||Θρονική εορτή της Εκκλησίας της Κύπρου||Barnabas was born in Cyprus with the name Joseph, of a noble family of Levites, and the apostles named him Barnabas, "son of consolation." He sold his field and gave the money to the apostles. // He was the one who introduced Paul to the Church of Jerusalem and they traveled together on the first missionary journey, to Cyprus and Asia Minor. Later, with Mark, he returned to Cyprus, where he preached and was martyred in Salamis, around 61. // In 488, Archbishop Anthemius found his tomb, with a copy of the Gospel of Matthew on his chest. The Emperor Zeno, after this, recognized the autocephaly of the Church of Cyprus. The feast of Barnabas is its patronal feast.

life|06-13||Άγιος Τριφύλλιος||Triphyllius was born in Constantinople, around 290, and studied law in Beirut. There he became a Christian. He came to Cyprus and became a disciple of Saint Spyridon. // He became Bishop of Ledra (modern Nicosia) and took part in the Council of Sardica (343). He became known for his eloquence and his writings. He died around 370.

life|07-13||Όσιοι Ηλιόφωτος||Heliophotus, Epaphroditus, Ammonius, Chuleleus and Eustathius were ascetics who lived in Cyprus, in the first years of Christianity on the island. // The sources for their lives are few; the Church of Cyprus honors them together as Venerable Fathers who practiced asceticism in the mountains and caves of the island.

life|09-07||Όσιος Σωζόμενος||Sozomenos was a shepherd from Cyprus, around the 4th century. According to tradition, he was known for his piety and humility, and became a monk. // It is said that, when robbers drove off his sheep, the sheep returned to the fold. His church is in the village of Orounta and he is honored as the protector of herdsmen.

life|10-17||Άγιος Λάζαρος ο τετραήμερος||Lazarus was the brother of Martha and Mary, from Bethany, and a friend of Jesus. According to the Gospel of John, he died and Christ raised him on the fourth day, before many people. // Tradition says that, after the Resurrection of Christ, the Jews pursued him and he came to Cyprus, where Paul and Barnabas made him Bishop of Kition (Larnaca). He lived another thirty years. // His tomb was found in 890 and the relics were taken to Constantinople, while in Larnaca they built the church of Saint Lazarus, one of the best known in Cyprus.

life|01-01||Περιτομή του Ιησού Χριστού||Eight days after his birth, according to the law of Moses, Jesus was circumcised and received his name, as the angel had told Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:21). // The feast shows that Christ was born under the law and kept it. It coincides with the memory of Basil the Great and with the first day of the civil year, which is why on this day the Church asks God's blessing for the new year.

life|01-02||Άγιος Σιλβέστρος Πάπας Ρώμης||Sylvester was Bishop of Rome from 314 to 335, in the years when Constantine the Great stopped the persecutions and favored the Christians. In his days great basilicas were built in Rome, among them Saint John Lateran. // He himself did not attend the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea (325), because of his age, but sent representatives. The Church honors his memory on January 2.

life|01-02||Οσία Ιουλιανή η Δικαία||Juliana lived in Russia in the late 16th and early 17th century, in Lazarevo, near Murom. She married early and raised many children. In the years of famine and the hardships of the time she distributed food and clothing to the poor, and she remained known for her almsgiving and patience. She died in 1604.

life|01-03||Οσία Γενεβιέβη εκ Παρισίων||Genevieve was born around 420 in Nanterre, near Paris, and from childhood dedicated her life to God. She remained in Paris as an ascetic and became famous for her faith and almsgiving. // According to tradition, in 451 she urged the Parisians not to leave the city before Attila, and the city was spared. Later, during the siege of the city by the Franks, she brought food by ships. She died around 502 and is considered the patron saint of Paris.

life|01-03||Οσία Θωμαΐς εκ Λέσβου||Thomais lived on Lesbos in the 10th century. She married and her husband treated her harshly. She endured everything with patience and prayer and took care of the poor. After her death the Church honored her as a venerable saint for her patience.

life|01-04||Οσία Απολλιναρία η Συγκλητική||Apollinaria was the daughter of a Roman nobleman of the 5th century. In order to dedicate herself to the monastic life, she dressed as a man and went to the desert of Egypt under the name Dorotheus, where she lived as a monk. It is said that she managed to keep her identity secret, and only after her death did it become known who she was.

life|01-04||Όσιος Ευθύμιος ο Νέος||Euthymius was born in 823 in Asia Minor. He married, but later became a monk on Olympus in Bithynia and then on Mount Athos, and finally practiced asceticism near Thessaloniki, at the Monastery of Peristerai. He died in 898.

life|01-04||Όσιος Θεόπροβος Επίσκοπος Καρπασίας||Theoprobus was Bishop of Karpasia in Cyprus and practiced asceticism in the years of the first Byzantine period. The Church of Cyprus honors his memory on January 4.

life|01-05||Άγιοι Θεόπεμπτος και Θεωνάς||Theopemptus was Bishop of Nicomedia and Theonas a sorcerer, who believed in Christ through the example of Theopemptus and was baptized. Both were martyred in Nicomedia, around 303, in the persecution of Diocletian.

life|01-07||Άγιος Cedd||Cedd was an English monk from Lindisfarne, brother of Saint Chad. He was sent as a missionary to the East Saxons and became their bishop. He founded monasteries, among them Lastingham. He took part in the Synod of Whitby in 664 as an interpreter and died in the same year.

life|01-08||Άγιος Αττικός Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Atticus was Patriarch of Constantinople from 406 to 425, after Arsacius, and had previously served in Sebasteia. He became patriarch in the years of the disputes over John Chrysostom and, later, restored his name to the diptychs of the Church. He confronted Pelagianism and cared for the poor of the capital.

life|01-08||Άγιος Σεβερίνος||Severinus lived in the 5th century and preached the Gospel in the provinces on the banks of the Danube (Noricum), in a time of upheaval, during the fall of the western empire. He founded monasteries, helped the inhabitants with food and died in 482.

life|01-08||Προφήτης Σαμέας||Shemaiah was a prophet in the time of King Rehoboam, son of Solomon. When the kingdom was divided, Shemaiah conveyed the word of God and dissuaded Rehoboam from civil war with the tribes of the North (1 Kings 12:22-24).

life|01-09||Άγιος Πέτρος Επίσκοπος Σεβαστείας||Peter was born around 340 and was the youngest brother of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa. He lived with his mother Emmelia and his sister Macrina in a community of ascetics. He became a presbyter and then Bishop of Sebasteia (about 380), and fought Arianism. He died in 391.

life|01-09||Άγιος Αδριανός Ηγούμενος Καντουαρίας||Hadrian was a monk of African origin, who lived near Naples. The pope sent him to England together with Theodore of Tarsus. He became abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter in Canterbury and taught Greek and Latin there, until his death in 710.
life|01-09||Άγιος Brithwald||Brithwald (Berhtwald) was Archbishop of Canterbury from 693 to 731. He succeeded Theodore of Tarsus and continued the work of organizing the Church in England.

life|01-10||Όσιος Δομετιανός Επίσκοπος Μελιτηνής||Domitian was a nephew or relative of the Emperor Maurice and became Bishop of Melitene in Armenia. He helped the emperor in diplomatic missions and died in 601.

life|01-11||Άγιος Υγίνος Επίσκοπος Ρώμης||Hyginus was Bishop of Rome in the middle of the 2nd century (about 138-142), in very early Christianity. Tradition mentions him as a Greek from Athens. The Church honors Hyginus as a martyr on January 11.

life|01-12||Άγιος Βενέδικτος||Benedict Biscop was born about 628 in Northumbria in England. He traveled many times to Rome and brought books, icons and craftsmen to his homeland. He founded the monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow, which became centers of learning, and in this monastery the historian Bede grew up. He died in 690.

life|01-12||Άγιος Πέτρος ο Αβεσαλαμίτης||Peter was from the region of Palestine and was martyred in Caesarea of Palestine, in 309, in the persecution of Maximinus Daia, burned in the fire. The Church honors him on January 12.

life|01-13||Άγιος Ιλάριος Επίσκοπος Πικτώνων||Hilary was born about 310 in Poitiers in Gaul and became bishop of the city. He defended the consubstantiality of the Son against the Arians and for this reason was exiled by the Emperor Constantius to Phrygia. In exile he wrote his work "On the Trinity." He returned to Gaul and died in 367. He was called "the Athanasius of the West."

life|01-13||Άγιος Κεντιγκέρνος Επίσκοπος Γλασκόβης||Kentigern, also known as Mungo, was the first bishop of Glasgow and a missionary to the Britons of Strathclyde, in Scotland, in the 6th century. He died around 614. Patron of Glasgow.

life|01-13||Άγιος Ρεμίγιος Επίσκοπος Ρημών||Remigius (Remi) was Bishop of Reims from about 459 to 533. He baptized the king of the Franks Clovis around 496, and thus the Franks became Christians, with an important consequence for the history of Europe.

life|01-14||Όσιος Σάββας ο πρώτος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Σερβίας||Sava was born about 1175 as Rastko, son of the grand župan Stefan Nemanja. He left secretly for Mount Athos and became a monk. Together with his father he founded the Monastery of Hilandar. // He returned to Serbia and with the consent of the Patriarchate, which was then in Nicaea, became in 1219 the first archbishop of the autocephalous Serbian church. He founded dioceses, wrote laws and traveled to the Holy Places. He died in 1236 in Tarnovo in Bulgaria. He is the national saint of the Serbs.

life|01-15||Αγία Ίτα εξ Ιρλανδίας||Ita lived in Ireland in the 6th century and founded a women's monastery at Killeedy, in County Limerick. She is considered the foster mother and teacher of many saints, among them Brendan. She died around 570.

life|01-15||Όσιος Αλέξανδρος ο Ακοίμητος||Alexander was born at the end of the 4th century in Asia Minor and left offices and wealth to live as an ascetic in Syria. He founded the monastic order of the Akoimetoi ("the Sleepless"), in which the praise of God never stopped, day and night, because the monks changed shifts. He brought the movement to Constantinople and died about 430.

life|01-16||Άγιος Γεράσιμος ο Παλλαδάς||Gerasimos Palladas was born in Crete in 1625. He studied in Italy and was Patriarch of Alexandria from 1688 to 1710. He was a scholar and as patriarch defended the Orthodox faith. He died in 1714.

life|01-16||Όσιος Ονωράτος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Αρελάτης||Honoratus was a Gallic nobleman, who became an ascetic and founded around 410 the monastery of Lérins, on an island near Cannes. This monastery became a great center of monasticism and teaching in Gaul. He became Bishop of Arles and died about 430.

life|01-17||Άγιος Θεοδόσιος ο Μέγας ο βασιλεύς||Theodosius I was born in 347 in Spain and ascended the throne of the eastern part of the empire in 379. With the edict of Thessaloniki (380) he proclaimed the Orthodox Christian faith the official religion of the state, and in 381 he convened the Second Ecumenical Council in Constantinople, which completed the Creed. // He died in 395 in Milan, and after his death the empire was permanently divided between his two sons.

life|01-19||Άγιος Μάρκος ο Ευγενικός Επίσκοπος Εφέσου||Mark was born in 1392 in Constantinople with the name Manuel. He studied philosophy and rhetoric, became a monk and in 1436 Metropolitan of Ephesus. // He went with the emperor to the Council of Ferrara-Florence (1438-1439) to discuss union with Rome. He was the only hierarch who refused to sign the union and became the defender of Orthodoxy. He died in 1444 and what he upheld became a symbol of resistance for the identity of the Church.

life|01-19||Άγιος Θεόδοτος Επίσκοπος Κυρήνειας||Theodotus was Bishop of Kyrenia in Cyprus, in the 4th century. He lived in the time of Constantine the Great and his memory is honored in the Church of Cyprus on January 19.

life|01-20||Άγιος Λέων Μακέλλης ο Μέγας||Leo I the Thracian was a Byzantine emperor from 457 to 474. He was crowned by Patriarch Anatolius, the first emperor to be set on the throne by the patriarch. He supported the decisions of the Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon. He also remained known as "Makelles" (that is, "the butcher"), a name connected with the murder of the powerful general Aspar in 471. His memory is honored on January 20.

life|01-21||Αγία Αγνή η Μάρτυς||Agnes was a young girl from Rome, who was martyred about 304 in the persecution of Diocletian, when she was about thirteen years old. She refused to offer sacrifice to the idols and they beheaded her. Her tomb in Rome has been venerated from very early on and Agnes is one of the best-loved saints of the ancient Church.

life|01-22||Άγιος Βικέντιος ο Διάκονος||Vincent was a deacon of Bishop Valerius in Saragossa in Spain. He was arrested in the persecution of Diocletian and, after undergoing tortures, died in 304 in Valencia. His veneration spread very quickly in the West.

life|01-22||Άγιος Αναστάσιος ο Οσιομάρτυρας ο Πέρσης||Anastasius was a Persian soldier, the son of a magus. When Khosrow captured Jerusalem (614), he took the Precious Cross to Persia, and Anastasius was impressed by the Christian faith. He was baptized and became a monk at the monastery of Saint Anastasius, near Jerusalem. Later he was arrested and put to death on January 22, 628.

life|01-22||Άγιος Ιωάσαφ Φωτιστής της Αλάσκας||Ioasaph (Bolotov) was born in 1761 in Russia and was a monk. He was sent as head of the first Orthodox mission to Alaska (1794), on Kodiak Island. He was ordained bishop but the ship that was bringing him back from Siberia was lost in the ocean in 1799. The missionaries of Alaska honor him as the apostle of the region.

life|01-23||Άγιος Αχόλιος Επίσκοπος Θεσσαλονίκης||Acholius (Ascholius) was Bishop of Thessaloniki from about 380 to 383. He was a friend of Basil the Great and baptized the Emperor Theodosius I when he fell ill in Thessaloniki in 380. He took part in the Second Ecumenical Council and died in 383 or 384.

life|01-24||Άγιος Βαβύλας ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Babylas was Bishop of Antioch in the middle of the 3rd century. He was martyred in 250 during the persecution of the Emperor Decius. It is said that he prevented an emperor from entering the church because he was in sin. John Chrysostom wrote a homily in his memory, and his relics were transferred to Daphne, near Antioch.

life|01-24||Άγιος Φίλωνας ο Θαυματουργός Επίσκοπος Καρπασίας||Philo was Bishop of Carpasia in Cyprus, around the 4th or 5th century, a disciple of Epiphanius of Constantia. He wrote a commentary on the Song of Songs and is known as a wonderworker.

life|01-25||Άγιος Βλαδίμηρος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Μητροπολίτης Κιέβου||Vladimir (Bogoyavlensky) was born in 1848 and became Metropolitan of Moscow, of Saint Petersburg, and finally of Kiev. At the beginning of the Russian Revolution, in 1918, the Bolsheviks killed him in Kiev. He was the first hierarch to be martyred in those years.

life|01-25||Όσιος Ανατόλιος της Όπτινα||Anatoly (Zertsalov) was born in 1824 and became a monk at Optina Monastery, one of the greatest spiritual centers of Russia. He became an elder and spiritual father to many people, monastics and laity. He was known for his humility and discernment. He died in 1894.

life|01-26||Άγιος Δαυΐδ βασιλεύς της Γεωργίας||David IV the Builder (1073–1125) was King of Georgia. He united the country and freed it from the Seljuks, with a victory at the Battle of Didgori (1121). He built monasteries and schools and founded the Gelati Academy. He died in 1125, and the Church of Georgia honors him as a saint.

life|01-28||Όσιος Ισαάκ ο Σύρος Επίσκοπος Νινευΐ||Isaac lived in the 7th century and came from the region of Qatar (Persian Gulf). He became a monk and Bishop of Nineveh, but after a few months he resigned and withdrew into the desert. His ascetic writings, which were written in Syriac and translated into Greek, are among the best-loved books of the monastics of Orthodoxy.

life|01-29||Άγιος Γκίλντας του Γουάϊς||Gildas (about 500–570) was a British monk. He wrote the work "On the Ruin and Conquest of Britain," one of the oldest sources for the history of the Britons after the departure of the Romans. In it he criticized the kings and the clergy of his time.

life|01-29||Όσιος Αφραάτης||Aphrahat lived in the first half of the 4th century in the Persian Empire and was called the "Persian Sage." He became a monk and possibly a bishop near Mosul. He wrote in Syriac 23 "Demonstrations," among the oldest Christian texts of the East.

life|01-30||Άγιος Πέτρος Βασιλέας των Βουλγάρων||Peter I was the son of Simeon and Tsar of the Bulgarians from 927 to 969. He made peace with Byzantium and married Maria Lekapene, granddaughter of the Emperor Romanos I. His reign was a period of peace and of the growth of Christian life. Before he died he became a monk.

life|01-31||Όσιος Αρσένιος ο εν Πάρω||Arsenios was born in 1800 on Paros. He became a monk and the founder of the Monastery of Christ in the Forest. He also founded a school, which children of Paros attended, and he cared for the inhabitants with charity. He died in 1877.

life|02-01||Κυριακή Τελώνου και Φαρισαίου||It is the first Sunday of the Triodion, the period of preparation for Pascha. The Gospel of the day (Luke 18:9-14) tells the parable of the Pharisee, who boasted of his works, and of the publican, who humbly asked God for mercy. // The Church teaches that humility and repentance open the way to God, while pride closes it. From this Sunday the Triodion begins to be chanted. The date changes every year, because it depends on Pascha.

life|02-01||Οσία Μπριντζίτα||Brigid (Bridget) was born around 451 in Ireland. She became a nun and founded a monastery at Kildare, which became a center of education and spiritual life for men and women. She was known for her charity and her care of the poor and the sick. She died around 525 and is one of the patrons of Ireland.

life|02-03||Όσιος Ανσέριος ο Απόστολος της Δανίας και της Σκανδιναβίας||Ansgar (Anskar) was born in 801 in France and became a monk. He was sent to preach the Gospel in Denmark and Sweden, and in 831 he became Archbishop of Hamburg and later of Bremen. Despite the difficulties and the destruction of churches by the Vikings, he continued his work. He died in 865 and was called the "Apostle of the North."

life|02-03||Άγιος Λαυρέντιος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Καντουαρίας||Laurence came to England in 597 with Augustine, the first Archbishop of Canterbury, and succeeded him in 604. He supported the young church of the Anglo-Saxons and tried to bring the Celtic Christians into contact with the rest of the Church. He died in 619.

life|02-03||Προφήτης Αζαρίας||Azariah was the son of Oded. In the days of King Asa of Judah he prophesied that God is with the people as long as the people remain faithful to Him. Asa listened to his words, and the people renewed their covenant with God (2 Chronicles 15).

life|02-03||Προφήτιδα Άννα||Anna, daughter of Phanuel of the tribe of Asher, was a widow who lived in the Temple of Jerusalem, praying and fasting night and day. When the Theotokos and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to the Temple, Anna recognized Him and spoke about Him to those who were awaiting the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:36-38).

life|02-03||Άγιος Νικόλαος ο Ισαπόστολος||Nicholas Kasatkin was born in 1836 in Russia and studied at the Academy of Saint Petersburg. In 1861 he was sent to Japan as a priest of the Russian consulate at Hakodate and carefully learned the language and culture. // He translated the liturgical books into Japanese and founded the Orthodox Church of Japan. He became a bishop and built the cathedral of Tokyo. He remained in Japan until his death in 1912, and he is honored as the apostle of that country.

life|02-04||Όσιος Νικόλαος ο Ομολογητής ο Στουδίτης||Nicholas was born in 793 in Crete and became a monk at the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople, with Theodore the Studite as his teacher. In the years of Iconoclasm he suffered persecution and exile for defending the holy icons. Later he became abbot of the monastery (846) and remained there until his death in 868.

life|02-05||Άγιος Πολύευκτος Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Polyeuktos was Patriarch of Constantinople from 956 to 970. He was a monk and abbot before becoming patriarch. When John Tzimiskes ascended the throne after the murder of Nikephoros Phokas, Polyeuktos asked him to repent and to remove those responsible for the murder before he crowned him. In this way he showed the independence of the Church in the face of authority.

life|02-06||Άγιος Άμανδος φωτιστής της Βελγικής||Amand was born around 584 in France and became a monk. He preached the Gospel in Flanders and in the regions of present-day Belgium, founded monasteries, among them the monastery of Elnon, and for a short time became Bishop of Maastricht. He died in 679, having reached deep old age.

life|02-06||Όσιος Βουκόλος Επίσκοπος Σμύρνης||Bucolus was Bishop of Smyrna at the end of the 1st century and, according to tradition, a disciple of the Apostle John. He prepared his successor, Saint Polycarp, who became bishop after his death.

life|02-08||Προφήτης Ζαχαρίας||Zechariah, son of Berechiah, was a prophet in Jerusalem after the return of the Jews from the Babylonian captivity (about 520 BC). He encouraged the people to rebuild the temple and wrote the Old Testament book of the same name, which contains visions and prophecies about the Messiah and the triumph of God.

life|02-08||ΚΥΡΙΑΚΗ ΤΟΥ ΑΣΩΤΟΥ||It is the second Sunday of the Triodion, and the parable of the Prodigal Son is read (Luke 15:11-32): the younger son asks for his inheritance, squanders it in a far country and, when he comes to be in need, returns in repentance. The father awaits him and receives him with love. // The parable recalls the boundless loving-kindness of God and invites to repentance. Its date changes every year, according to Pascha.

life|02-11||Αγία Θεοδώρα η Βασίλισσα||Theodora was the wife of the Emperor Theophilos, who was an iconoclast. After his death (842) she assumed the regency for her young son Michael III and supported the restoration of the veneration of icons. // In 843, with Patriarch Methodios, the Triumph of Orthodoxy took place, which the Church celebrates on the first Sunday of Lent. Later she was removed from the palace and died around 867.

life|02-12||Όσιος Αλέξιος ο Θαυματουργός Αρχιεπίσκοπος Μόσχας||Alexis was born around 1293 in Moscow and became a monk. In 1354 he became Metropolitan of Kiev and all Russia, with his seat in Moscow. He was adviser and regent of the young Grand Prince Dmitry Donskoy, and he supported the unification of the Russian principalities around Moscow. He died in 1378.

life|02-12||Οσία Μαρία η μετονομασθείσα Μαρίνος||Maria was the daughter of a pious father, who entered a men's monastery under the name Marinos in order to live as a monk. In the monastery she was accused of being the father of a child, and she accepted the slander with patience, without revealing her secret. After her death it became known that she was a woman.

life|02-13||Άγιοι Ακύλας και Πρίσκιλλα οι Απόστολοι||Aquila and Priscilla were a couple of Jewish Christians who worked as tentmakers. Aquila came from Pontus. They came to Corinth when the Emperor Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome, and they hosted the Apostle Paul. They followed him to Ephesus, where they carefully explained the faith to Apollos. // Paul calls them his fellow workers and says that they "risked their necks" for his life (Romans 16:3-4). The church gathered in their house.

life|02-13||Όσιος Ευλόγιος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Αλεξάνδρειας||Eulogios was Patriarch of Alexandria from 580 to 607. Before becoming patriarch he was an abbot in Antioch. He was a friend of Pope Gregory the Great, with whom he exchanged letters, and he confronted the heresies that were developing in Egypt.

life|02-13||Όσιος Συμεών ο Μυροβλήτης Κτήτορας της Μονής Χιλανδαρίου||Symeon was Stefan Nemanja, Grand Zhupan of Serbia and founder of the Serbian state. In 1196 he resigned the throne in favor of his son and became a monk with the name Symeon. He went to Mount Athos, where his son Sava was already a monk, and together they founded the Monastery of Hilandar. He died in 1199. Myrrh, it is said, flowed from his body.

life|02-14||Άγιος Ουαλεντίνος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Τέρνι||Valentine was Bishop of the city of Terni in Italy and was martyred in the 3rd century, in the persecutions of the Roman emperors. His commemoration on February 14 was linked in the West, during the Middle Ages, with the festival of lovers ("Saint Valentine's Day").

life|02-14||Όσιος Μάρων||Maron lived at the end of the 4th and the beginning of the 5th century in Syria, near Cyrrhus. He practiced asceticism in the open countryside, on a mountaintop. He became known for his discernment and his working of miracles and gathered disciples. John Chrysostom wrote him a letter from exile. The Maronites of the Middle East take their name from him.

life|02-14||Ψυχοσάββατον||It is the Saturday before Meatfare Sunday, and the Church holds a memorial service for all the departed, from the forefathers to the most recent. This day shows the unity of the living and the dead in the body of the Church. The date changes every year according to Pascha.

life|02-15||ΚΥΡΙΑΚΗ «ΤΗΣ ΑΠΟ-ΚΡΕΩ»||It is Meatfare Sunday, the third of the Triodion, which is also called the Sunday "of the Great Judgment." The parable of the Last Judgment is read (Matthew 25:31-46), in which Christ says that He will judge people according to the love they showed to the hungry, the strangers, the sick and the imprisoned. // From the next day meat is no longer eaten and the preparation for Lent begins. The date changes every year.

life|02-16||Άγιος Φλαβιανός Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Flavian was Patriarch of Constantinople from 446 to 449. In 448 he convened a synod in Constantinople that condemned Eutyches, an abbot who taught that Christ had one nature. But Eutyches had the protection of the emperor, and the "Robber Council" of Ephesus (449) deposed Flavian and exiled him. He died shortly afterwards, in exile. Pope Leo had sent him his "Tome," which was read at the Council of Chalcedon (451).

life|02-17||Άγιοι Μαρκιανός και Πουλχερία οι βασιλείς||Marcian was Byzantine emperor from 450 to 457. He married Pulcheria, sister of the previous emperor Theodosius II, who already had great influence in the state. Together they convened in 451 the Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon, which defined the dogma of the two natures of Christ.

life|02-17||Άγιος Ερμογένης ο Ιερομάρτυρας Πατριάρχης Μόσχας||Hermogenes was born around 1530 and became Metropolitan of Kazan and in 1606 Patriarch of Moscow. In the Time of Troubles, when Russia was being invaded by the Poles, he refused to compromise and called the people to resist. The Poles imprisoned him in the Chudov Monastery, where he died of hunger in 1612.

life|02-19||Αγία Φιλοθέη η Οσιομάρτυς η Αθηναία||Philothei was born in 1522 in Athens, of the Benizelos family, and was married young. After the death of her husband she became a nun and founded a women's monastery, the Andrianou, in Athens. The monastery became a refuge for poor women and for captives whom Philothei tried to ransom from the Turks. // The Turks attacked her monastery and struck her severely. She died of her wounds in 1589. Athens honors her as its protectress.

life|02-19||Άγιος Ιεροσλάβος ο Σοφός||Yaroslav the Wise (978–1054) was Grand Prince of Kiev from 1019 until his death. In his days Kievan Rus became one of the most powerful countries of Europe.
