He built the church of Saint Sophia in Kiev, founded schools and libraries, and issued its first written code of laws, the "Russkaya Pravda."

life|02-20||Άγιος Αγάθων Πάπας Ρώμης||Agatho was pope from 678 to 681. He sent representatives to the Sixth Ecumenical Council in Constantinople (680–681), which condemned Monothelitism, and his letter to the Council became an important text for doctrine. He died in 681.

life|02-21||Άγιος Ζαχαρίας Πατριάρχης Ιεροσολύμων||Zacharias was Patriarch of Jerusalem from 609 to 632. In 614 the Persians captured Jerusalem, burned churches and took with them the Precious Cross and the patriarch as a captive to Persia. He returned to Jerusalem in 628, when the Emperor Heraclius defeated the Persians and recovered the Precious Cross.

life|02-21||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο από Σχολαστικών Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||John III the Scholastic was Patriarch of Constantinople from 565 to 577. He was a lawyer (scholastic) in Antioch. He is known for the collection of ecclesiastical canons that he compiled, a basis for the later canon law of the Church.

life|02-21||Άγιος Μαξιμιανός Αρχιεπίσκοπος Ραβέννης||Maximian was Archbishop of Ravenna from 546 to 556, in the days of Justinian. In 547 he consecrated the church of Saint Vitalis, which is adorned with the well-known mosaics in which Maximian is depicted beside the Emperor Justinian.

life|02-22||ΚΥΡΙΑΚΗ «ΤΗΣ ΤΥΡΟΦΑΓΟΥ»||It is Cheesefare Sunday, the last before Great Lent, which is also called the Sunday "of forgiveness." It recalls the expulsion of Adam from Paradise and calls the faithful to begin the fast with repentance. In the evening Forgiveness Vespers is held, in which people ask forgiveness of one another. // The date changes every year according to Pascha.

life|02-22||Άγιος Τελεσφόρος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Ρώμης||Telesphorus was Bishop of Rome in the middle of the 2nd century (about 125–136), one of the first bishops after the Apostles. Tradition says that he was martyred under the Emperor Hadrian. The Church honors him on February 22.

life|02-23||Αγία Γοργονία αδελφή του Αγίου Γρηγορίου του Θεολόγου||Gorgonia was the elder sister of Gregory the Theologian, daughter of Bishop Gregory and of Nonna, in Nazianzus of Cappadocia. She married and raised children. Her brother wrote a funeral oration in which he regards her as a model of a Christian wife and mother. She died around 370.

life|02-23||Καθαρά Δευτέρα||It is the first day of Great Lent. In the Orthodox Church the fast begins, and the celebration is linked with the purification of body and soul. The faithful pray with the Great Canon of Saint Andrew of Crete and the Prayer of Saint Ephraim. // In Greece the day is a public holiday, and it is customary to go out to the countryside, to fly kites, and to eat fasting foods such as lagana bread, taramas and legumes.

life|02-24||Άγιος Εθελμπέρτος βασιλιάς της Αγγλίας||Ethelbert was King of Kent from about 560 to 616. He married a Christian Frankish princess, Bertha, and in 597 he received Augustine and his missionaries. He was baptized and became the first English king to become a Christian. He also issued the first written laws in Anglo-Saxon.

life|02-24||Όσιος Μποϊζίλ εκ Σκωτίας||Boisil was a monk and abbot of the monastery of Melrose, in southern Scotland, in the 7th century. He was the teacher of the young Cuthbert, who later became one of the best-known saints of Northern England. He died in 664 of the plague.

life|02-26||Αγία Φωτεινή η Μεγαλομάρτυς η Σαμαρείτιδα||Photini is the Samaritan woman who met Christ at Jacob's well and spoke with Him (John 4). After the meeting she believed and brought many of her countrymen to Christ. // According to tradition, she preached the Gospel in Carthage and in Rome and was martyred under the Emperor Nero together with her sons and her sisters.

life|02-27||Άγιος Λέανδρος Επίσκοπος Σεβίλλης||Leander (about 534–600) was the brother of Isidore of Seville and Bishop of Seville in Spain. He converted from Arianism to the Orthodox faith the prince Hermenegild and later the Visigothic king Reccared, and he was the chief inspirer of the Council of Toledo (589). He was a friend of Pope Gregory the Great.

life|02-27||Άγιος Ραφαήλ Επίσκοπος Μπρούκλυν||Raphael Hawaweeny was born in 1860 in Damascus, studied at the theological school of Halki and in Russia, and in 1895 arrived in New York. He founded parishes for the Arab Orthodox immigrants and cared for the Orthodox of all North America. In 1904 he was consecrated Bishop of Brooklyn, the first Orthodox bishop to be consecrated in America. He died in 1915.

life|02-28||Άγιοι Νυμφάς και Εύβουλος οι Απόστολοι||Nymphas was a Christian of Laodicea, in whose house the church gathered, and Paul greets him in the Epistle to the Colossians (Colossians 4:15). Eubulus was a Christian of Rome, who sends greetings to Timothy through Paul (2 Timothy 4:21). Tradition numbers them among the seventy apostles.

life|02-28||Άγιος Ιαροσλάβος ο Σοφός||Yaroslav the Wise (978–1054) was Grand Prince of Kiev from 1019 until his death. In his days Kievan Rus became one of the most powerful countries of Europe. He built the church of Saint Sophia in Kiev, founded schools and libraries, and issued its first written code of laws, the "Russkaya Pravda."

life|02-28||Άγιος Νικόλαος ο διά Χριστόν Σαλός του Πσκώφ||Nicholas lived in Pskov, in northwestern Russia, in the 16th century, as a fool for Christ, that is, as a man who played the madman out of love for Christ. According to tradition, in 1570 or 1571 Tsar Ivan the Terrible visited Pskov and Nicholas rebuked him for the massacres in Novgorod, and in this way, it is said, he saved the city from plunder. He died in 1576.

life|02-28||Άγιος Προτέριος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Αρχιεπίσκοπος Αλεξανδρείας||Proterius was Patriarch of Alexandria from 451, after the Council of Chalcedon, in the place of Dioscorus, who had been deposed. He supported the decisions of the Council, and this brought him into conflict with the Monophysites of Egypt. In 457, when the Emperor Marcian died, the mob killed him in the church.

life|02-28||Όσιος Κασσιανός ο Ρωμαίος||Cassian was born around 360 in the region of Scythia (Dobruja). He became a monk in Bethlehem and went to Egypt, where he lived near great ascetics. Later, in Marseilles, he founded two monasteries and wrote the works "Institutes" and "Conferences," which carried the monasticism of the East to the West. He died around 435.

life|03-01||Άγιος Δαβίδ ο Αρχιεπίσκοπος||David lived in the 6th century in Wales and is considered the patron of the country. He founded monasteries and became known for his strict ascetic life and his teaching; the center of his activity was the area of present-day St Davids. The Welsh honor him as their national saint, and his commemoration is celebrated on March 1.

life|03-02||Άγιος Τσάντ εκ Σκωτίας||Chad (Ceadda) was a Northumbrian monk of the 7th century, a disciple of Saint Aidan at Lindisfarne. He became Bishop of York and later of Mercia, with his seat at Lichfield, where he taught with humility and traveled on foot in his regions. He died on March 2, 672.

life|03-02||Άγιος Θεόδοτος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Κυρηνείας Κύπρου||Theodotos was Bishop of Kyrenia in Cyprus at the beginning of the 4th century, at the time of the persecutions of Licinius. He was imprisoned and tortured for his faith and died as a martyr. The Church of Cyprus honors him as one of the saints of the island.

life|03-04||Άγιος Δανιήλ ο Πρίγκιπας||Daniel was the youngest son of Alexander Nevsky and the first ruler of Moscow; he governed in 1283–1303. He founded the Monastery of Saint Daniel in Moscow and is famed for his peaceful policy toward the neighboring princes. He died in 1303, having become a monk.

life|03-05||Άγιος Θεόφιλος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Καισαρείας||Theophilus was Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine at the end of the 2nd century. Around 190 he presided over a synod of the bishops of Palestine, which dealt with the date of Pascha. The Church honors him as a defender of unity and of tradition.

life|03-05||Άγιος Νικόλαος Επίσκοπος Αχρίδος και Ζίτσης||Nikolaj Velimirović (1881–1956) was a Serbian bishop, theologian and writer; he served as Bishop of Ohrid and Žiča. In the Second World War he was held by the Germans in a monastery and at Dachau. After the war he lived in the United States, where he died in 1956. His sermons and prayers are widely read, and he was glorified as a saint by the Church of Serbia in 2003.

life|03-07||Άγιος Εφραίμ Πατριάρχης Αντιόχειας||Ephraim (Ephraemius) was Patriarch of Antioch in the days of Justinian (527–545). Before becoming patriarch he held high offices of the state in the East. He defended the Orthodox faith of the Council of Chalcedon and wrote theological texts, of which only fragments survive.

life|03-07||Όσιος Παύλος ο Απλός||Paul was an Egyptian farmer who became a disciple of Anthony the Great in the desert, at an advanced age. He was called "the Simple" for the simplicity and obedience with which he received every instruction of his teacher. Anthony considered him spiritually mature and called him a model of obedience.

life|03-10||Αγία Αναστασία η Πατρικία||Anastasia was an aristocratic woman of Constantinople in the days of Justinian. In order to avoid the admiration and the pressures of the court, she secretly left for Egypt and lived as a monk with the name Anastasios the Eunuch, near the Venerable Daniel of Scetis. She died around 567, and only then was it revealed that she was a woman.

life|03-11||Οσία Θεοδώρα η βασίλισσα Άρτης||Theodora Petraliphaina was the wife of Michael II Doukas, despot of Epirus, in the 13th century. She lived in Arta, cared for the poor and supported the Church. After the death of Michael she became a nun and died in 1270. Arta regards her as its protectress, and her relics are kept in the city.

life|03-11||Άγιος Ευλόγιος ο Ιερομάρτυρας και οι συν αυτώ εν Κορδούη Ισπανίας||Eulogius was a priest in Córdoba in Spain, at the time when the city was under Arab rule (9th century). He supported the Christians who were led to martyrdom and wrote about their struggle. He was arrested and beheaded on March 11, 859.

life|03-12||Άγιος Γρηγόριος ο Διάλογος πάπας Ρώμης||Gregory was born around 540 into an aristocratic family of Rome and became prefect of the city before becoming a monk. As pope (590–604) he cared for the poor, organized the Church and sent missionaries to England. He wrote the "Dialogues," with lives of the saints of Italy, and the "Moralia." Because the "Dialogues" were translated into Greek, he is known in the East as the Dialogist. The Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts is attributed to him.

life|03-12||Όσιος Συμεών ο Νέος Θεολόγος||Symeon (949–1022) was born in Paphlagonia and was educated in Constantinople, where he served at the court. He became a monk at the Stoudios Monastery and later abbot of the monastery of Saint Mamas. He taught that a Christian can know God personally, and he wrote hymns of divine love and homilies. His teachings provoked opposition, and he was exiled to Paloukiton in Bithynia, where he died. He is the third saint whom the Church has called "the Theologian," after John and Gregory.

life|03-12||Άγιος Φινεές ο Δίκαιος||Phinehas was the son of the priest Eleazar and a grandson of Aaron. In the desert, after the idolatry of the people at Baal-peor, he intervened with zeal, and the plague that had struck the people ceased (Numbers 25). God gave him the covenant of priesthood and of peace.

life|03-13||Κοίμηση Αγίου Λεάνδρου Επισκόπου Σεβίλλης||Leander (about 534–600) was Bishop of Seville in Spain and brother of Isidore. He persuaded the Visigothic king Reccared to abandon the heresy of Arius, and at the Third Council of Toledo (589) the faith of Nicaea became official in the kingdom. He wrote a rule for nuns and died around 600.

life|03-15||Άγιος Αριστόβουλος ο Απόστολος Επίσκοπος Βρετανίας||Aristobulus is one of the Seventy Apostles, and Paul mentions "those who belong to Aristobulus" in the Epistle to the Romans (16:10). According to tradition he was the brother of Barnabas, a fellow worker of Paul, and he preached the word of God in Britain, where he became a bishop.

life|03-16||Όσιος Χριστόδουλος ο εν Πάτμω||Christodoulos was born around 1021 in the region of Nicaea and became a monk on Mount Olympus in Bithynia and in other monasteries of Asia Minor. The Emperor Alexios I Komnenos gave him Patmos in 1088, where he founded the monastery of Saint John the Theologian, which exists to this day. He died in 1093 on Euboea.

life|03-17||Άγιος Πατρίκιος Απόστολος της Ιρλανδίας||Patrick was born in Britain in the 5th century. At sixteen he was abducted by Irish pirates and worked as a shepherd until he escaped. He became a cleric and bishop, returned to Ireland and preached the Gospel to its people; he founded churches and monasteries. His work, the "Confession," describes his life. Ireland honors him as its patron, and his commemoration is celebrated on March 17.

life|03-18||Άγιος Εδουάρδος βασιλέας της Αγγλίας||Edward became King of England in 975, as a child, after the death of his father Edgar. He died, murdered, on March 18, 978, at Corfe Castle, at about the age of sixteen; the faithful honored him as a martyr, and he was called "Edward the Martyr."

life|03-20||Όσιος Κουθβέρτος εκ Βρετανίας||Cuthbert (about 634–687) was a monk at Melrose and at Lindisfarne, in Northumbria, and became a renowned preacher and pastor. He lived as a hermit on the small island of Farne, and in 685 he became Bishop of Lindisfarne, a position that he accepted reluctantly. He died on March 20, 687. His tomb became a place of pilgrimage.

life|03-21||Άγιος Θωμάς Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Thomas I was Patriarch of Constantinople in the days of the Emperor Phokas (607–610). He lived in a time of internal disturbances and external dangers for the state. The Church honors him as a saint and holds that he served with piety.

life|03-25||Άγιος Τύχων Πατριάρχης Μόσχας||Tikhon (Vasily Belavin, 1865–1925) was elected Patriarch of Moscow in 1917, when the patriarchate was restored in Russia after two centuries. He faced the persecution of the Church by the Soviet state, cared for the poor during the famine of 1921 and refused to submit to the political authority. He died in 1925 and was glorified as a saint in 1989.

life|03-26||Διήγησης ωφέλιμος Μάλχου μοναχού αιχμαλωτισθέντος||The narrative comes from the Life of Malchus, which Jerome wrote in the 4th century. Malchus was a monk in Syria who was captured by Saracens and worked as a shepherd. He spent years as a slave, refused to break his monastic vow, and finally escaped together with a woman. Their story shows the faith and purity that were preserved in difficult circumstances.

life|03-26||Άγιος Ειρηναίος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Σιρμίου||Irenaeus was Bishop of the city of Sirmium (today Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia). In the persecution of Diocletian he was arrested and refused to sacrifice to the idols; he was beheaded in 304. The Church honors him as a hieromartyr.

life|03-27||Άγιος Ανανί ο Προφήτης||Hanani was a prophet of the kingdom of Judah in the days of King Asa, and the father of the prophet Jehu. He rebuked Asa for relying on the king of Syria instead of trusting in God, and Asa threw him into prison (2 Chronicles 16).

life|03-30||Άγιος Ιωήλ ο Προφήτης||Joel was one of the Twelve Minor Prophets, son of Pethuel. His book speaks of a disaster caused by locusts, calls the people to repentance and prophesies the outpouring of the Holy Spirit "upon all flesh." The Apostle Peter quotes the passage in his sermon at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21).

life|03-31||Άγιος Ιννοκέντιος Μητροπολίτης Μόσχας και Ιεραπόστολος Αλάσκας||John Veniaminov (1797–1879) was a priest who became a missionary in the Aleutian Islands and Alaska. He learned the local languages, created an alphabet and translated church texts, and built schools and churches. He became a bishop and in 1868 Metropolitan of Moscow. He was glorified as a saint in 1977.

life|03-31||Άγιος Ιωνάς Μητροπολίτης Μόσχας και πασών των Ρωσιών||Jonah became Metropolitan of Moscow in 1448, when the Russian bishops chose him without the approval of Constantinople, a development that became a milestone for the autocephaly of the Russian Church. He helped to calm the civil quarrels of the princes. He died in 1461.

life|04-01||Όσιος Βαρσανούφιος της Όπτινα||Barsanuphius (1845–1913) was an elder of the Optina Monastery in Russia, to which he came after a career in the army. People flocked to him for advice and consolation, and he was the spiritual father of many. He died in 1913, and the Church honors him as a venerable father.

life|04-04||Άγιος Ισίδωρος Επίσκοπος Σεβίλλης||Isidore (about 560–636) succeeded his brother Leander as Bishop of Seville in Spain. He was the most learned man of his time in the West and wrote the "Etymologies," a kind of encyclopedia with the knowledge of antiquity. He presided at the Fourth Council of Toledo (633) and died on April 4, 636.

life|04-05||Άγιοι Δίδυμος και Θεοδώρα οι Μάρτυρες||Theodora was a Christian virgin from Alexandria who, in the persecution of Diocletian, was condemned to be taken to a brothel. The soldier Didymus, a Christian, helped her to escape by exchanging clothes with her. When Theodora returned to defend him, both were condemned and were martyred around 304.

life|04-06||Άγιος Ειρηναίος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Σιρμίου||Irenaeus was Bishop of Sirmium (today Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia). In the persecution of Diocletian he refused to sacrifice to the idols and was beheaded, in 304. The Church honors him as a hieromartyr.

life|04-06||Όσιος Γρηγόριος ο Σιναΐτης||Gregory (about 1255–1346) was a monk from Asia Minor who practiced asceticism on Sinai and in Crete, and brought to Mount Athos the teaching on hesychast prayer. Later he founded a monastery at Paroria in Bulgaria, where he taught many disciples, and he died in 1346. His "Discourses" on prayer and stillness are included in the Philokalia.

life|04-08||Άγιος Κελεστίνος πάπας Ρώμης||Celestine I was Pope of Rome in 422–432. He took up the dispute over Nestorius, and at a synod in Rome in 430 he condemned his teachings, and he sent representatives to the Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus (431). He died in 432.

life|04-09||Όσιος Ακάκιος Επίσκοπος Αμίδης Μεσοποταμίας||Acacius was Bishop of Amida (present-day Diyarbakır) at the beginning of the 5th century. When the Romans took thousands of Persian prisoners, Acacius sold the sacred vessels of the church in order to ransom and feed them, and sent them back to the king of Persia. His act became an example of charity.

life|04-10||Άγιος Μιλτιάδης πάπας Ρώμης||Miltiades (or Melchiades) was Pope of Rome in 311–314, at the time when Constantine the Great put a stop to the persecutions. In 313 he presided at a synod in Rome that examined the case of the Donatists of Africa. He himself had lived through the persecutions.

life|04-10||Άγιος Γρηγόριος Ε’ Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Gregory V (1746–1821) was born in Dimitsana and became Ecumenical Patriarch three times, in 1797, 1806 and 1818. When the Greek Revolution of 1821 began, the Ottomans held him responsible, although he had excommunicated the revolutionaries. He was hanged on Pascha Sunday, April 10, 1821, at the central gate of the Patriarchate. His body was thrown into the sea and was recovered by Greek sailors, who carried it to Odessa; in 1871 his relics were transferred to Athens, to the Metropolitan Cathedral. The Church honors him as an ethnomartyr.

life|04-12||Άγιος Σάββας ο Μάρτυρας εν Μπουζάου Ρουμανίας||Sabbas was a Gothic Christian in the region of Buzău in present-day Romania, in the 4th century. In the persecution by the Gothic ruler he refused to eat the food offered to the idols and, in 372, was drowned in the river. His martyrdom became known from a letter of the Church of Gothia to Cappadocia.

life|04-13||Άγιος Αρσένιος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Ελασσώνος||Arsenios was born in Elassona in Thessaly and became archbishop of the city. Later he went to Russia, where he served at the Cathedral of the Archangel Michael in the Moscow Kremlin and became Archbishop of Suzdal. He died in Suzdal in 1626, and his relics are venerated there. He is one of the Greeks who helped the Church of Russia to stand firm.

life|04-14||Άγιος Αρδαλίων ο Μάρτυρας ο μίμος||Ardalion was an actor (mime) in the days of Maximian. While he was performing in a play that mocked the Christians, he believed in Christ and publicly confessed Christianity. He was tortured and put to death for his faith.

life|04-17||Άγιος Ανίκητος ο Ιερομάρτυρας πάπας Ρώμης||Anicetus was Pope of Rome in the middle of the 2nd century (about 155–166). He received Polycarp of Smyrna in Rome, and the two discussed the date of Pascha; they did not agree, but remained in communion. According to tradition he died as a martyr.

life|04-17||Άγιος Αγαπητός πάπας Ρώμης||Agapetus I was Pope of Rome in 535–536. He was sent by the king of the Goths to Constantinople to intercede with Justinian, and there he persuaded Patriarch Anthimus to step down, because he supported Monophysitism. He died in Constantinople in 536 and his body was carried to Rome.

life|04-17||Άγιος Μακάριος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Κορίνθου||Makarios Notaras (1731–1805) was born in Athens and became Archbishop of Corinth. Together with Nikodemos the Hagiorite he published the Philokalia of the Holy Neptic Fathers (1782), and he was among the spiritual leaders of the Kollyvades movement. He died on Chios in 1805 and is considered one of the revivers of the neptic tradition.

life|04-17||Άγιος Συμεών ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Περσίδος και οι συν αυτώ Μαρτυρήσαντες||Symeon was Bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, the capital of Persia, and the first of the Christians of the country. In the persecution of King Shapur II he refused to worship the sun and to pay the exceptional tax that was demanded of the Christians. He was martyred on April 14, 341, together with many clergy and other faithful.

life|04-19||Άγιος Αλπέγιος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Αρχιεπίσκοπος Καντουαρίας||Alphege was Archbishop of Canterbury from 1006. In 1011 Danish raiders captured the city and held him hostage. He refused to ask for a ransom that would burden the people and was killed on April 19, 1012, at Greenwich.

life|04-20||Άγιος Ζακχαίος ο Απόστολος||Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector in Jericho, short in stature, who climbed a sycamore tree in order to see Jesus. Christ called him and stayed in his house; Zacchaeus promised to give half of his possessions to the poor and to restore fourfold to those whom he had wronged (Luke 19). According to tradition he became Bishop of Caesarea.

life|04-20||Όσιος Αθανάσιος ο Μετεωρίτης||Athanasios (about 1302–1383) was born in Neai Patrai (Hypati) and became a monk on Mount Athos. In Thessaly he climbed up on the rocks of Meteora and founded the Great Meteoron, the first and largest of the monasteries of the region, in the 14th century. He died in 1383.

life|04-20||Όσιος Ιωάσαφ ο Μετεωρίτης||Joasaph was John Uroš Palaiologos, son of the Serbian ruler Symeon, who governed Thessaly. He resigned the throne and became a monk at Meteora, where he succeeded Athanasios as abbot of the Great Meteoron. He gave his wealth to the monastery and died around 1423.

life|04-21||Άγιος Μαξιμιανός Επίσκοπος Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Maximian was Patriarch of Constantinople in 431–434, after Nestorius, at the time of the Third Ecumenical Council. He was a presbyter of the city with a reputation for piety; as patriarch he took care to calm the disputes of the Church. He died in 434.

life|04-22||Άγιος Ναθαναήλ ο Απόστολος||Nathanael came from Cana of Galilee. Philip spoke to him about Jesus, and Christ called him "an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile" (John 1:45–51). In tradition he is often identified with Bartholomew, one of the Twelve.

life|04-24||Άγιος Μελίτων Αρχιεπίσκοπος Καντουαρίας||Mellitus came from Rome in 601 with the second group of missionaries that Pope Gregory I sent to England. In 604 he became the first Bishop of London, and in 619 he succeeded Laurence as Archbishop of Canterbury. He died in 624.

life|04-25||Άγιος Αννιανός Επίσκοπος Αλεξανδρείας||Anianus was a shoemaker in Alexandria. According to tradition, the Apostle Mark healed his hand, and he believed and became his disciple. Mark made him a bishop, and Anianus was the second bishop of the city, in the 1st century.

life|04-25||Άγιος Μακεδόνιος Β’ Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Macedonius II was Patriarch of Constantinople in 496–511. He defended the Council of Chalcedon against the Emperor Anastasius I, who favored the Monophysites. Anastasius deposed him in 511 and exiled him; he died in exile, in 517.

life|04-26||Άγιος Στέφανος Επίσκοπος Πέρμ||Stephen (about 1340–1396) was a missionary to the Komi, a people of northern Russia. He learned their language and created the Old Komi (Permic) alphabet, into which he translated church texts. In 1383 he became Bishop of Perm. He died in 1396 in Moscow.

life|04-28||Άγιος Κύριλλος Επίσκοπος Τούρωφ||Cyril of Turov (12th century) was a bishop in the Russian land of Kiev and is considered one of the greatest orators and writers of the early Russian Church. He wrote sermons for the feasts of Pascha and of Thomas Sunday, and prayers. He died around 1182.

life|04-30||Άγιος Ερκονγουάλδος Επίσκοπος Λονδίνου||Erkenwald was Bishop of London in 675–693. He founded the monasteries of Chertsey and Barking and cared for the Church of the region. He died in 693, and his tomb in Saint Paul's Cathedral became a place of pilgrimage.

life|04-30||Άγιος Ιγνάτιος Επίσκοπος Σταυρουπόλεως||Ignatius Brianchaninov (1807–1867) was a military engineer who became a monk and, in 1857, Bishop of the Caucasus and the Black Sea, with his seat at Stavropol. He resigned in 1861 and devoted himself to study and writing. His works on prayer and the neptic life are among the most widely read in the Russian Church. He was glorified as a saint in 1988.

life|05-01||Αγία Ταμάρα η βασίλισσα||Tamar (about 1160–1213) reigned in Georgia from 1184 until her death, the daughter of King George III. Under her rule the state reached its greatest flourishing: the borders were extended, the monasteries and the spiritual life were strengthened, and her era is the "golden age" of Georgian literature and art, the best-known work being the poem "The Knight in the Panther's Skin" by Shota Rustaveli. The Church of Georgia honors her as a saint and calls her "King" Tamar.

life|05-01||Οσία Ισιδώρα η διά Χριστόν Σαλή||Isidora lived in the 4th century in a women's monastery of Tabennisi in Egypt. According to tradition, preserved by Palladius, she pretended to be mad and did the humblest chores of the monastery, so as to remain unnoticed. The other nuns despised her, and she endured without complaint. When an ascetic perceived her holiness, Isidora secretly left the monastery and was not seen again. She is considered the first woman to follow the path of foolishness for Christ.

life|05-02||Άγιος Βόρις – Μιχαήλ ο Ισαπόστολος||Boris was ruler of the Bulgarians from about 852. He was baptized around 864–865 and took the name Michael, and thus his country became Christian. Later he welcomed the disciples of Cyril and Methodius, who had been driven out of Moravia, and with their help the Slavonic language was established in worship and in letters, and schools were founded in Pliska, in Preslav and in Ohrid. In 889 he resigned and became a monk. He died in 907, and the Church honors him as equal to the apostles.

life|05-02||Άγιοι Έσπερος και Ζωή||Hesperus and Zoe were slaves of a pagan, Catullus, in Attalia of Pamphylia, under the Emperor Hadrian (2nd century). They became Christians, and together with their two sons, Cyriacus and Theodulus, they refused to take part in the sacrifices of their master and in the pagan banquets. According to tradition, they were thrown into a fiery furnace and died as martyrs, while Catullus later believed.

life|05-03||Άγιος Οικουμένιος Επίσκοπος Τρίκκης||Oikoumenios was Bishop of Trikka (Trikala) in Thessaly and lived, according to the prevailing view, in the 10th century. He remained known as an interpreter of Holy Scripture: his commentaries on the Acts of the Apostles, on the epistles of Paul and the catholic epistles, as well as on the Apocalypse, gather the interpretations of the ancient Fathers and were widely used by later interpreters.

life|05-03||Όσιος Θεοδόσιος καθηγούμενος της Λαύρας||Theodosius was born around 1008 in Vasilkov, near Kiev. He was one of the founders of the Kiev Caves Lavra, the first great monastery of Russia, and became its abbot around 1062. He introduced there the cenobitic rule of the Stoudios Monastery of Constantinople, which became a model for the Russian monasteries. He cared for the poor and the sick and boldly rebuked even the rulers. He died in 1074.

life|05-04||Αγία Μόνικα μητέρα του Αγίου Αυγουστίνου||Monica was born around 331 in Tagaste in North Africa. She married a pagan, Patricius, and with patience and prayer she cared for her family. Her eldest son, Augustine, lived many years far from the faith, and Monica followed him with tears and prayers as far as Rome and Milan. She saw Augustine baptized in 387 by Ambrose. A little later she died in Ostia, on the way to her homeland. Augustine himself tells her story in the "Confessions."

life|05-04||Άγιος Φλωριανός ο Μάρτυρας||Florian was an official of the Roman army in the region of Noricum (present-day Austria). When the persecution of Diocletian broke out, he did not deny his faith and, in 304, he was thrown into the river Enns with a millstone tied around his neck. The place of the martyrdom became a pilgrimage site, and the monastery of Saint Florian near Linz took its name from him.

life|05-05||Άγιος Ιλάριος Επίσκοπος Αρελάτης||Hilary (about 403–449) became a monk at the monastery of Lérins, near Cannes, and in 429 he succeeded his relative Honoratus as Bishop of Arles in Gaul. He was a zealous pastor, cared for the poor and convened synods, but he came into conflict with Pope Leo I over the rights of the Bishop of Arles in other provinces. He died in 449.

life|05-08||Όσιος Αρσένιος ο Μέγας||Arsenius (about 354–450) was a Roman deacon and nobleman, whom the Emperor Theodosius I made the teacher of his sons, Arcadius and Honorius. In 394 he left the court and went to Scetis in Egypt, where he lived as an ascetic, loving silence and humility. Later he moved to the region of Troe, near Cairo. His sayings are preserved in the Gerontikon, the best known being "Flee, be silent, pray always." He died at about the age of 95.

life|05-09||Άγιος Χριστοφόρος ο Μεγαλομάρτυρας||Christopher was martyred in Lycia in Asia Minor, according to tradition under the Emperor Decius, in the middle of the 3rd century. Popular tradition has him carrying people across a river and lifting Christ on his shoulders in the form of a child, and for this reason his name means "the one who bears Christ." In Orthodox iconography he is often depicted with the head of a dog. He is honored as the patron of travelers.

life|05-10||Άγιοι Αλφειός, Κυπρίνος και Φιλάδελφος||Alphius, Philadelphus and Cyprian were brothers from Lentini in Sicily. According to tradition, in the middle of the 3rd century, under Valerian, they were arrested because they confessed Christ and were cruelly tortured before they died as martyrs. The Churches of the East and of the West honor their memory.

life|05-12||Άγιος Παγκράτιος ο Μάρτυρας||Pancras was a young man from Phrygia in Asia Minor who arrived in Rome together with his uncle. According to tradition, he became a Christian and was beheaded at about the age of fourteen, in the persecution of Diocletian (around 304). His tomb in Rome became a place of pilgrimage, and the church of Saint Pancras was built there.

life|05-12||Άγιοι Αχιλλέας και Νερέος||Nereus and Achilleus were Roman soldiers who became Christians and, according to tradition, served Flavia Domitilla, a cousin of the Emperor Domitian. They refused to take up arms again and to sacrifice to the idols, and they were martyred by beheading. Their tombs are in the catacombs of Domitilla in Rome.

life|05-12||Αγία Δομιτίλλα η Μάρτυς||Flavia Domitilla was a Roman noblewoman, a niece of the Emperor Domitian. According to tradition, because she was a Christian, she was exiled to the island of Pontia, where she lived and died for her faith. The catacombs of Domitilla in Rome, among the oldest Christian catacombs, take their name from her.

life|05-12||Άγιος Ερμογένης ο Ιερομάρτυρας Πατριάρχης||Hermogenes (about 1530–1612) became Patriarch of Moscow in 1606, in the Time of Troubles, when Russia was without stable authority and a large part of Moscow was under Polish occupation. Despite the threat, he ordered the Russians to resist the foreign conquerors and to defend the Orthodox faith. The Poles imprisoned him in the Chudov monastery, where he died of hunger in 1612. The liberation of Moscow followed almost immediately.

life|05-13||Όσιος Ευθύμιος ο Αθωνίτης||Euthymius (955–1028) was born in Georgia and was the son of John, a nobleman who became a monk on Athos and founded the Monastery of the Iberians. He lived in that monastery and, as its abbot, continued the work of his father. He devoted himself to translating Greek books, especially liturgical and patristic ones, into the Georgian language, and thus became a cultural bridge between Byzantium and Georgia. He died in 1028.

life|05-13||Όσιος Γεώργιος ο Ίβηρας||George the Hagiorite (1009–1065) was born in Georgia and became a monk on Athos, in the Monastery of the Iberians, where he succeeded Euthymius as abbot. He continued the work of translating Greek ecclesiastical and patristic texts into Georgian and wrote the lives of John and Euthymius. He died in 1065 in Constantinople, where he had gone to defend the rights of the monastery.

life|05-15||Άγιος Αχίλλιος Επίσκοπος Λαρίσης||Achillios was Bishop of Larissa in Thessaly at the beginning of the 4th century and took part in the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea in 325. He fought against Arianism, and tradition attributes miracles to him, especially healings. His relics were transferred in 986 by King Samuel to Prespa, to the lake whose islet bears the name Saint Achilleios.

life|05-16||Άγιος Νικόλαος ο Α’ ο||Nicholas Mystikos was Patriarch of Constantinople from 901 to 907 and again from 912 to 925. As patriarch he refused to give his consent to the fourth marriage of Emperor Leo VI and was persecuted for it, but he returned when Leo died and became regent for the young Constantine VII. He wrote many letters, which survive and are of great historical value. He died in 925.

life|05-16||Όσιος Βρενδανός ο Αναχωρητής||Brendan (about 484–577) was an Irish abbot, founder of the monastery of Clonfert. He became known as "the Navigator": his Life, written centuries later, tells of a wondrous voyage of his with monks across open seas to the "Promised Land of the Saints". His historical personality is nevertheless certain: he founded monasteries in Ireland and Scotland and is regarded as one of the great monks of Ireland.

life|05-16||Άγιος Μακάριος ο Νοταράς||Makarios Notaras (1731–1805) was born in Corinth and became Archbishop of Corinth. Together with Nikodemos the Hagiorite and Athanasios of Paros he is counted among the Kollyvades, the movement that called for a return to the patristic tradition and to frequent Holy Communion. With Nikodemos he published the "Philokalia of the Holy Neptic Fathers" (Venice, 1782). He died in 1805 on Chios.

life|05-18||Άγιος Στέφανος Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Stephen I was the son of Emperor Basil I and the brother of Leo VI. He became a monk, and in 886, when Leo ascended the throne and deposed Photios, he made him Patriarch of Constantinople at about nineteen years of age. He remained on the throne until his death in 893.

life|05-19||Άγιος Δουνστάνος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Καντουαρίας||Dunstan (about 909–988) was an English monk, abbot of Glastonbury and, from 959, Archbishop of Canterbury. He renewed monasticism in England on the basis of the Rule of Benedict, worked with the kings of his time, and crowned King Edgar in 973. He was also a musician and a craftsman. He died in 988.

life|05-20||Αγία Λυδία η Φιλιππησία||Lydia came from Thyatira and lived in Philippi in Macedonia, where she traded in purple. When the Apostle Paul came to Philippi around the year 50, she listened to his teaching and was baptized together with her household, becoming the first known Christian of Europe (Acts 16:14–15). She hosted Paul and his companions, and her house became the nucleus of the first Christian community of Philippi.

life|05-23||Αγία Μαρία η Μυροφόρος του Κλωπά||Mary of Clopas is mentioned in the Gospels among the women who stood near the cross of Jesus (John 19:25) and who went to the tomb on the morning of the Resurrection bearing myrrh (Mark 16:1). Tradition regards her as the mother of James the Less and of Joses and honors her among the Myrrh-bearers.

life|05-24||Όσιος Βικέντιος των Λερίνων||Vincent (died before 450) was a monk at the monastery of Lérins, in southern Gaul. In his work the "Commonitorium" (434) he formulated the well-known criterion for distinguishing true faith from innovations: that which has been believed "everywhere, always and by all". His work has influenced the theological thought of both East and West.

life|05-25||Άγιος Αλδέλμος Επίσκοπος Σέρμπορν||Aldhelm (about 639–709) was an English monk, abbot of Malmesbury and, from 705, Bishop of Sherborne. He was among the first English writers of Latin, a poet and theologian, and was renowned for his learning and eloquence. He founded monasteries and churches in Wessex and died in 709.

life|05-25||Άγιος Διονύσιος Επίσκοπος Μιλάνου||Dionysius was Bishop of Milan in the middle of the 4th century. At the Council of Milan in 355 he refused to sign the condemnation of Athanasius of Alexandria demanded by Emperor Constantius, and for this he was exiled to Cappadocia, where he died around 360.

life|05-26||Άγιος Ελευθέριος Επίσκοπος Ρώμης||Eleutherius was Bishop of Rome from about 175 until 189, in the time of Marcus Aurelius and Commodus. In his time the Church had to face the teaching of Montanism and Gnosticism, and Irenaeus of Lyons, who knew him, wrote of him with respect.

life|05-26||Άγιος Αυγουστίνος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Καντουαρίας||Augustine was a monk of Rome whom Pope Gregory the Great sent in 596, with about forty monks, to bring Christianity to the Anglo-Saxons. They arrived in Kent in 597, where King Ethelbert received them and was baptized. Augustine became the first Archbishop of Canterbury and died in 604 or 605. He is regarded as the "Apostle of the English".

life|05-26||Άγιοι Αλφαίος και Κάρπος οι Απόστολοι||Carpus is mentioned in the Second Epistle to Timothy (4:13), where Paul writes that he left his cloak and his books at Carpus's house in Troas. According to tradition, he was one of the seventy apostles and became bishop in Beroea of Thrace. For Alphaeus the information from tradition is brief: he is honored together with him as a co-worker of the apostles.

life|05-27||Όσιος Βεδέας ο Ομολογητής||Bede, also known as the Venerable Bede (672/673–735), was a monk of the monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow in Northumbria, England. He wrote many works of scriptural interpretation and history, and the most important of them is the "Ecclesiastical History of the English People" (731), a source for early English history. He died in 735, and his death is movingly described by his disciple Cuthbert.

life|05-28||Άγιος Γερμανός Επίσκοπος Παρισίων||Germanus (about 496–576) became Bishop of Paris in 555. He was an adviser to the Frankish king Childebert I, with whom he founded the monastery of Saint Vincent, which later took the name of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. He cared for the poor and the imprisoned and did not hesitate to rebuke rulers for their violence.

life|05-31||Άγιος Φιλόθεος Μητροπολίτης Τομπόλσκ||Philotheus (Leshchinsky, 1650–1727) became a monk in Kiev and in 1702 Metropolitan of Tobolsk and All Siberia. He organized missionary work among the peoples of Siberia, baptized thousands of Khanty and Mansi, built churches and schools, and saw to the education of the clergy. In his last years he withdrew to a monastery, where he died in 1727.

life|06-02||Αγία Βλανδίνη η Μάρτυς||Blandina was a slave and a Christian in Lyons in Gaul. In 177, under Marcus Aurelius, a storm of persecution struck the Christian communities of Lyons and Vienne. Blandina, weak in body, was tortured from morning until evening and showed extraordinary courage: with the confession "I am a Christian" she encouraged the others. She was exposed to the beasts and finally thrown to a bull and put to death. Her story is preserved in the letter of the Churches of Lyons and Vienne, which Eusebius quotes in the Ecclesiastical History.

life|06-02||Άγιος Ευγένιος Επίσκοπος Ρώμης||Eugene I was Bishop of Rome from 654 to 657. He was elected when his predecessor, Martin I, had been exiled by Emperor Constans II and was still alive. He became known for his compassion toward the poor and for his efforts to preserve peace with Constantinople without accepting the teaching of Monothelitism.

life|06-02||Άγιοι Μαρκελλίνος και Πέτρος||Marcellinus was a presbyter and Peter an exorcist in Rome. They were arrested in the persecution of Diocletian and beheaded around 304, according to tradition in a forest outside the city, where they themselves were forced to dig their own grave. Pope Damasus, who heard the story from their executioner, wrote an epigram for their tomb, and their relics were venerated in the catacomb of the same name in Rome.

life|06-03||Άγιος Κέβιν ο εξ Ιρλανδίας||Kevin (died around 618) was an Irish ascetic and founder of the monastery at Glendalough, in a valley with two lakes in County Wicklow. He began as a hermit and attracted disciples, and his monastery became an important center of learning and a place of pilgrimage in medieval Ireland. Accounts of his life present him as a lover of nature and quiet.

life|06-03||Άγιος Καικίλιος διδάσκαλος του Αγίου Κυπριανού||Caecilian was a presbyter of Carthage who, according to tradition, led the orator Cyprian to Christianity. Cyprian, after his baptism, took the name Caecilius out of respect. When Caecilian died, Cyprian took over the care of his family.

life|06-05||Άγιος Βονιφάτιος ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Boniface was born around 675 in Wessex in England with the name Winfrid and became a monk. With the approval of the pope he left for Germany and became the "Apostle of the Germans": according to tradition he cut down Thor's oak at Geismar, founded monasteries and bishoprics, and organized the Church of the Franks. He became Archbishop of Mainz. In his old age he returned as a missionary to Frisia, where he was killed by robbers in 754 near Dokkum.

life|06-06||Άγιος Ζαρλάθιος Επίσκοπος Τούαμ||Jarlath (about 6th century) founded a monastery and school at Tuam in Ireland and became its first bishop. Many pupils were taught by him, among them, according to tradition, Brendan the Navigator. The later Archdiocese of Tuam regards him as its founder.

life|06-07||Άγιος Βιλλιβάλδος ο Απόστολος||Willibald (about 700–787) was an Englishman from Wessex. He made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, with stops in Rome, Cyprus, Constantinople and Palestine, and the account of his journey, recorded by a nun, is among the first English travel narratives. Later he became a monk at Monte Cassino, and Boniface ordained him bishop of Eichstätt in Germany, and he founded monasteries.

life|06-07||Άγιος Μάρκελλος Επίσκοπος Ρώμης||Marcellus I was Bishop of Rome in 308–309, after a vacancy of many years on the throne, because the persecution had thrown the Church into turmoil. He organized the Roman parishes and dealt with the reconciliation of Christians who had denied the faith during the persecution and asked to return. This provoked reactions, and Emperor Maxentius exiled him. He died in exile.

life|06-07||Οσία Ευφροσύνη η εν Πολώκ||Euphrosyne of Polotsk (about 1101–1167) was a princess of the region of present-day Belarus. She refused marriage and became a nun. She founded two monasteries, copied books and distributed them to the poor, and commissioned her famous cross, which Lazar Bogsha made in 1161. She went on pilgrimage to the Holy Land and died in Jerusalem in 1167.

life|06-08||Οσία Μελανία η Πρεσβυτέρα||Melania the Elder (about 350–417) was a wealthy Roman noblewoman. She was widowed at the age of 22, and in 372 she left for Egypt, where she visited the ascetics of the desert. Later she settled in Jerusalem and founded a monastery on the Mount of Olives, where she hosted Rufinus of Aquileia. She helped many exiles and ascetics and gave a large part of her property to the poor. She died in 417. She is the grandmother of Melania the Younger.

life|06-09||Όσιος Κολούμπα ο Ιεραπόστολος||Columba, or Columcille (521–597), was born in Ireland, became a monk and founded several monasteries. Around 563 he left with twelve companions for the island of Iona, off the west coast of Scotland, and there he founded a monastery that became the center of Christianity in Scotland. He traveled into the interior of the country to preach to the Picts. He died on Iona in 597.

life|06-10||Άγιος Βασσιανός Επίσκοπος Λόντι||Bassian (about 320–409) was Bishop of Lodi in northern Italy. He was a friend of Ambrose of Milan and took part in the Council of Aquileia in 381, against Arianism. He founded a church dedicated to the apostles and became known for his care for the poor.

life|06-10||Άγιος Μακάριος ο Απόστολος των||Makary (Glukharev, 1792–1847) was a Russian priest and monk who from 1830 founded a mission in the Altai of Siberia. He learned the local languages, preached to the native populations and translated sacred texts. He was also engaged in translating the Old Testament into Russian. He died in 1847.

life|06-11||Άγιος Λουκάς Αρχιεπίσκοπος Κριμαίας||Luke (Valentin Felixovich Voyno-Yasenetsky, 1877–1961) was a Russian physician, surgeon and archbishop. As a surgeon he wrote the book "Essays on Purulent Surgery" (1934), for which he was awarded a Stalin Prize, and he became a bishop in 1923 without giving up medicine. He spent many years in exile and in prison under the Soviet regime. He became Archbishop of Simferopol and Crimea in 1946, despite his blindness in his last years. He died in 1961.

life|06-13||Άγιος Ευλόγιος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Αλεξανδρείας||Eulogius was Patriarch of Alexandria from 580 to 607. He was a contemporary and friend of Pope Gregory the Great, with whom he exchanged letters, and he struggled against the heresies, especially Monophysitism, and defended the Orthodox faith of Chalcedon. He was known for his preaching and his writings.

life|06-14||Άγιος Μεθόδιος ο Ομολογητής Πατριάρχης||Methodius (about 788–847) was born in Syracuse in Sicily and became a monk. During the iconoclast period he suffered imprisonment and exile for the defense of the icons. After the death of Emperor Theophilos he became Patriarch of Constantinople in 843, and on the first Sunday of Lent of that year the restoration of the icons was celebrated, the "Sunday of Orthodoxy". He died in 847.

life|06-15||Άγιος Αυγουστίνος Επίσκοπος Ιππώνος||Augustine (354–430) was born in Thagaste in Algeria to a pagan father and a Christian mother, Monica. He studied rhetoric in Carthage, followed Manichaeism for years and taught in Rome and in Milan, where the influence of Ambrose and the prayer of his mother led him to Christianity. He was baptized in 387. He became a priest and, in 395, Bishop of Hippo. He wrote many works, among them the "Confessions" and the "City of God". He died in 430, while the Vandals were besieging the city.

life|06-15||Άγιοι Βίτος, Μόδεστος και Κρησκεντία||Vitus was a youth from Sicily who, according to tradition, was martyred under Diocletian, around 303, together with his tutor Modestus and his nurse Crescentia. He was greatly venerated in the Middle Ages in the West, especially in Germany and Bohemia.

life|06-15||Άγιος Ιωνάς Μητροπολίτης Μόσχας||Jonah (died 1461) became Metropolitan of Moscow in 1448, elected by the Russian bishops without the approval of Constantinople, an event that became the starting point of the independence of the Russian Church. He was the first metropolitan who did not receive the office from the Patriarchate. He supported the Trinity-Saint Sergius Monastery and lived in austerity. He died in 1461.

life|06-15||Όσιος Ιερώνυμος||Jerome (about 347–420) was born in Stridon in Dalmatia and studied in Rome. He lived as an ascetic in the desert of Chalcis and later in Rome, where Pope Damasus entrusted him with translating the Bible into Latin. In 386 he settled in Bethlehem and founded a monastery. His translation, the "Vulgate", became the principal text of the Bible in the West. He also wrote commentaries and many letters. He died in 420.

life|06-16||Όσιος Μωυσής της Όπτινα||Moses (Putilov, 1782–1862) was abbot of the Optina Monastery, near Kozelsk in Russia. Together with his brother Anthony he gave the monastery new life and made it a center of the elders (startsy), people of spiritual experience who guided those who asked for advice. Optina later became a place of pilgrimage and attracted writers and intellectuals.

life|06-17||Άγιος Αλβανός ο Πρωτομάρτυρας||Alban was a pagan in Verulamium (present-day St Albans) in Roman Britain. He gave shelter to a priest who was being hunted and, influenced by his teaching and faith, became a Christian. When they came to arrest the priest, Alban put on his cloak and gave himself up in his place. He refused to sacrifice to the idols and was beheaded. He is regarded as the first known martyr of Britain.

life|06-19||Άγιοι Γερβάσιος, Προτάσιος||Gervasius and Protasius were, according to tradition, twin brothers and martyrs of Milan. Their relics were discovered in 386 by Ambrose of Milan beneath the floor of the church, and were carried in a great festal procession to the Basilica of Ambrose, where they remain. The discovery helped to strengthen the Orthodox of Milan, who were then facing the Arians.

life|06-20||Όσιος Νικόλαος Καβάσιλας||Nicholas Kabasilas (about 1319–after 1391) was born in Thessaloniki and was a lay theologian and writer. He studied in Thessaloniki and in Constantinople and took part in the political and theological events of his time. He wrote "On the Life in Christ" and the "Commentary on the Divine Liturgy", works that brought out the experience of the mysteries. The Church recognized him as a saint in 1983.

life|06-20||Άγιος Κάλλιστος Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Callistus I was Patriarch of Constantinople from 1350 to 1353 and again from 1355 to 1363. He supported the hesychast tradition and the teaching of Gregory Palamas,. He died in 1363 in Serbia, on a mission to resolve the ecclesiastical dispute.

life|06-23||Οσία Εθελδρέδα η βασίλισσα||Etheldreda (about 636–679) was the daughter of the king of East Anglia. She married and became queen of Northumbria, but she kept her virginity and, despite her husband's displeasure, became a nun. In 673 she founded a monastery at Ely and became its abbess. She died in 679 and her tomb became a place of pilgrimage.

life|06-24||Όσιος Αθανάσιος ο Πάριος||Athanasios of Paros (1721–1813) was born on Paros. He became a monk and taught at the Athonite School on Mount Athos and on Chios. He belonged to the Kollyvades movement, which defended tradition and the patristic texts, and he wrote many works, among them anthologies and commentaries. He died in 1813 on Chios.

life|06-25||Άγιος Θεόληπτος Μητροπολίτης Φιλαδελφείας||Theoleptos (about 1250–1322) was born in Nicaea and became a monk on Mount Athos. In 1283 he became Metropolitan of Philadelphia in Asia Minor, and his metropolis was among the last Byzantine cities of the region. He was a spiritual father and teacher of hesychasts and exercised great influence, among others on Gregory Palamas. He died in 1322.

life|06-25||Όσιος Διονύσιος κτίτωρ Ιεράς Μονής||Dionysios the Athonite, from Korisos in Kastoria, was a monk of Mount Athos who around 1374, with the support of Emperor Alexios III Komnenos of Trebizond, founded the Monastery of Dionysiou on Athos. The monastery, dedicated to the Honorable Forerunner, is today fifth in the hierarchy of the Athonite monasteries.

life|06-25||Άγιος Πρόσπερος εξ Ακουϊτανίας||Prosper (about 390–455) was a French theologian from Aquitaine. He defended Augustine's teaching on grace against the so-called Semi-Pelagians and wrote works on the subject. He also wrote a Chronicle that reaches to 455. According to some sources he worked in Rome near Pope Leo I; the place of his death is not certain.

life|06-26||Άγιοι Ιωάννης και Παύλος οι Μάρτυρες||John and Paul were, according to tradition, brothers and officials of the court of Constantia, the daughter of Constantine. Under Julian the Apostate they refused to serve the emperor and to sacrifice to the idols and were beheaded secretly in their house, around 362. Over their house was built in Rome, on the Caelian Hill, the Basilica of Saints John and Paul.

life|06-27||Οσία Ιωάννα η Μυροφόρος||Joanna was the wife of Chuza, steward of Herod Antipas. The Gospel of Luke (8:3) mentions her among the women who had been healed by Jesus and who followed him and supported him with their possessions. She was among the Myrrh-bearers who went to the tomb on the morning of the Resurrection (Luke 24:10).

life|06-30||Αγία Μαρία η μητέρα του Ευαγγελιστού Μάρκου||Mary was the mother of John Mark, the Evangelist Mark. The Acts of the Apostles (12:12) mentions that her house in Jerusalem was a meeting and prayer place of the first Christians, and Peter took refuge there when he was released from prison. She was a relative of Barnabas.

life|07-01||Άγιος Λέων Β’ ο Επίσκοπος Ρώμης||Leo II was Bishop of Rome for a short time, from 682 to 683. He confirmed the decisions of the Sixth Ecumenical Council, which condemned Monothelitism, and the Church honors him for this stance of his.

life|07-01||Άγιος Γάλλος ο Επίσκοπος Κλερμόν||Gallus was Bishop of Clermont in France in the middle of the 6th century. He was the uncle of Gregory of Tours, who wrote his Life and told of his kindness and his care for the poor and the sick of his city.

life|07-01||Άγιος Μαυρίκιος ο Μάρτυρας||Maurice was the leader of the so-called Theban Legion, a Roman unit of Christian soldiers. According to tradition, the men refused to sacrifice to the idols and to turn against other Christians, and were put to death at Agaunum in Switzerland at the end of the 3rd century. The place later took the name Saint-Maurice.

life|07-02||Άγιος Ιουβενάλιος ο Πατριάρχης Ιεροσολύμων||Juvenal was Bishop of Jerusalem from 422 to 458. He took part in the Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus and in the Fourth of Chalcedon, in 451, where the patriarchal rank of the Church of Jerusalem was recognized, with jurisdiction over Palestine.

life|07-02||Άγιος Ιώβ ο Πατριάρχης Μόσχας||Job was the first Patriarch of Moscow, from 1589, when the Russian Church became a patriarchate with the consent of Patriarch Jeremias II of Constantinople. He supported the Church in the difficult years of the "Time of Troubles" and died in 1607.

life|07-02||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Αρχιεπίσκοπος Σαγκάης||John Maximovich (1896–1966) was born in Ukraine and left Russia after the revolution. He became a bishop in China and cared for the refugees and orphans of Shanghai, and later served in Western Europe and in San Francisco. He was beloved for his ascetic life and his charity.

life|07-02||Άγιος Στέφανος ο Μέγας ο Πρίγκηπας Μολδαβίας||Stephen the Great ruled Moldavia from 1457 until his death in 1504. He successfully faced the Ottomans and other neighbors, and built many monasteries and churches. He was glorified as a saint by the Church of Romania in 1992.

life|07-03||Άγιος Ανατόλιος ο Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Anatolius was Patriarch of Constantinople from 449 to 458. He stood by the decisions of the Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon and contributed to their implementation.

life|07-04||Άγιος Μιχαήλ ο Χωνιάτης ο Μητροπολίτης Αθηνών||Michael Choniates (about 1138–1222) was Metropolitan of Athens from 1182. When Leo Sgouros besieged the Acropolis and, in 1204, the Franks seized the city, he defended his flock. He was forced to leave and died on Kea. He was also a scholar, the brother of the historian Niketas Choniates.

life|07-05||Άγιος Παλλάδιος ο Απόστολος και Επίσκοπος Σκωτίας||Palladius was sent in 431 by Pope Celestine to the Christians of Ireland as bishop, before Patrick. According to tradition, he also worked in Scotland.

life|07-06||Οσία Σεξβούργα η βασίλισσα του Κέντ||Seaxburh was queen of Kent in England in the 7th century. After the death of her husband she founded a monastery and became a nun, and later abbess at Ely, where she died around 699.

life|07-07||Αγία Ευφροσύνη η Μεγάλη Πριγκίπισσα της Ρωσσίας||Euphrosyne was the wife of Grand Prince Dmitry Donskoy. After his death she became a nun and founded the Ascension Convent in the Moscow Kremlin, where she died in 1407.

life|07-07||Οσία Εθελβούργα η εκ Βρεττανίας||Ethelburga was an Anglo-Saxon abbess of the convent of Faremoutiers in France in the 7th century, and died around 664. She became known for the piety and the brotherly love of the members of the monastery.

life|07-08||Αγία Θεοδοσία η Μάρτυς η μητέρα του Αγίου Προκοπίου||Theodosia lived in Palestine and, according to tradition, was the mother of the martyr Procopius. In the persecution of Diocletian, at the beginning of the 4th century, she was put to death for her faith in Christ.

life|07-09||Άγιος Παγκράτιος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Ταυρομενίας||According to tradition, Pancras was the first bishop of Tauromenium (Taormina) in Sicily and preached the Gospel in the region. The Church honors him as a hieromartyr.

life|07-10||Άγιοι Ιανουάριος, Φήλιξ, Φίλιππος, Σιλβανός, Αλέξανδρος, Βιτάλιος και Μαρτιάλιος||The seven brothers were sons of Saint Felicitas, a Christian woman of Rome. According to tradition, they were martyred in the 2nd century under Emperor Antoninus Pius, and their mother was put to death after them, having encouraged them to remain faithful.

life|07-11||Αγία Όλγα η Ισαπόστολος||Olga was a princess of Kiev. After the death of her husband Igor she ruled on behalf of her young son. She was baptized in Constantinople around 957 and tried to spread Christianity in Russia. She died in 969 and was the grandmother of Vladimir, who brought the Russians to baptism. She is honored as equal to the apostles.

life|07-11||Άγιος Ευσέβιος ο Α’ ο Επίσκοπος Ρώμης||Eusebius was Bishop of Rome in 309 or 310, in a period when the Church, after the persecution of Diocletian, was divided over the question of the "lapsed". He was exiled to Sicily, where he died.

life|07-11||Όσιος Σωφρόνιος Σαχάρωφ||Sophrony Sakharov (1896–1993) was a Russian painter who became a monk on Mount Athos and a disciple of Saint Silouan. He published the writings of Silouan and, in 1959, founded in Essex, England, the Monastery of Saint John the Baptist, where he wrote and taught about prayer.

life|07-12||Αγία Βερονίκη η αιμορροούσα||The woman who suffered from bleeding for twelve years approached Christ and touched his garment, and was healed, as the Gospels relate. According to tradition, she came from Paneas (Caesarea Philippi) and later erected a statue of Christ.

life|07-12||Άγιος Ερμαγόρας ο Ιερομάρτυρας||According to tradition, Hermagoras was the first bishop of Aquileia in northern Italy, ordained by the Apostle Mark, and he was martyred together with his deacon Fortunatus.

life|07-12||Όσιος Μιχαήλ ο Μαλεΐνος||Michael Maleinos (about 894–962) was an ascetic at Kyminas in Bithynia and a relative of Emperor Nikephoros Phokas. He was the spiritual father of Saint Athanasios the Athonite, who became his disciple before going to Mount Athos.

life|07-13||Άγιος Ανάκλητος ο Επίσκοπος Ρώμης||Anacletus, also known as Cletus, was one of the first bishops of Rome, at the end of the 1st century. The sources for his life are few; the Church honors him as a martyr.

life|07-13||Άγιος Ευγένιος ο Επίσκοπος Καρθαγένης||Eugenius was Bishop of Carthage in Africa at the end of the 5th century. Under the Vandals, who were Arians, he was exiled and suffered for the Orthodox faith. He died in exile in 505.

life|07-13||Άγιος Ονησίφορος||Onesiphorus was a Christian of Ephesus whom the Apostle Paul mentions in the Second Epistle to Timothy, because he supported him and was not ashamed of his chains when Paul was imprisoned in Rome. Tradition counts him among the Seventy.

life|07-13||Όσιος Στέφανος ο Σαββαΐτης||Stephen was a monk of the Monastery of Saint Sabbas in Palestine in the 8th century, and a nephew of John of Damascus. He lived with ascetic strictness and was regarded as a wonderworker.

life|07-14||Άγιος Ιωσήφ ο Ομολογητής ο Αρχιεπίσκοπος Θεσσαλονίκης||Joseph (about 762–830) was the brother of Theodore the Studite, a monk of the Monastery of Saccudio and then of Stoudios, and later Archbishop of Thessaloniki. He stood by Theodore in the struggle for the icons and suffered exile during the iconoclast period. He also wrote hymns.

life|07-14||Άγιος Φρίθων ή Δεουσδεδίτος ο Αρχιεπίσκοπος Καντέρμπουρι||Deusdedit was the first Englishman to become Archbishop of Canterbury, from 655 to 664. He continued the work of spreading Christianity in England and died of the plague.

life|07-14||Όσιος θεοφόρος Νικόδημος ο Αγιορείτης||Nikodemos was born on Naxos in 1749 and became a monk on Mount Athos. Together with Makarios of Corinth he published the Philokalia, and he wrote and compiled a multitude of works: the Pedalion, with the canons of the Church, the Synaxaristes of the Orthodox saints, Unseen Warfare and others. He died in 1809 and is regarded as one of the great teachers of Orthodox spirituality.

life|07-15||Άγιος Βλαδίμηρος ο Ισαπόστολος και Φωτιστής των Ρώσσων||Vladimir was Grand Prince of Kiev. Originally a pagan, he was baptized in 988 and called the Russians to become Christians. He brought priests and teachers from Byzantium and built churches. He died in 1015 and is honored as equal to the apostles.

life|07-17||Αγία Συμφορόζα η Μάρτυρας και τα τέκνα αυτής||Symphorosa was a Christian of Rome, the widow of the martyr Getulius. According to tradition, she was martyred under Hadrian together with her seven children at Tivoli, because they refused to sacrifice to the idols.

life|07-17||Άγιοι Σάββας, Κλήμης, Αγγελάριος, Γόρασδος και Ναούμ οι Ισαπόστολοι||The five saints were disciples of Cyril and Methodius. They continued the work of their teachers in Moravia and in the Balkans in the 9th and 10th centuries. Clement and Naum founded in Ohrid a school that educated clergy and spread the Slavonic script and liturgical language.

life|07-17||Άγιοι Νικόλαος ο Β’ τσάρος Ρωσσίας||Tsar Nicholas II, his wife Alexandra and their five children were executed by the Bolsheviks on the night of 16 to 17 July 1918 in Yekaterinburg. The Russian Church proclaimed them saints, as "passion-bearers", in 2000.

life|07-17||Άγιος Αλβανός ο Πρωτομάρτυς της Βρεττανίας||Alban lived in Verulamium in Britain in the 3rd or 4th century. According to tradition, he sheltered a persecuted priest and, influenced by him, became a Christian. When they came to arrest the priest, he put on his cloak and gave himself up in his place, and was beheaded. He is regarded as the first known martyr of Britain.

life|07-18||Αγία Ελισάβετ η Μάρτυς και η συν αυτή Αγία Βαρβάρα||Grand Duchess Elizabeth Feodorovna (1864–1918) was the sister of Empress Alexandra. After the murder of her husband, in 1905, she founded in Moscow the Convent of Martha and Mary and devoted herself to the poor and the sick. The Bolsheviks threw her, together with Barbara and others, into a mine at Alapayevsk, on 18 July 1918.

life|07-19||Αγίες Ρουφίνη και Ιούστα οι Μάρτυρες||Justa and Rufina were sisters and potters in Seville in Spain. According to tradition, they refused to sell pots for pagan ceremonies and were martyred around 287.

life|07-19||Άγιος Σύμμαχος ο Επίσκοπος Ρώμης||Symmachus was Bishop of Rome from 498 to 514. He was elected in a divided election and faced the antipope Laurentius. He cared for the poor and took on the governance of the Church in difficult circumstances.

life|07-20||Αγία Μαργαρίτα η Παρθενομάρτυς||Margaret (in Greek also Marina) came from Antioch in Pisidia and, according to tradition, was martyred around 304, in the persecution of Diocletian, because she refused to deny Christ and to marry a pagan ruler. She is honored in the West as well.

life|07-20||Άγιος Φλαβιανός Β’ ο Ομολογητής ο Πατριάρχης Αντιοχείας||Flavian was Patriarch of Antioch from 498 to 512. He resisted the pressures of Emperor Anastasius and of Severus of Antioch in favor of Monophysitism and was exiled, and he died in exile.

life|07-21||Αγία Πραξέδη η Μάρτυς||Praxedes was a Christian of Rome, according to tradition the sister of Pudentiana and the daughter of Pudens, who hosted the Apostle Peter. She cared for imprisoned Christians and buried the martyrs, and the Church honors her as a martyr.

life|07-22||Άγιος Σαλβιανός ο Απολογητής||Salvian (about 400–480) was a priest of Marseille. In his work "On the Governance of God" he argued that the calamities of the Roman Empire were also due to the moral decline of people, and he denounced the injustice done to the poor.

life|07-23||Προφήτης Ιεζεκιήλ||Ezekiel was a priest and prophet. He was carried captive to Babylon in 597 BC and, near the river Chebar, saw the vision of the glory of God. His book also contains the vision of the dry bones that come to life and the vision of the new temple. He comforted the exiles and called them to repentance.

life|07-23||Άγιος Σαλλούστιος ο Πατριάρχης Ιεροσολύμων||Sallustius was Patriarch of Jerusalem from 486 to 494. He had a close relationship with Saint Sabbas, who founded his lavra in Palestine, and he supported the Orthodox faith of Chalcedon.
life|07-23||Άγιος Θύρσος ή Θέρισσος ο Αναχωρητής ο Επίσκοπος Καρπασέων||Thyrsus was Bishop of Karpasia in Cyprus. As the tradition reports, he lived as an ascetic and was regarded as a wonderworker.

life|07-24||Άγιοι Βόρις και Γκλέμπ οι Μάρτυρες||Boris and Gleb were sons of Vladimir of Kiev. After the death of their father, in 1015, their brother Sviatopolk murdered them in order to take power. They did not resist, and the Russian Church honors them as "passion-bearers", among its first saints.

life|07-24||Άγιος Αθηναγόρας ο Απολογητης||Athenagoras was an Athenian philosopher of the 2nd century who became a Christian. He wrote the "Plea for the Christians", which he addressed around 177 to the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus, to defend the Christians against the accusations, and a work on the resurrection of the dead.

life|07-25||Οσία Ολυμπιάδα η Διακόνισσα||Olympias (about 368–408) was a wealthy and noble woman of Constantinople. She was widowed young and, ordained a deaconess, distributed her property to the poor and to the Church. She was a spiritual daughter and friend of John Chrysostom and supported him in his persecutions and in his exile.

life|07-26||Άγιος Ερμόλαος ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Hermolaus was a presbyter of Nicomedia and the teacher of Saint Panteleimon. According to tradition, he was martyred around 305 in the persecution of Maximian, together with other Christians.
life|07-27||Άγιος Ιωάσαφ ο Μητροπολίτης Μόσχας||Joasaph was Metropolitan of Moscow from 1539 to 1542. It is said that he suffered from the internal rivalries of the boyars of the time.

life|07-28||Άγιος Βίκτωρ ο Ιερομάρτυρας ο Επίσκοπος Ρώμης||Victor I was Bishop of Rome from 189 to 199, and was of African origin. He stood in opposition to the Churches of Asia Minor over the date of Easter and tried to impose unity. Tradition honors him as a martyr.

life|07-28||Όσιος Σαμψών ο εξ Ουαλίας||Samson (about 485–565) was a monk in Wales and then Bishop of Dol in Brittany, France. He founded monasteries, was present at the Council of Paris, and is among the great missionaries of the region.

life|07-29||Άγιος Όλαφ ο βασιλέας||Olaf II Haraldsson became king of Norway and tried to establish Christianity there. He lost his throne and was killed in the Battle of Stiklestad, on 29 July 1030. He was soon venerated as a saint, and is the patron of Norway.

life|07-29||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Στρατιώτης ο Μάρτυρας||John was a soldier in the time of Julian the Apostate. According to tradition, he secretly helped the persecuted Christians, hiding and caring for them, and he is honored as patron of prisoners and of the wronged.

life|07-30||Άγιος Πέτρος ο Χρυσολόγος ο Επίσκοπος Ραβέννας||Peter (about 380–450) was Bishop of Ravenna, the capital of the Western Empire. He became known for his short, lively sermons, which won him the epithet "Chrysologus", that is, one who speaks with golden words. He also wrote to Eutyches, encouraging him to accept the Tome of Leo.

life|07-30||Άγιος Λούπος ο Επίσκοπος Τροίας||Lupus (about 383–479) was Bishop of Troyes in France. In 429 he went with Germanus of Auxerre to Britain to fight Pelagianism and, according to tradition, in 451 he saved his city from the attack of Attila.

life|07-30||Αγία Αγγελίνα η πριγκίπισσα των Σέρβων||Angelina was a Greek, the daughter of the ruler of Epirus, and married Despot Stefan Branković of Serbia. After the Ottoman conquest she left for Hungary and then became a nun. She died in 1520 in the Krušedol monastery.

life|07-31||Άγιος Ιωσήφ ο από Αριμαθαίας||Joseph of Arimathea was wealthy and a member of the Sanhedrin, a secret disciple of Christ. After the crucifixion he asked Pilate for the body of Jesus, wrapped it in a linen sheet and laid it in a new tomb which he had hewn for himself, as the Gospels relate.

life|08-01||Άγιοι Επτά Μακαβαίοι||The seven Maccabee brothers, with their mother and the elder Eleazar, were martyred around 167 BC in Antioch, under King Antiochus IV Epiphanes, because they refused to eat pork and to transgress the law of God. The account is found in the Second Book of Maccabees, and the Church honors them as forerunners of the Christian martyrs.

life|08-03||Αγία Σαλώμη η Μυροφόρος||Salome was one of the women who followed Jesus and served him. According to tradition she was the mother of the apostles James and John, sons of Zebedee. She stood near the cross and went with myrrh to the tomb on the morning of Sunday, where she learned of the Resurrection.

life|08-03||Άγιος Στέφανος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Πάπας Ρώμης||Stephen I was Bishop of Rome from 254 to 257. He disagreed with Cyprian of Carthage over whether those who had been baptized by heretics had to be baptized again. According to tradition, he was martyred in 257 in the persecution of Valerian.

life|08-03||Όσιοι Δαλμάτιος, Φαύστος, και Ισαάκιος||Isaac was an ascetic in Constantinople at the end of the 4th century. Dalmatius, a military man who became a monk, was his disciple and abbot of the monastery that took his name, and Faustus was his son. The three were models of ascetic life and defended Orthodoxy in Ephesus and in Constantinople.

life|08-05||Αγία Νόννα||Nonna was the mother of Gregory the Theologian, of Gorgonia and of Caesarius. By her steadfast faith and prayer she led her husband Gregory, who was a pagan, to baptism, and he later became Bishop of Nazianzus. She died in 374.

life|08-05||Άγιος Ευθύμιος Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Euthymius was Patriarch of Constantinople from 907 to 912. He opposed the fourth marriage of Emperor Leo VI, and this led to his deposition and exile. He expressed the view of the Church on the sanctity of marriage and was honored by the faithful.

life|08-05||Άγιος Φάβιος||Fabian was Bishop of Rome from 236 and was martyred in 250 in the persecution of Emperor Decius. He organized the administration of the Church of Rome into districts and cared for the cemeteries of the Christians.

life|08-07||Άγιος Νάρκισσος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Πατριάρχης Ιεροσολύμων||Narcissus was Bishop of Jerusalem at the end of the 2nd century and the beginning of the 3rd. He took part in the dispute over the date of Easter and was respected for his holiness and his age. Tradition also relates a miracle with the oil of the lamps.

life|08-08||Άγιος Τριαντάφυλλος ο Μάρτυρας από τή Ζαγορά||Triantaphyllos came from Zagora on Pelion and is one of the new martyrs of the period of Turkish rule, who was martyred for his faith in Christ. The Church honors him as a new martyr.

life|08-09||Άγιος Oswald (Αγγλος)||Oswald was king of Northumbria in England from 634. He had been baptized in the monastery of Iona and invited Aidan from there to preach to his people. He was killed in 642 in battle with the pagan king of Mercia, Penda, and was immediately venerated as a saint.

life|08-09||Όσιος Γερμανός ο εν Αλάσκα||Herman (about 1756–1837) was a Russian monk who came in 1794 from the Valaam monastery to Alaska as a missionary. He settled on Spruce Island, where he lived an ascetic life and protected the natives from exploitation. He was canonized in 1970.

life|08-11||Άγιος Νήφων Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Niphon II was Patriarch of Constantinople in 1486–1488 and 1497–1498. He was deposed and later went to Wallachia, where he helped organize the Church and founded monasteries. He withdrew to Mount Athos and died in 1508 at the Monastery of Dionysiou.

life|08-11||Ανάμνηση Θαύματος Αγίου Σπυρίδωνα||On this day the people of Corfu remember the salvation of the island from the Ottoman siege of 1716, when, according to tradition, Saint Spyridon protected the city. The memory is celebrated with a litany of the relics of the saint, which are kept in Corfu.

life|08-13||Αγία Ευδοκία η βασίλισσα||Eudocia (about 401–460) was born in Athens with the name Athenais, was the daughter of a philosopher and became the wife of Emperor Theodosius II. She wrote poems on religious themes and, after leaving Constantinople, lived in Jerusalem, where she founded churches and monasteries and died in 460.

life|08-14||Άγιος Μάρκελλος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Απαμείας||Marcellus was Bishop of Apamea in Syria. At the end of the 4th century he destroyed pagan temples of the region and, according to tradition, was killed by pagans around 389.

life|08-16||Άγιος Αλκιβιάδης ο Μάρτυρας||Alcibiades was one of the Christians of Lyons who were martyred in 177. He was an ascetic and, as the letter of the church of Lyons relates, lived only on bread and water, and after the urging of the martyr Attalus he began to eat of everything with thanksgiving.

life|08-20||Άγιος Στέφανος ο Α’ Βασιλεύς Ουγγαρίας||Stephen (about 975–1038) was the first king of Hungary, and was crowned in the year 1000 or 1001. He established bishoprics, built monasteries and churches and organized the state. The Church proclaimed him a saint in 1083.

life|08-20||Άγιος Ιερόθεος ο Α’ Επίσκοπος Ουγγαρίας||Hierotheos was ordained by the Patriarch of Constantinople, around 950, and was sent as a missionary to the Hungarians. Tradition regards him as the first bishop of Hungary.

life|08-23||Άγιος Ειρηναίος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Λουγδούνου||Irenaeus (about 130–202) came from Smyrna and had heard Polycarp in his youth. He became Bishop of Lugdunum (Lyons) in Gaul. In his work "Refutation and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So Called" he defended the tradition of the Church against the Gnostics. Tradition regards him as a martyr.

life|08-23||Άγιος Ποθεινός ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Λουγδούνου||Pothinus was the first known bishop of Lugdunum (Lyons) in Gaul. At about ninety years of age, in 177, he was arrested in the persecution in the city and died in prison from the tortures, as the letter of the Christians of Lyons relates.

life|08-23||Άγιος Ειρηναίος ο Μάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Σιρμίου||Irenaeus was Bishop of Sirmium, in present-day Serbia. In the persecution of Diocletian, in 304, he refused to sacrifice to the idols and was beheaded.

life|08-25||Άγιος Μηνάς Αρχιεπίσκοπος Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Menas was Patriarch of Constantinople from 536 to 552, under Emperor Justinian. He was ordained by Pope Agapetus, who had come to Constantinople, and took part in the theological controversies of the time.

life|08-27||Άγιος Λιβέριος ο Ομολογητής Πάπας Ρώμης||Liberius was Bishop of Rome from 352 to 366. He refused to condemn Athanasius of Alexandria and was exiled by Constantius II, who favored the Arians. He returned to Rome in 358.

life|08-27||Άγιος Όσιος Επίσκοπος Κορδούης της Ισπανίας||Hosius (about 256–358) was Bishop of Córdoba and an adviser to Constantine on ecclesiastical matters. He took part in, and probably presided over, the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea. Later he resisted Constantius and suffered exile. He died at a very advanced age.

life|08-27||Βάπτιση του Αιθίοπα Ευνούχου από τον Άγιο Φίλιππο||The Acts of the Apostles relates that the deacon Philip met, on the road from Jerusalem to Gaza, an Ethiopian official, treasurer of Queen Candace. He was reading the prophet Isaiah, and Philip explained to him that the text speaks of Christ. The Ethiopian asked to be baptized in water they found on the road.

life|08-28||Άγιος Εζεκίας ο Δίκαιος Βασιλιάς||Hezekiah was king of Judah, about 715–686 BC. He cleansed the temple of the worship of idols, renewed the Passover and built the water system of Jerusalem, the "Siloam tunnel". When the Assyrian king Sennacherib besieged the city, he prayed with the prophet Isaiah and the city was saved.

life|08-28||Αγία Άννα θυγατέρα του Φανουήλ||The prophetess Anna, of the tribe of Asher, was a widow and very advanced in years. She did not leave the temple and served with fasting and prayer. When the Theotokos and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to the temple, she gave glory to God and spoke about him to all who were waiting for the salvation of Israel, as the Gospel according to Luke relates.

life|08-29||Άγιος Sebbi (Άγγλος)||Sebbi was king of the East Saxons of England for about thirty years, from 664. He was pious and charitable, and in his old age he abdicated and became a monk. He died around 694 and was buried in London.

life|08-29||Οσία Θεοδώρα η εν Θεσσαλονίκη||Theodora was born around 812 on Aegina. She married and had a daughter, Theopiste. When the Arabs captured Aegina, the family took refuge in Thessaloniki, where Theodora became a nun together with her daughter. She died in 892 and her relics are in Thessaloniki.

life|08-31||Άγιος Aidan (Σκωτσέζος)||Aidan was a monk from Iona. In 635 King Oswald of Northumbria summoned him to preach to his people, and Aidan founded the monastery of Lindisfarne. He traveled on foot, spoke to ordinary people and the poor, and died in 651.

life|08-31||Αγία Cuthburge (Βρετανίδα)||Cuthburga was the sister of King Ine of Wessex. She married the king of Northumbria, but their marriage was annulled and she became a nun. She founded the monastery of Wimborne and died around 725.

life|09-01||Άγιος Ιησούς ο Δίκαιος||Jesus, who was also called Justus, is mentioned in Paul's Epistle to the Colossians among his fellow workers who came from Judaism and stood by his side "for the kingdom of God" and were a comfort to him. The Church honors his memory as one of the first fellow workers of the Apostle to the Gentiles.

life|09-02||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Νηστευτής||John was Patriarch of Constantinople from 582 to 595, in the time of the emperors Tiberius and Maurice. He became known for his strict fasting, his simple life and his care for the poor.
