In his days the title "Ecumenical" was used in his patriarchal signature, which provoked a reaction from Pope Gregory the Dialogist. He died in 595.

life|09-03||Αγία Φοίβη η διακόνισσα||Phoebe was a deaconess of the Church of Cenchreae, the port of Corinth. The Apostle Paul mentions her at the end of the Epistle to the Romans as "our sister" and "a helper of many, and of myself also," and asks the Christians of Rome to receive her. According to tradition, she herself carried the epistle to Rome.

life|09-07||Οσία Κασσιανή||Cassiane (or Kassia) was born in Constantinople around 810 and lived in the time of the emperor Theophilus. She became a nun, founded a monastery, and was one of the few women of the Byzantine era who wrote hymns and poetry. Her best-known work is the troparion "Lord, the woman who had fallen into many sins," which is chanted every year on the evening of Holy Tuesday.

life|09-12||Άγιος Χρυσόστομος Σμύρνης ο Εθνοϊερομάρτυρας||Chrysostomos Kalafatis was born in 1867 in Triglia in Bithynia and was Metropolitan of Smyrna from 1910. When the Turkish army entered Smyrna in September 1922, he refused to abandon his flock. He was handed over to a mob and put to death with torture in the streets of the city. The Church of Greece proclaimed him a saint in 1992.

life|09-13||Άγιος Μελέτιος Πηγάς||Meletios Pegas was born in 1549 in Heraklion, Crete, which was then a Venetian possession. He studied at Padua, became a monk and a scholar, and from 1590 until his death in 1601 was Patriarch of Alexandria. He defended the Orthodox faith against the pressures of the Latins and the problems caused by the calendar reform, and he raised up Cyril Lucaris. He died in Alexandria.

life|09-14||Οσία Πλακίλλα η Ευσεβέστατη Βασίλισσα||Aelia Flaccilla was the first wife of the emperor Theodosius I and the mother of Arcadius and Honorius. She became known for her piety and almsgiving; she visited the sick and the poor and cared for them herself. She died in 386.

life|09-15||Άγιος Συμεών Αρχιεπίσκοπος Θεσσαλονίκης||Symeon was Archbishop of Thessaloniki in the early 15th century and an important author of liturgical and theological works, such as his interpretations of worship and of the mysteries. He stood by the people of Thessaloniki in the time of the Ottoman danger and died in 1429, shortly before the fall of the city in 1430.

life|09-15||Άγιος Πορφύριος ο μίμος||Porphyrius, according to tradition, was an actor and mime in the time of the emperor Julian the Apostate. While mocking the baptism of Christians in a performance, he suddenly believed and confessed the new faith. Despite the emperor's pressure, he did not deny it and was martyred.

life|09-16||Αγία Λουντμίλα||Ludmila was born around 860 and was Duchess of Bohemia, grandmother of Saint Wenceslaus. She was baptized a Christian and saw to her grandson's Christian upbringing. She was killed in 921 at Tetín, after a clash with the pagan faction of the court, and is regarded as one of the first martyrs of the Czechs.

life|09-16||Άγιος Νινιάν (Βρετανός)||Ninian was a British missionary to the Picts, around the 5th century. At Whithorn in southwestern Scotland he founded a church and monastery, which became a center for the Christianization of the region.

life|09-16||Όσιος Κυπριανός Μητροπολίτης Κιέβου, Ρώσος||Cyprian was born in Bulgaria around 1330 and was a disciple of Patriarch Philotheos Kokkinos. He became Metropolitan of Kiev and All Russia and united in his person the sees of Kiev and Moscow. He translated and copied liturgical books from Greek, and died in 1406.

life|09-17||Άγιοι Ηρακλείδης και Μύρων Επίσκοποι Ταμάσου της Κύπρου||Heraclidius was a disciple of the apostles Paul and Barnabas and, according to tradition, the first bishop of Tamassos in Cyprus. Myron is honored together with him as a bishop of the same city. The two are connected with the Monastery of Saint Heraclidius in Politiko, Cyprus.

life|09-21||Άγιος Δημήτριος Μητροπολίτης Ροστοβίας (Ρώσος)||Demetrius was born in 1651 near Kiev and became a monk. He was Metropolitan of Rostov from 1702 until his death in 1709 and a distinguished writer: he wrote the great synaxarion of the Russian Church, the "Menaion of Readings." He was proclaimed a saint in 1757.

life|09-23||Οσίες Ξανθίππη και Πολυξένη||Xanthippe and Polyxena, according to tradition, were sisters in the time of the apostles. They heard the preaching of the Apostle Paul and believed, and lived with piety and charity. The Church honors their memory on September 23.

life|09-24||Άγιος Σιλουανός ο Αγιορείτης||Silouan was born in 1866 in a village in the Tambov region of Russia. He became a monk on Mount Athos, at the Monastery of Saint Panteleimon, and lived there for about fifty years in deep prayer and humility. He died in 1938. His teaching became known through his disciple Sophrony, and the Ecumenical Patriarchate proclaimed him a saint in 1987.

life|09-25||Όσιος Σέργιος ο Θαυματουργός (Ρώσος)||Sergius was born around 1314 near Rostov and founded the Lavra of the Holy Trinity in the forests north of Moscow, which became the spiritual center of Russia. He is regarded as the greatest saint of the Russians. He blessed Prince Dmitry of the Don before the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380 and died in 1392.

life|09-26||Άγιος Γεδεών ο Δίκαιος||Gideon was a judge of Israel, around the 12th century BC, and his story is told in the Book of Judges. He was called to deliver his people from the Midianites, and with a very small force, three hundred men, he won a complete victory. The New Testament mentions him among the men of faith.

life|09-27||Άγιοι Μάρκος, Αρίσταρχος και Ζήνων οι Απόστολοι||Mark was a cousin of Barnabas and a traveling companion of the apostles Paul and Barnabas. Aristarchus came from Thessaloniki, followed Paul on his journeys and was in danger together with him at Ephesus and on the voyage to Rome, as the Acts of the Apostles relates. The three are honored as disciples of the apostles.

life|09-28||Προφήτης Βαρούχ ο Δίκαιος||Baruch was the scribe and fellow worker of the prophet Jeremiah, in the time of the fall of Jerusalem to the Babylonians (586 BC). He wrote down Jeremiah's words at his dictation and read them publicly in the temple. The Book of Baruch belongs to the deuterocanonical books of the Old Testament.

life|09-30||Άγιος Μιχαήλ ο Θαυματουργός πρώτος Μητροπολίτης Κιέβου||Michael came to Kiev after the Christianization of the Rus under Prince Vladimir, at the end of the 10th century, and is regarded as the first metropolitan of the region. He baptized and taught the first Christians of Kiev and took the first steps in organizing the Church of Russia.

life|10-01||Άγιος Ανανίας ο Απόστολος||Ananias was a disciple in Damascus. According to the Acts of the Apostles, the Lord asked him to visit Saul (Paul), who had been blinded on the road to Damascus. Ananias followed the command, laid his hands on him, healed him and baptized him. According to tradition, he later became a bishop and was martyred.

life|10-01||Όσιος Ιωάννης ο ψάλτης ο καλούμενος Κουκουζέλης||John Koukouzeles was born in Dyrrachium and lived in the 13th or 14th century. He became a chanter at the imperial court of Constantinople and later a monk at the Great Lavra on Mount Athos. He was one of the greatest composers of Byzantine chant and reformed the musical notation and the melody of the hymns.

life|10-02||Αγία Δάμαρις η Αθηναία||Damaris was an Athenian woman who believed when the Apostle Paul spoke on the Areopagus in Athens, around 51. The Acts of the Apostles mention her by name together with Dionysius the Areopagite, as one of the first persons in the city to embrace Christianity.

life|10-03||Όσιος Ιωάννης ο Χοζεβίτης επίσκοπος Καισαρείας||John was bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. He gave up his office and withdrew as a monk to the monastery of Choziba, in the desert of Judea, where he spent the last years of his life in ascetic struggle.

life|10-04||Όσιος Ιωάννης ο Λαμπαδιστής||John was a Cypriot ascetic of the Middle Ages, who lived in the region of Marathasa. He is honored as the protector of the area of Kalopanagiotis, where the monastery that bears his name stands and where his relic is kept.

life|10-05||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Μαυρόπους, επίσκοπος Ευχαΐτων||John Mauropous was born in Paphlagonia, became a teacher in Constantinople and was the teacher of Michael Psellos. From about 1050 he was Metropolitan of Euchaita. He was a poet and the author of homilies and hymns. According to tradition, the feast of the Three Hierarchs on January 30 was established on his initiative. He died around 1075.

life|10-10||Όσιος Αμβρόσιος της Όπτινα (Ρώσος)||Ambrose was born in 1812 and became a monk at the Optina Monastery in Russia, where he served as an elder and spiritual father. Crowds of the faithful, as well as writers and thinkers such as Dostoevsky, visited him for counsel. He died in 1891 and was proclaimed a saint in 1988.

life|10-11||Άγιοι Νεκτάριος, Αρσάκιος και Σισίνιος Πατριάρχες Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Nectarius was Patriarch of Constantinople from 381, the successor of Gregory the Theologian, and presided at the end of the Second Ecumenical Council. Arsacius was patriarch in 404-405, after the exile of John Chrysostom, and Sisinnius in 426-427. The Church honors the three patriarchs together.

life|10-12||Άγιος Wilfrid (Άγγλος)||Wilfrid lived in the 7th century and was Bishop of York in Northumbria. At the Synod of Whitby in 664 he upheld the uniform date of Easter and the Roman method of determining it, and he carried out missionary work in Frisia and Sussex. He died in 709 or 710.

life|10-12||Όσιος Συμεών ο Νέος Θεολόγος||Symeon was born in 949 in Galatai in Paphlagonia and served at the court in Constantinople before becoming a monk at the Monastery of Stoudios and later abbot of the Monastery of Saint Mamas. Through his works and hymns he shaped the mystical theology of the personal experience of God. He was exiled by the patriarch and died in 1022.

life|10-14||Άγιος Κοσμάς ο Μελωδός||Cosmas was born in Jerusalem in the late 7th century and was raised with John of Damascus, whose adoptive brother and fellow ascetic he was at the Monastery of Saint Sabbas. He became Bishop of Maiouma, near Gaza, and was one of the great hymnographers, with canons for great feasts such as Christmas, Theophany and Pentecost. He died around 752.

life|10-16||Άγιος Γάλλος||Gall was an Irish monk who followed Columbanus to Europe, around 590. He founded a hermitage near Lake Constance, in Switzerland, around which the famous abbey and the town of Saint Gall later grew up. He died around 646.

life|10-18||Άγιος Μνάσων ο Μάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Κύπρου||Mnason was a Cypriot, an "early disciple" of Christ as the Acts of the Apostles call him, in whose house Paul was hosted in Jerusalem. According to tradition, he became a bishop in Cyprus and was martyred.

life|10-19||Άγιος Μνάσων ο αρχαίος μαθητής||Mnason of Cyprus was one of the first disciples of Christ. The Acts of the Apostles mention him as the host with whom Paul stayed when he arrived in Jerusalem toward the end of his third missionary journey.

life|10-21||Αγία Ursula (Βρεταννίδα)||Ursula, according to medieval tradition, was a British princess who was killed in Cologne, Germany, together with a large group of her companions, on the return from a pilgrimage. Her veneration spread widely in the West during the Middle Ages.
life|10-21||Άγιος Finan (Ιρλανδός)||Finan was an Irish monk of Iona and was Bishop of Lindisfarne in Northumbria from 651 to 661. He baptized kings and founded churches in England.

life|10-24||Άγιος Πρόκλος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Proclus was Patriarch of Constantinople from 434 to 446, the successor of Nestorius. He was a distinguished preacher and defended the teaching about the Theotokos. In his days, in 438, the relics of John Chrysostom were solemnly transferred to Constantinople.

life|10-25||Αγία Ταβιθά||Tabitha (in Greek Dorcas) was a disciple of Christ in Joppa, known for her kindness and her works of charity, especially her sewing for poor widows. When she died, the Apostle Peter prayed and raised her up, as the Acts of the Apostles relate.

life|10-27||Αγία Πρόκλα σύζυγος του Πιλάτου||Procla (in the Latin tradition Claudia Procula) was, according to tradition, the wife of Pontius Pilate. The Gospel of Matthew reports that she sent word to Pilate not to become involved in the trial of Christ, because she had seen much about Him in her sleep.

life|10-27||Άγιος Κυριάκος Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Cyriacus was Patriarch of Constantinople from 596 to 606, in the time of the emperors Maurice and Phocas. He was the successor of John the Faster and became known for his piety and character.

life|10-28||Αγία Lioba (Βρετανίδα)||Leoba was born in England around 710 and became a nun at the monastery of Wimborne. Her kinsman, the missionary Boniface, summoned her there to help spread Christianity in Germany. She became abbess at Tauberbischofsheim and died in 782.

life|10-28||Όσιος Αθανάσιος ο Α’ Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Athanasius was born around 1230 and became a monk, well known for his strict life. He was Patriarch of Constantinople twice (1289-1293 and 1303-1309). He cared for the poor of the capital, resisted the relaxation of the clergy's life and corruption, and died around 1310.
life|10-28||Όσιος Στέφανος ο Σαββαΐτης||Stephen was a nephew of John of Damascus and a monk at the Lavra of Saint Sabbas in the desert of Judea. He was a hymnographer and died in 794.

life|10-30||Άγιος Κλεόπας ο Απόστολος εκ των 70||Cleopas was one of the two disciples who were going to Emmaus on the evening of the Resurrection and met the risen Christ, as the Gospel of Luke relates. Tradition counts him among the Seventy Apostles.

life|10-30||Άγιοι Τέρτιος, Μάρκος, Ιούστος (ή Ιησούς) και Αρτεμάς||Tertius is the one who wrote the Epistle to the Romans at Paul's dictation, and he sends his own greeting at the end of it. Mark, Justus and Artemas were fellow workers of the Apostle Paul. The Church honors them as disciples from among the Seventy.

life|10-31||Άγιος Αριστόβουλος ο Απόστολος||Aristobulus is mentioned by Paul in the Epistle to the Romans, where he sends greetings to "those of the household of Aristobulus." According to tradition, he was one of the Seventy Apostles, preached the Gospel in Britain and became a bishop there.

life|11-01||Όσιος Δαβίδ ο εν Ευβοία||Venerable David lived in the 16th century and practiced asceticism in northern Euboea. According to tradition, he restored the monastery that today bears his name, near Rovies, and became a spiritual guide to the people of the region. His memory is honored on November 1.

life|11-04||Άγιοι Ερμάς, Πατρόβας||Hermas, Patrobas, Linus, Gaius and Philologus were disciples of the Apostles and are counted among the Seventy. Five of their names are found in the epistles of the Apostle Paul (Romans, Second Timothy). According to tradition, they taught the Gospel in various cities and became bishops.

life|11-04||Άγιος Αβιμέλεχ||Abimelech was the Ethiopian courtier of King Zedekiah, who, according to the book of the prophet Jeremiah (chapter 38), took courage to ask the king to save the prophet from the cistern into which he had been thrown. He drew him up with ropes, and God promised him that he would be saved when Jerusalem fell. He is honored as a Righteous man of the Old Testament.

life|11-04||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Βατατζής||John III Doukas Vatatzes was emperor of Nicaea from 1221 to 1254. He continued the recovery of territories lost after 1204 and strengthened the economy through care for agriculture and livestock farming. He became known for his almsgiving and for the hospitals and homes for the aged that he founded. He died in 1254 at Nymphaion and the Church honors him as a Saint.

life|11-04||Όσιος Γεώργιος Καρσλίδης||Elder George was born in 1901 in the region of Kars, in Pontus, and came to Greece as a refugee. He lived in Drama as an ascetic, with prayer and love for the poor, and many visited him for counsel. He died in 1959 and was officially recognized as a Saint by the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 2012.

life|11-06||Άγιος Iltud||Illtud was a monk and abbot in Wales, in the late 5th and early 6th century. He founded a large monastery and school at Llantwit Major, where many later saints of Britain were educated. He is regarded as one of the principal teachers of Celtic monasticism.

life|11-06||Άγιος Δημητριανός Επίσκοπος Κηθηρίας||Saint Demetrianos lived in Cyprus in the late 9th and early 10th century and, according to tradition, became bishop of Chytroi (Kythrea). He became known for his kindness and his care for the poor. In Cyprus his memory is honored especially in the region of Kythrea.

life|11-06||Όσιος Βαρλαάμ ο εν Χουτινή||Venerable Barlaam was a Russian monk from Novgorod. Around 1192 he founded near the city the Monastery of the Transfiguration at Khutyn, where he lived in strict asceticism and became the father of many monks. He died in 1192 and his monastery remained an important spiritual center of the region.

life|11-07||Άγιος Willibrord||Willibrord was born around 658 in Northumbria in England and studied in monasteries of Britain and Ireland. He became a missionary to the Frisians, in present-day Holland, and was ordained by the pope as bishop of Utrecht. He founded the abbey of Echternach in Luxembourg, where he died in 739.

life|11-07||Όσιος Λάζαρος ο Θαυματουργός||Venerable Lazarus was born in 966 in Asia Minor and became a monk, traveling as a pilgrim to the Holy Places. He settled on Mount Galesion, near Ephesus, where he lived as a stylite and founded three monasteries. He died in 1053 and his memory is honored as that of Lazarus of Galesion.

life|11-09||Όσιοι Ευθύμιος και Νεόφυτος||Venerable Euthymius and Neophytus are regarded as the founders of the Monastery of Docheiariou on Mount Athos, which was built in the late 10th century. The monastery was dedicated to the Archangels, and generations of monks have lived there since. Their memory is honored at the monastery and on the Mountain.

life|11-09||Οσία Θεοκτίστη||Venerable Theoktiste was born on Lesbos in the 9th century. According to tradition, after an Arab raid on Lesbos, she reached the island of Paros, where she lived alone for many years without seeing any people. According to tradition, a hunter found her, brought her the Immaculate Mysteries and later buried her. On Paros there is a monastery that honors her memory.

life|11-09||Όσιος Ιωάννης ο Βραχύσωμος||Venerable John the Dwarf, or the Short, was born around 339 in Egypt and became a monk at Scetis, a disciple of Abba Ammoes. Tradition says that, to practice obedience, he watered a dry stick for years, and it finally blossomed. He became famous for his humility and for his sayings in the Gerontikon. He died in the early 5th century.

life|11-09||Όσιος Συμεών ο Μεταφραστής||Symeon was a high official of Constantinople, logothete of the course, in the 10th century. He gathered the lives of the saints and rewrote them in a higher style in one great work, the Menologion, which greatly influenced Byzantine hagiography. He wrote other texts as well, and died around 1000.

life|11-10||Άγιος Justus||Justus was a Roman monk whom Pope Gregory I sent to England in 601 to help Augustine of Canterbury. He became bishop of Rochester and, in 624, the fourth Archbishop of Canterbury. He died in 627.

life|11-10||Άγιος Νόννος ο κατηχητής||Nonnus was a bishop in Syria in the 5th century. After a sermon of his in Antioch, the actress Pelagia repented, was baptized by him and became a nun on the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem. The account of her repentance became very well known in the Church.

life|11-10||Άγιος Μίλος ή Μίλης||Miles was bishop of Susa in Persia, in the 4th century. Under King Shapur II, and after many persecutions of Christians, he was arrested and martyred around 341, together with his disciples. His memory is honored as that of a hieromartyr and wonderworker.

life|11-11||Αγία Στεφανίδα||Stephanis was a young Christian woman of Damascus, who was martyred in the 2nd century, under the emperor Antoninus. According to tradition, the soldier Victor who interrogated her saw her faith, confessed Christ himself, and they were martyred together.

life|11-11||Άγιος Άβιβος||Abibus was one of the thirteen Syrian Fathers who came to Georgia in the 6th century and founded monasticism there. He became bishop of Nekresi, in Kakheti, and preached among pagans and fire-worshippers. According to tradition, he was martyred by fire-worshippers and is honored as a hieromartyr in Georgia.

life|11-11||Άγιος Μάξιμος ο διά Χριστόν Σαλός||Maximus lived in Moscow in the 15th century and died in 1434. According to tradition, he wandered without shoes and with very little clothing, even in winter, and counseled people to live with repentance and humility. The Church of Russia honors him as a fool for Christ.

life|11-11||Όσιος Θεόδωρος ο Ομολογητής||Theodore was born in Constantinople in 759, into a family of pious and wealthy people, and became a monk with his uncle Plato. In 799 he became abbot of the Stoudios Monastery and reformed monastic life; the rule of his monastery, the Stoudite typikon, influenced monasticism in Byzantium and Russia. // He resisted imperial policy: first over the matter of the second marriage of Constantine VI and then over iconoclasm, for which he was exiled many times. In his writings he defended the relation of the icon to the incarnation of Christ. // He wrote catechetical sermons, letters, hymns and iambic poems. He died in 826 on Prinkipo, and the Church honors him as a confessor.

life|11-12||Όσιος Νείλος ο Ασκητής||Nilus was a high official of Constantinople and a disciple of John Chrysostom. Around 390 he left his position and his family and went with his son to Sinai as an ascetic. He wrote ascetic works and many letters and died around 430.

life|11-12||Όσιος Νείλος ο Μυροβλύτης||Venerable Nilus practiced asceticism on Mount Athos in the 17th century and died in 1651. According to tradition, fragrant myrrh flows from his relics, and for this reason he was called the Myrrh-Streamer. His memory is honored especially on Mount Athos.

life|11-12||Προφήτης Αχιά||Ahijah was a prophet from Shiloh, in the time of King Solomon. According to First Kings (chapter 11), he prophesied to Jeroboam that the kingdom would be divided and that he himself would reign over the ten northern tribes. Later he also prophesied the fall of his family.

life|11-14||Άγιος Γρηγόριος ο Παλαμάς||Gregory was born around 1296 in Constantinople, into a family of the court, and studied philosophy. At a young age he became a monk on Mount Athos and practiced hesychasm, the discipline of the prayer of the heart. // When Barlaam of Calabria attacked the hesychasts, Palamas defended them, and his teaching on the distinction between the essence and energies of God was confirmed by councils in Constantinople, in 1341 and 1351. In 1347 he became Archbishop of Thessaloniki. // In 1354 the Turks captured him as he was traveling, and he remained a captive for about a year. He died in 1359 in Thessaloniki and was glorified in 1368. The Second Sunday of Lent is dedicated to his memory.

life|11-14||Άγιος Dubritius||Dubricius (Dyfrig) was a bishop in Wales in the late 5th and early 6th century. Tradition connects him with southeastern Wales and with the church of Llandaff, and he is regarded as one of the first pastors of the Church there.

life|11-14||Άγιος Κωνσταντίνος ο Νεομάρτυρας ο Υδραίος||Constantine was born on Hydra and was a sailor. At the end of the 18th century he confessed his faith in Constantinople, where he was martyred in 1800. The Church honors him as a new martyr and his memory is celebrated especially on Hydra.

life|11-15||Όσιος Παΐσιος Βελιτσκόφσκυ||Paisius was born in 1722 in Poltava in Ukraine and studied at the Kiev Academy, but left it to become a monk. He lived on Mount Athos and then in Moldavia, in the monasteries of Dragomirna and Neamt, where he gathered hundreds of monks. // He translated the patristic texts and the Philokalia (1793) into Slavonic and revived hesychasm throughout Russia and Romania. He died in 1794 at Neamt.

life|11-16||Αγία Ιφιγένεια||According to tradition, Iphigenia was the daughter of the king of Ethiopia, who was baptized by the Apostle and Evangelist Matthew and dedicated herself to God. She became the head of a monastic community of women. Her memory is celebrated on the same day as Matthew.

life|11-17||Αγία Hilda||Hilda (614-680) was an Anglo-Saxon noblewoman who became a nun and abbess. She founded and directed the monastery of Whitby, at first a monastery of both men and women, which became an important center of learning. The Synod of Whitby was hosted there in 664, and the poet Caedmon lived there.

life|11-17||Όσιος Λάζαρος ο Ζωγράφος||Lazarus was a Byzantine icon painter of the 9th century. Under the emperor Theophilus, during the second iconoclasm, he was imprisoned because he painted icons. According to tradition, his hands were burned with red-hot irons, but after his release he continued to paint. He died around 867.

life|11-17||Όσιος Νίκων ο Θαυματουργός||Nikon was a Russian monk and abbot of the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Saint Sergius of Radonezh. He succeeded Sergius as abbot and kept the monastic life in the monastery. He died in the 15th century and is honored as a wonderworker.

life|11-18||Άγιοι Ζακχαίος και Αλφαίος||Zacchaeus, deacon of Gadara, and Alphaeus, reader of Eleutheropolis, were Christians of Palestine. They were martyred in Caesarea in Palestine in 303, at the beginning of the great persecution of Diocletian, as the historian Eusebius relates.

life|11-18||Άγιος Ρωμανός ο Μάρτυρας από την Παλαιστίνη||Romanus was a deacon and exorcist of Caesarea in Palestine. At the beginning of the persecution of Diocletian, in 303, he came to Antioch and encouraged the Christians not to be afraid. He was arrested and, according to tradition, his tongue was cut out and later he was strangled in prison.

life|11-20||Άγιος Edmund||Edmund was king of East Anglia in the 9th century. In 869 the Danes invaded and captured him, and, according to tradition, he refused to renounce his Christian faith or to submit as their vassal. They killed him and the English honored him as a martyr; around his tomb the monastery of Bury St Edmunds grew up.

life|11-20||Άγιος Πρόκλος Αρχιεπίσκοπος||Proclus was a disciple of John Chrysostom and became Patriarch of Constantinople in 434, after Maximian. He was an outstanding orator, whose first great homily, on the Theotokos, was delivered in 428 or 429, on the matter of Nestorius. In 438 he transferred the relics of Chrysostom to Constantinople. He died in 446.

life|11-22||Άγιοι Κικιλία, Βαλεριανός||Cecilia was a Roman noblewoman, according to tradition in the 3rd century. She persuaded her husband Valerian and his brother Tiburtius to be baptized, and the three were martyred in Rome. Cecilia is honored in the West as the patroness of church music.

life|11-22||Άγιος Κλήμης ο Θαυματουργός||Clement was born around 840 and was a disciple of Cyril and Methodius in Moravia, where he contributed to the spread of the Slavonic alphabet and the Slavonic liturgy. After the expulsion of the disciples, he went to Bulgaria, taught and founded a school at Ohrid, where he became bishop. He died in 916 and is regarded as one of the teachers of the Slavs.

life|11-23||Άγιος Deiniol||Deiniol was a monk in Wales in the 6th century and the first bishop of Bangor, where he founded a monastery. He died around 584. The Church of Wales honors him as the founder of the see of Bangor.

life|11-24||Άγιος Πέτρος ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Peter became Bishop of Alexandria in 300 and was one of the chief pastors of Egypt in the time of the persecutions. He expelled Meletius and Arius from the Church and established canons for those who had denied the faith during the persecutions and wished to return. He was beheaded under Maximinus Daia in 311.

life|11-25||Άγιος Μερκούριος ο Μεγαλομάρτυρας||Mercurius was a soldier of the Roman army and, according to tradition, was martyred in Caesarea in Cappadocia in the 3rd century, under the emperor Decius. The Church honors him as a military saint and great martyr.

life|11-26||Όσιος Αλύπιος ο Κιονίτης||Alypius was a monk of the 6th and 7th century in Paphlagonia. According to tradition, he lived for about fifty years on a pillar, as a stylite, and was the father of many monks. His memory is celebrated on November 26.

life|11-29||Άγιος Φιλούμενος ο νέος Ιερομάρτυρας||Philoumenos was born in 1913 in Cyprus and became a monk, and later abbot of Jacob's Well, near Nablus, in Palestine. In 1979 a fanatical intruder murdered him, and the Patriarchate of Jerusalem recognized him as a Saint in 2009.

life|11-30||Άγιος Φρουμέντιος||Frumentius was born in Tyre and, as a young man, was shipwrecked in the Red Sea together with his brother Aedesius, and they were taken to the court of the king of Axum, in Ethiopia. Frumentius became the teacher of the heir Ezana and introduced the Christians. Around 328 the Great Athanasius of Alexandria ordained him bishop, and he converted Ezana and the kingdom to Christianity. The Church of Ethiopia honors him as the "Father of Peace."

life|12-01||Άγιος Φιλάρετος ο Ελεήμων||Philaretos was born around 702 in Amnia in Paphlagonia and was a wealthy landowner with a family. When Arab raids destroyed his estates, and he gave away to the poor whatever was left to him, he lived on very little. His granddaughter Maria became in 788 the wife of the emperor Constantine VI and they brought him to Constantinople, but he remained humble. He died in 792 and the Church honors him as the Merciful.

life|12-02||Όσιος Πορφύριος ο Θαυματουργός||Porphyrios was born in 1906 at Saint John of Karystia in Euboea, and at a young age went to Mount Athos. Later he became a priest and served for decades at the Polyclinic of Athens, while also founding the monastery of the Transfiguration at Milesi in Attica. Many people sought his counsel, and he was known for his discernment, humility and love. He died in 1991 and the Ecumenical Patriarchate recognized him as a Saint in 2013.

life|12-02||Όσιος Κύριλλος ο Φιλεώτης||Cyril was born around 1015 in Phileas, on the coast of Thrace on the Black Sea. He married, and with the consent of his wife became a monk and ascetic. At Phileas he lived in strict asceticism and gathered disciples. He died in 1110 and his life was written by Nicholas Kataskepenos.

life|12-03||Άγιος Birinus||Birinus was a bishop whom Pope Honorius sent in 634 to preach the Gospel to the Saxons of western England. In 635 he baptized Cynegils, king of Wessex, and became the first bishop of Dorchester. He died around 650 and is honored as the apostle of Wessex.

life|12-04||Όσιος Ιωάννης ο Δαμασκηνός||John was born in Damascus around 675, into a Christian family that served in the administrative system of the caliphs. After some years at court, he left his offices and became a monk at the monastery of Saint Sabbas, near Jerusalem. // He wrote three discourses against those who fought against the icons, in which he distinguishes veneration from worship. His great work, the "Fount of Knowledge," presents Christian teaching systematically. // He was also a great hymnographer: his canons for Pascha and for other feasts are still chanted in the services. He died around 749.

life|12-04||Άγιος Κρύσπος||Crispus was the ruler of the synagogue in Corinth, who believed in Christ and was baptized by the Apostle Paul, as the Acts (18:8) and First Corinthians (1:14) mention. According to tradition, he was one of the Seventy Apostles and became bishop of Aegina.

life|12-06||Όσιος Νείλος ο Θαυματουργός ο Νέος||Nilus was a Russian ascetic who lived on Lake Seliger, in the region of Tver. He settled on an island, Stolobny, and lived there with prayer and labor for many years. He died in 1554, and many pilgrims still go to the monastery that was founded there.

life|12-07||Όσιος Αμμούν||Ammoun of Nitria was born around 295 in Egypt. He was married by force, but on the first night he persuaded his wife to live as brother and sister, and later he went to the mountain of Nitria, where he became the founder of monasticism in that region. He was a disciple and friend of Anthony the Great, and died around 350.

life|12-08||Άγιος Τυχικός ο Απόστολος||Tychicus was a disciple and fellow worker of the Apostle Paul. He is mentioned in the Acts (20:4) and in the epistles to the Ephesians, Colossians, Timothy and Titus, as a "beloved brother and faithful minister." According to tradition, he was one of the Seventy and became a bishop.

life|12-09||Προφήτιδα Άννα||Anna was the mother of the prophet Samuel and the wife of Elkanah. Because she was childless, she prayed with tears at Shiloh, and God gave her a son, whom she dedicated to worship. Her hymn, in First Kings (chapter 2), is a model of the prayer of the humble and is among the texts that inspired the hymn of the Theotokos.

life|12-11||Άγιος Νικηφόρος Φωκάς||Nikephoros Phokas was born around 912 into a family of generals of Cappadocia and was one of the greatest generals of Byzantium. He recovered Crete from the Arabs in 961 and Cyprus in 965, and became emperor in 963. He was a friend of Athanasius the Athonite and financed the founding of the Great Lavra on Mount Athos. He was murdered on December 11, 969, by John Tzimiskes.

life|12-12||Άγιος Finian of Clonard||Finian of Clonard (about 470-549) was an Irish monk and founded the abbey of Clonard, an important school of Ireland. He is regarded as the teacher of the "twelve apostles of Ireland," among them Columba of Iona and Brendan.

life|12-13||Άγιοι Ιουβενάλιος και Πέτρος||Juvenaly was one of the missionaries who arrived in 1794 on Kodiak Island in Alaska, to preach the Gospel to the natives. He was killed in 1796, and the Church honors him as the first martyr of Alaska. Tradition also mentions Peter the Aleut, who is said to have been martyred in 1815 in California. On the same day all the Saints of Alaska are honored.

life|12-13||Άγιοι Νεόφυτος, Ιγνάτιος||Neophytus, Ignatius, Procopius and Nilus are regarded as the founders of the Machairas Monastery, on the Kionia mountain in Cyprus, in the 12th century. According to tradition, the ascetics found an icon of the Theotokos in the area, and with the permission of the emperor Manuel Komnenos the monastery was built. Machairas Monastery is today one of the great pilgrimage sites of Cyprus.

life|12-15||Άγιος Στέφανος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Σουρόζας||Stephen was bishop of Surozh (Sougdaia), present-day Sudak in Crimea, in the 8th century. He lived in the time of iconoclasm and defended the icons. The Church of Russia honors him because tradition connects his life with the first contact of the Russian people with Christianity.

life|12-16||Αγία Θεοφανώ||Theophano was born around 866 and married Leo VI the Wise, by the will of his father, Basil I. The marriage was not happy, and Theophano lived with virtue and prayer, with charity and care for the poor. She died in 897 or 895 and the Church commemorates her as a saint.

life|12-16||Άγιος Μέμνων||Memnon was bishop of Ephesus in the 5th century. At the Third Ecumenical Council, in 431 at Ephesus, he stood with Cyril of Alexandria against Nestorius, and hosted the council in his city. The day of his memory is December 16.

life|12-17||Άγιος Διονύσιος ο Θαυματουργός ο εκ Ζακύνθου||Dionysios was born in 1547 on Zakynthos, into a noble family, and became a monk at the monastery of the Strophades. He became archbishop of Aegina, but later resigned and returned to Zakynthos. // Tradition singles out the forgiveness he gave to the murderer of his brother, when the latter took refuge in the monastery. He died in 1622 and his relics are kept on Zakynthos, where he is the patron saint of the island.

life|12-18||Άγιος Μοδεστός Αρχιεπίσκοπος||Modestus was abbot of a monastery in Palestine and became Patriarch of Jerusalem in 632. After the conquest of Jerusalem by the Persians in 614, Modestus had organized the rebuilding of the destroyed churches, and especially of the Church of the Resurrection. He died in 634.

life|12-18||Όσιος Μιχαήλ ο Ομολογητής||Michael was born around 761 in Jerusalem and became a monk, and later syncellus of the Patriarch of Jerusalem. In Constantinople he defended the icons during iconoclasm, and for this reason he was imprisoned and exiled. He died in 846.

life|12-19||Όσιος Γρηγέντιος||Gregentius was bishop of Taphar, in the kingdom of the Himyarites in southern Arabia (Yemen), in the 6th century. According to tradition, he taught Christianity and wrote laws for the kingdom. The Church honors him as the enlightener of the Himyarites.

life|12-20||Άγιος Ιωάννης της Κρονστάνδης||John Sergiev was born in 1829 in a poor village of northern Russia and studied at the Theological Academy of Saint Petersburg. From 1855 he served as a priest at the cathedral of Saint Andrew in Kronstadt, a poor naval town. // He cared for the poor and founded a house of industry and schools. He became known for his frequent liturgies, for the frequent Holy Communion of the faithful, and for his prayers, which many believed to heal. He wrote the spiritual diary "My Life in Christ." He died in 1908 and was recognized as a Saint by the Russian Church in 1990.

life|12-21||Άγιος Πέτρος ο Θαυματουργός||Peter was born around 1260 in Volhynia and became a monk. In 1308 he became Metropolitan of Kiev and All Russia and, around 1325, moved his see to Moscow, which from then on became the spiritual center of Russia. He supported Prince Ivan Kalita in building the Church of the Dormition. He died in 1326.

life|12-22||Άγιος Ναούμ ο Θαυματουργός||Naum was born around 830 in Bulgaria or Macedonia and was a disciple of Cyril and Methodius. After the death of Methodius, in 885, he was driven out of Moravia with his fellow disciples and went to Bulgaria. He taught in Preslav and founded a monastery and school on Lake Ohrid, where he lived and died in 910.

life|12-23||Όσιος Παύλος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Νεοκαισαρείας||Paul was bishop of Neocaesarea on the Euphrates in the 4th century. He was a confessor of the faith during the persecutions of Licinius, when, according to tradition, his hands were burned with a red-hot iron. His memory is honored on December 23.

life|12-25||Προσκύνησις των Μάγων||According to the Gospel of Matthew (chapter 2), magi from the East followed a star and arrived in Jerusalem, asking about the king of the Jews. They worshipped the infant in Bethlehem and offered him gifts, gold, frankincense and myrrh. God warned them in a dream not to return to Herod, and they went back by another road. The Church honors their memory together with the Nativity.

life|12-26||Άγιος Ευθύμιος ο Ομολογητής||Euthymius was Metropolitan of Sardis in the late 8th and early 9th century. He defended the icons during iconoclasm, and for this reason was exiled and imprisoned. According to tradition, he was cruelly tortured and died around 831, and the Church honors him as a confessor.

life|12-26||Όσιος Νικόδημος της Τισμάνα||Nicodemus was born around 1320 in Prilep, in Macedonia, and became a monk on Mount Athos. He came to Wallachia and founded monasteries, among them Vodita and, around 1378, Tismana, and was important for the monasticism of the Romanians. He died in 1406.

life|12-26||Φυγή Στήν Αίγυπτο||According to the Gospel of Matthew (chapter 2), an angel warned Joseph in a dream that Herod would seek the child in order to kill him, and so the family fled by night to Egypt. It stayed there until the death of Herod and then returned to Nazareth. Tradition connects the Massacre of the Infants in Bethlehem with this event.

life|12-27||Άγιος Θεόδωρος ο Γραπτός||Theodore and his brother Theophanes were monks of the monastery of Saint Sabbas in Palestine. During iconoclasm, under the emperor Theophilus, they were arrested and had verses inscribed on their faces with a red-hot iron, and for this reason they were called the Inscribed. He died around 841 as a confessor and was also a hymnographer.

life|12-28||Όσιος Σίμων ο Μυροβλήτης||Simon was an ascetic of the 13th century on Mount Athos. According to tradition, he saw a star over a steep rock and there founded, around 1257, the monastery that was named Simonopetra. He also became its abbot and died there. His relics, according to tradition, give off a fragrance.

life|12-29||Όσιος Γεώργιος Επίσκοπος Νικομήδειας||George was bishop of Nicomedia in the 9th century and a hymnographer. He wrote canons and troparia, which are chanted in the services of the Church. He was among those who defended the Orthodox faith in the period after iconoclasm.

life|12-31||Άγιος Ζωτικός ο Ορφανοτρόφος||Zoticus was a priest in Constantinople in the 4th century, in the time of Constantine the Great. He founded and directed an orphanage and cared for the poor and the sick. The Church honors him as a benefactor of orphans.
